bullets: The newly released Evidence-State Drift framework evaluates web-connected large language model agents at the claim level across repeated retrievals. Its replay benchmark records normalized claims, supporting passages, source identity, timestamps, content fingerprints, and source-authority labels for 67 claims across 871 observations, separating substantive evidence changes from formatting-only changes. Why it matters: If you evaluate an agent that repeatedly consults the web, this provides a way to test whether its evidence actually changed rather than treating every page revision as knowledge drift. That distinction can make longitudinal regression alerts more specific and auditable. Evidence: E006. High confidence.

The newly captured versioned package “Honest agent scores” recomputes 3,300 Terminal-Bench 4.0 runs from raw trials and tests whether defective tasks or alternative repeat aggregation change agent rankings. It reports that neither removing 30 flagged tasks nor using pass^5 instead of pass@1 materially changes the ranking, while score differences of roughly 9.5 points or less are ties with 66 tasks. Why it matters: If you select agents from a leaderboard, this package supplies a reproducible method for testing whether the apparent winner survives task-quality and repeated-run uncertainty. It changes the decision from comparing point estimates to checking whether candidates are statistically distinguishable. Evidence: E025. Medium confidence.

The newly released MLOps-Bench evaluates agents on executable machine-learning operations changes inside real repositories. Its tasks span data pipelines, feature engineering, training, serving, monitoring, continuous integration and delivery, governance, and end-to-end integration, rather than limiting evaluation to model experiments or generic software issues. Why it matters: If you are choosing an agent for production machine-learning maintenance, this benchmark tests the lifecycle work that the agent would encounter instead of using coding success as a proxy. Repository evidence, buggy baselines, and executable changes also permit more concrete failure diagnosis. Evidence: E018. High confidence.

The newly released NAME-Bench changes how object hallucination is measured in vision-language models. It distinguishes assertions that an object exists from non-assertive mentions such as describing what a bench is for, covering 25,497 object mentions rather than counting every named object as a visual claim. Why it matters: If you compare image-captioning systems, this benchmark can prevent legitimate explanatory language from being scored as hallucination. That may change both model rankings and the kinds of captions a product team discourages during tuning. Evidence: E050. High confidence.

The newly released ProPerMem benchmark tests proactive assistants against year-long personal memories averaging about 618,000 tokens, with distracting information and human-verified windows for when assistance is appropriate. Its protocol scores both what the assistant says and when it intervenes. Why it matters: If you evaluate an assistant that acts without a direct request, answer correctness alone misses premature, late, or unjustified interventions. ProPerMem makes memory retrieval and intervention timing part of the same product decision. Evidence: E021. High confidence.

The newly released RAP dataset frames paper-to-poster generation as reconstructing human-designed posters through declarative markup. It supports objective rendering comparisons, rather than relying only on a vision-language model judge or human checklist, while preserving human posters as design examples and supervision. Why it matters: If you are selecting a system for visual document generation, RAP offers a repeatable test of whether the produced layout and rendering match a verified target. This separates implementation fidelity from the preferences of another model acting as judge. Evidence: E007. High confidence.

The newly released MuninAI framework combines a locally hosted open-weight model with an indexed research group corpus, citation graph, and specialized reading, search, and computation tools. It ships an evaluation suite designed to test the authors’ claim that the agent harness contributes more than the choice of underlying model. Why it matters: If a research group is deciding between upgrading a model and improving its local retrieval and tool system, this artifact provides a direct evaluation structure for that comparison while keeping unpublished literature on local infrastructure. Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 Evidence-State Drift 框架在多次检索过程中，以声明为单位评估联网大型语言模型智能体。其回放基准针对 67 条声明的 871 次观测，记录规范化声明、支持段落、来源身份、时间戳、内容指纹和来源权威性标签，从而区分实质性证据变化与仅涉及格式的变化。Why it matters: 如果评估的是反复查阅网络的智能体，该框架可以检验其证据是否确实发生变化，而不是将每次页面修订都视为知识漂移。这一区分可以让纵向回归警报更具针对性且更易审计。Evidence: E006. High confidence.

新收录的版本化软件包“Honest agent scores”基于原始试验重新计算 3,300 次 Terminal-Bench 4.0 运行，并检验缺陷任务或其他重复运行聚合方式是否会改变智能体排名。结果显示，无论移除 30 个被标记的任务，还是使用 pass^5 而非 pass@1，排名都没有实质性变化；在包含 66 个任务时，约 9.5 分或更小的分数差异均属平局。Why it matters: 如果依据排行榜选择智能体，该软件包提供了一种可复现的方法，用于检验表面上的胜者能否经受住任务质量和重复运行不确定性的考验。它将决策方式从比较点估计，转变为检查候选者之间是否在统计上可区分。Evidence: E025. Medium confidence.

新发布的 MLOps-Bench 在真实代码仓库中，通过可执行的机器学习运维变更来评估智能体。其任务覆盖数据流水线、特征工程、训练、服务、监控、持续集成与交付、治理及端到端集成，而不是将评估局限于模型实验或通用软件问题。Why it matters: 如果要为生产环境中的机器学习维护选择智能体，该基准测试的是智能体实际会遇到的全生命周期工作，而不是用编码成功率作为替代指标。代码仓库证据、有缺陷的基线和可执行变更也有助于进行更具体的故障诊断。Evidence: E018. High confidence.

新发布的 NAME-Bench 改变了视觉语言模型中物体幻觉的衡量方式。它区分了断言某个物体存在的表述与非断言式提及，例如描述长椅的用途；其覆盖 25,497 次物体提及，而不是将每个被点名的物体都计为视觉声明。Why it matters: 如果要比较图像描述系统，该基准可以避免将合理的解释性语言判定为幻觉。这可能会改变模型排名，也会改变产品团队在调优期间不鼓励生成的描述类型。Evidence: E050. High confidence.

新发布的 ProPerMem 基准使用跨度长达一年的个人记忆来测试主动式助手，这些记忆平均约含 618,000 个词元，并包含干扰信息以及经人工核验的适宜协助时间窗口。其协议既评估助手说了什么，也评估其何时介入。Why it matters: 如果评估的是无需直接请求便采取行动的助手，仅看回答正确性会遗漏过早、过晚或缺乏依据的介入。ProPerMem 将记忆检索和介入时机纳入同一项产品决策。Evidence: E021. High confidence.

新发布的 RAP 数据集将论文到海报的生成定义为通过声明式标记重建人工设计的海报。它支持客观的渲染对比，而不是仅依赖视觉语言模型裁判或人工检查清单，同时保留人工制作的海报作为设计示例和监督信号。Why it matters: 如果要为视觉文档生成选择系统，RAP 提供了一种可重复的测试，用于检验生成的布局和渲染是否与经过验证的目标一致。这将实现保真度与充当裁判的另一个模型的偏好区分开来。Evidence: E007. High confidence.

新发布的 MuninAI 框架将本地托管的开放权重模型与建立了索引的研究团队语料库、引文图谱，以及专门的阅读、搜索和计算工具相结合。它附带一套评估工具，用于检验作者的主张：相比底层模型的选择，智能体运行框架带来的贡献更大。Why it matters: 如果研究团队需要在升级模型与改进本地检索和工具系统之间作出决定，该成果可为这种比较提供直接的评估结构，同时将未发表文献保留在本地基础设施中。Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.

organizations: Alfred-Wegener-Institut Helmholtz-Zentrum für Polar- und Meeresforschung
evidence_items.summary: The measurement of ice thickness is of great importance for the accurate estimation of glacier volume and the delineation of their bedrock topography. In particular, this is a crucial factor in forecasting the future evolution of glaciers in the context of a changing climate. In order to derive the ice thickness, the travel time of electromagnetic waves in radargrams acquired by radio-echo sounding (RES) systems is analyzed. This can only be achieved by identifying the ice surface and underlying ice bottom in corresponding radargrams. Manually identifying these two reflection horizons in RES data is a laborious and time-consuming process. Consequently, scientists are attempting to automate this task through the use of techniques such as deep learning. Such automation can significantly reduce the time between a field campaign and the calculation of the glacier's ice thickness distribution. In this paper, we present the first benchmark dataset for delineating the ice surface and bottom boundaries in RES data, to facilitate straightforward comparisons of deep learning models in the future. The IceAnatomy'' dataset comprises radargrams and the corresponding manual picks, amounting to a total of over 45,000km of observations. The RES data originates from three sources: FAU, CReSIS, and AWI. The dataset comprises different RES systems as well as different pre-processing methods. In addition, the data was acquired over a large range of geographical and glaciological settings, featuring different thermal regimes present in Antarctica and the Southern Patagonian Icefield. This diversity ensures that the models' behaviors can be analyzed in different scenarios. We define a standardized train-test split for each source in the dataset. This allows us to introduce not only a baseline model trained on the entire training set (the omni'' model), but also three source-specific baseline models.
evidence_items.title: Ice Anatomy: A Benchmark Dataset and Methodology for Automatic Ice Boundary Extraction from Radio-Echo Sounding Data

evidence_items.summary: Research groups that want a language model grounded in their own literature face a choice between hosted services that receive their unpublished work and self-hosted deployments that keep the data local but give the model no access to the corpus. Munin is an open-source framework for a self-hosted scientific assistant that indexes a group's corpus and its citation graph, and wraps whichever open-weight model the group can serve in an agent harness with specialised reading, search, and computation tools. We claim that the harness, rather than the specific model, is what makes the system useful on domain literature, and we ship the evaluation suite that tests this claim with the software. On 199 paired literature questions, the harness more than doubles the accuracy of the base model, from 0.387 to 0.874 (+0.487, 95% CI [0.407, 0.568]), while naive retrieve-then-answer scores below the unaided model on every backbone tested. Under the harness, roughly twice as many answer claims trace to a passage the model read itself as with fixed top-5 retrieval. When the source paper for a question is removed from the corpus, the system abstains on about nine in ten of the questions it had answered correctly on the Qwen backbones and eight in ten on gpt-oss-20b, and it produces no fabricated local citation across 300 fabricated references. The pattern holds on three backbones from two developers, including a 20-billion-parameter model that runs on a single consumer-grade GPU. With all outbound network access disabled, both Qwen backbones still exceed the published PaperQA2 accuracy. The evaluation suite runs as a single command, so an adopting group can re-run it on its own corpus and model.
evidence_items.title: MuninAI: A Self-Hosted Agentic Framework for Independent Research Groups

rationale: Matched: annotation quality, benchmark, dataset, evaluat
evidence_items.summary: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
evidence_items.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases

rationale: Matched: agents~evaluating, benchmark, evaluat, synthetic data
evidence_items.summary: A fundamental challenge in evaluating and training autonomous agents is measuring the intrinsic difficulty of the tasks they attempt. Estimating this quantity can be useful for environment designers creating synthetic data or benchmarks, as well as for constructing training curricula, thereby offering a way to reduce compute costs. Such an estimation becomes increasingly important as agents (particularly LLM-based) move into longer-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error becomes a severe computational bottleneck. However existing work is largely confined to static tasks and relies on evaluation metrics that, as we show, can give an incomplete picture of predictive performance. In this paper we study ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We find that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and demonstrate how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts

rationale: Matched: agents~benchmark, benchmark, data provenance, evaluat
evidence_items.summary: This paper introduces Evidence-State Drift, a claim-level framework for monitoring changes in evidence used by web-connected large language model (LLM) agents over repeated retrieval events. The framework represents evidence using a normalized claim, evidence span, source identity, retrieval and publication timestamps, content fingerprint, and source-authority label. It aims to distinguish material changes in claim-associated evidence from non-material modifications, such as formatting changes, that do not alter the monitored claim. The study evaluates the proposed representation using a longitudinal replay benchmark containing 67 claims and 871 observation events, including 47 oracle-defined material changes. Within this benchmark, the claim-state detector achieved an F1 score of 0.989 against a predefined deterministic change oracle, with no false positives among 824 oracle-defined non-material events. These results indicate consistency with the benchmark’s predefined change rules. They do not establish independent semantic validation or improved factual accuracy in deployed LLM agents. Independent human evaluation and end-to-end agent testing remain areas for future work. This research contributes to the study of evidence monitoring, information freshness, data provenance, and reliability in web-connected AI systems.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-State Drift: A Claim-Level Framework and Replay Benchmark for Web-Connected LLM Agents

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: RAP: A Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars

evidence_items.summary: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1\,=\,0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1\,=\,0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.
evidence_items.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments

evidence_items.summary: Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) remain a major source of preventable morbidity and mortality in healthcare settings. Proper execution of the central line dressing change (CLDC) procedure is essential for infection prevention, yet current approaches to competency assessment rely primarily on manual ob- servation by clinical educators, making evaluation time-intensive, difficult to scale, and limited in consistency and granularity. These challenges highlight the need for AI-assisted skill evaluation methods that can support more objective, reproducible, and scalable assessment of clinical performance. However, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of broad-scale, clinically grounded datasets for developing and evaluating such methods. In this work, we present the collection process of a large-scale video dataset for CLDC skill evaluation, comprising 365 recordings of registered nurses collected during the 2026 annual competency exam at Houston Methodist Hospital. Each video is paired with subtask-level temporal annotations and clinical performance assessments spanning 17 subtasks of the procedure. We describe the data collection and curation pipeline, including pilot testing of record- ing configurations, annotation protocol design, and post-collection processing. We further establish the feasibility of video-based skill assessment through benchmark experiments with spatiotemporal deep learning models. This dataset provides a foundation for future research on automated clinical skill assessment, feedback generation, and AI-assisted training in nursing education.
evidence_items.title: The Collection of a Real-World, Large-Scale Dataset for Automated Skill Evaluation in Central Line Dressing Change

evidence_items.summary: Comparing climate-policy search methods requires accounting for differences in policy control, available observations, feedback timing, and simulator budgets. We introduce GCAM-Gym, a Gymnasium-compatible environment that supports full-policy evaluation and stepwise control through a common interface and exposes the components of the policy objective. We compare seven search and control systems in three settings: target attainment and cost, cost-temperature trade-offs, and one-step delayed feedback. Each system is evaluated with ten seeds per setting, for a total of 3,210 attempted GCAM evaluations. Four systems share a budget of 24 attempts per seed; among these, CMA-ES achieves the highest interquartile mean (IQM) of the best returns from completed policy evaluations in all three settings. We release the evaluation archive and analysis tools to reconstruct the reported comparisons without running GCAM.

evidence_items.summary: Personalization is classically a two-party problem: a sender chooses what to say, and a receiver with independent objectives decides whether to act. A salesperson pitching the same analytics product leads with HIPAA compliance for a hospital and real-time reporting for a retailer, expecting a different argument to work on each. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure a narrower, one-party property: whether output matches the preferences of the same user it serves—sender and receiver being the same, as when RLHF aligns an assistant to its own user. The two-party case is harder to study automatically, since it needs ground truth linking specific content to an observed receiver action.Sales outreach provides this: a message written for one prospect, recorded against whether it produced a reply, a call, or a closed deal. We introduce SDR-Arena, a framework for benchmarking two-party generative personalization at scale, and SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 50,000 customer success stories across 22 industries and 3500 enterprises. Given only pre-outcome information, an agent must reconstruct the arguments that won the deal, scored by a weighted nugget-recall metric (WCS). The best model, Claude Sonnet 4.6, reaches 55.8% WCS indicating it recovers only half the winning content—a plateau we observe across model families that costly deep-research pipelines do not close. An ablation shows the cause is retrieval, not reasoning: models improve substantially given the facts a human researcher would gather, but rarely find them through web search alone. Two studies with professional SDRs support the metric: only 48% of generated pitches were rated usable without editing, and WCS yields model rankings consistent with evaluation against expert strategies authored independently of any model output.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation

evidence_items.summary: Rare malignant cells in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), including circulating tumor cells (CTCs), minimal residual disease (MRD) cells, and small malignant populations in heterogeneous tumor microenvironments (TME), represent an important clinical challenge. These cells occur at very low frequency, requiring separation from a large non-malignant background. Existing methods show inconsistent evaluation, using different datasets, label definitions, prevalence settings, scoring strategies, and failure handling. We present Rare-cell Evaluation Across Cancer Heterogeneity (REACH), treating inter-lineage rare malignant cell detection as an imbalanced ranking task. REACH benchmarks CNV-supported malignant cells (P HC) against immune, stromal, and normal epithelial cells (B HC), modeling the CTC and MRD screening setting. REACH excludes intra-lineage state discovery, including drug-tolerant persisters, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), and transitional malignant states, evaluating these separately in Track F. REACH combines confidence tiered multi-arm labels with five evaluation tracks, covering controlled real spike-ins, synthetic Splatter stress tests, null background controls, natural blood/CTC prevalence, and supervised label noise diagnostics. Applying standardized method wrappers, fallback-aware metrics, non-parametric statistics, and audited figure regeneration, REACH provides a reproducible evaluation framework. REACH evaluates 10 computational methods on 10 curated scRNA-seq cancer datasets containing 359,739 cells. This benchmark produces 11,250 performance measurements across 1,125 benchmark tasks. The supervised highly variable gene logistic regression ceiling achieves a median average precision of 1.0, indicating strong expression differences between tumor and non-tumor cells. Current unsupervised methods recover only part of this signal.
evidence_items.title: REACH: a reproducible benchmark for inter-lineage rare malignant cell detection in single-cell RNA sequencing

evidence_items.summary: Bengali hallucination detection must distinguish unsupported factual claims from incorrect reasoning, often without a supplied reference passage. We present and characterize an inference-only system that combines response-conditioned query rewriting, hybrid retrieval, and task-specific language-model judging. Six retrieval routes search question-answer and passage collections; a router directs each example to a 27B textual judge or a 14B agent that can compare retrieved answers, reason directly, or generate and execute Python. We characterize the system using version-specific code, saved predictions, execution traces, and corpus metadata from the Olikbochon challenge. Kaggle associates a displayed private macro-F1 of 0.956 with Version 2; its saved run processes 2,516 examples in 220.99 minutes on two T4 GPUs. Of 253 math-routed examples, 88 terminate through candidate matching, while execution traces expose 49 stderr-bearing run events across 35 examples. A later run changes six predictions despite identical core worker code. A bounded audit of 1,090 benchmark-related corpus records finds exact question or context overlap for 38 processed evaluation inputs, precluding an unqualified claim of corpus-independent generalization. The contribution is a concrete retrieval-and-computation judging architecture with an auditable operational characterization, not a controlled estimate of component gains. We distinguish the reported leaderboard result from independently recomputed diagnostics and identify the evidence needed for stronger effectiveness and reproducibility claims.
evidence_items.title: Bengali Hallucination Detection with Retrieval and Programs: A System Study

evidence_items.summary: FOR-species20K is the largest public LiDAR benchmark for tree-species classification, pooling 25 independently collected terrestrial, mobile, and airborne laser-scanning datasets across 33 species. We introduce a multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves official hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at the time of submission. We then examine what this score measures. Because the hidden test is species-balanced, its overall accuracy is more comparable to a macro metric than to accuracy under the public set's long-tailed distribution. Moreover, the official random split places every source dataset in both training and evaluation. A logistic probe recovers source identity from out-of-fold model probabilities with 69% accuracy, while geometric features identify the source above 90% within two widely shared species; 18 of the 33 species occur in only one source. Under a source-species-cell holdout, evaluated on 5,566 trees from eight eligible species that retain the same LiDAR-type training support in other sources, the unweighted species mean falls from 82% to 36%, and tree-weighted accuracy falls from 95% to 60%. Count-matched retraining and experiments with two alternative backbones indicate that this gap is not explained by reduced training support alone, while an external PureForest experiment shows a smaller but consistent grouped-split effect. These results establish the 85% leaderboard score as strong in-distribution performance, but not as an estimate of source-disjoint generalization, motivating balanced metrics and source-aware evaluation. The code is available at: https://github.com/JaeLee18/FOR20K-lidar-tree-species
evidence_items.title: Three LiDARs, Twenty-Five Datasets: Cross-Source Generalization in Tree-Species Recognition

evidence_items.summary: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions

evidence_items.summary: Ultrasound is the most widely deployed imaging modality worldwide, yet clinical AI remains fragmented into narrow single-task models that fail when device, operator, or anatomy changes. Here we present SonoCorpus, an open resource unifying 456,963 images and 1,626,085 expert masks from 53 public datasets spanning 24 clinical applications and 17 countries, and SonoBase, an interactive segmentation foundation model pretrained on it. Across fifteen evaluation datasets introducing new organs, devices, operators, and geographies, SonoBase outperforms SAM2, MedSAM2, and the concept-promptable MedSAM3 on every dataset and matches per-dataset specialist models trained on the same data; on fully external data it exceeds the accuracy these baselines achieve on their own in-distribution benchmarks. Ejection fraction derived from its segmentations falls within inter-observer variability (6.63\% error), with fewer misclassifications at the defibrillator-candidacy threshold than either promptable baseline (13\% versus 18--42\%); fetal head-circumference (1.81~mm) and gestational-age (1.2 days) errors fall below inter-observer variability. Where a baseline fails outright, one in four test cases, SonoBase recovers a usable segmentation in 81\% of them, including on handheld probes operated by minimally trained users in two low- and middle-income countries (Sierra Leone and Tanzania). Five labeled examples can help the model adapt to a new setting, and the identical training protocol transfers well to newer models such as SAM3, locating the advantage in ultrasound-specific pretraining rather than any single architecture. To ensure reproducibility and enable the community to build on SonoBase as a platform, we release all checkpoints, optimizer states, data-split indices, deduplication hashes, and starter code at https://github.com/AlfredQin/sonobase.
evidence_items.title: Open ultrasound foundation model for robust segmentation and clinical measurement across heterogeneous settings

evidence_items.summary: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations

evidence_items.summary: Panoptic occupancy unifies 3D geometry, semantics, and instance identities, but its development is limited by scarce instance-aware annotations. Existing benchmarks mainly provide semantic labels reconstructed from incomplete sensor observations, while panoptic datasets have limited domain coverage or annotation completeness. We introduce PanoBench, a camera-centric panoptic occupancy prediction benchmark spanning synthetic and real-world driving scenes. It combines PanoBench-CarlaOcc, PanoBench-nuScenes, and PanoBench-KITTI360 through canonical data interfaces and unified evaluation protocols, providing multi-resolution annotations with persistent instance identities. The synthetic branch derives complete panoptic geometry from simulated meshes. For real-world data, a new pipeline reconstructs backgrounds using geometric priors and topology constraints, generates foreground mesh assets from multi-frame multi-view images, and fuses them into sparse panoptic voxels. A unified valid-mask protocol evaluates complete thing instances supported by temporal observations while scoring stuff regions at the voxel level. Analyses of observation fidelity, geometric completeness, spatial continuity, and temporal consistency demonstrate the benefits of the resulting annotations over existing occupancy benchmarks. We benchmark representative methods on semantic occupancy prediction, panoptic occupancy prediction, and 4D occupancy forecasting, and study voxel resolution, synthetic-to-real transfer, and storage efficiency. These results reveal complementary strengths of volumetric and ray-based metrics and persistent challenges in real-world instance-aware prediction. PanoBench is available at https://mias.group/PanoBench.
evidence_items.title: PanoBench: A Panoptic Occupancy Prediction Benchmark for Autonomous Driving

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to modify and maintain machine-learning systems in production, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate either competition-style ML experimentation or generic repository issue resolution. We introduce MLOps-Bench, a repository-grounded benchmark for production ML engineering. Unlike prior ML-agent benchmarks, MLOps-Bench evaluates executable lifecycle changes inside real ML repositories, spanning data pipelines, feature engineering, model training, model serving, monitoring, CI/CD and governance, and end-to-end integration. Each task is grounded in repository evidence and includes a natural-language requirement, oracle patch, plausible buggy baseline, fail-to-pass tests, pass-to-pass tests, and provenance metadata. The benchmark contains 212 validated tasks from 31 public ML repositories, with 636 fail-to-pass tests and 856 pass-to-pass tests. We evaluate six agents and find that the best system solves 31.2% of tasks while passing 68.7% of tests, showing that current agents often make partial progress but still fail production-relevant behavioral requirements. MLOps-Bench shifts agent evaluation beyond model building and issue fixing toward repository-native MLOps work where correctness depends on lifecycle reasoning, behavioral robustness, and preservation of existing system behavior.
evidence_items.title: MLOps-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Production ML Engineering in Real Repositories

evidence_items.summary: Physical reasoning about humans in videos has largely focused on everyday interactions, where contact, pressure, pose, and motion support embodied perception and contact-aware applications. Still, short and forceful properties like impact events remain relatively underexplored, despite their relevance to broader understanding of how abrupt physical events affect the human body. To fill this gap, we introduce human-centric impact localization, a new task that localizes target physical impacts temporally within a video and spatially on the human body. We further present HAPACT, a HumAn-centric imPACT dataset and benchmark built from movie clips, containing over 2.8K video-query pairs with more than 20K fine-grained human-annotated frames. We built HAPACT around viewer-grounded annotation, text-conditioned localization, and supervision at frame-level temporal and SMPL-X-based spatial granularity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our benchmark, we conduct extensive evaluations of existing methods, employing video moment retrieval models for temporal localization and human-scene contact models for spatial localization. For the spatial task, we propose a text-conditioned baseline by reformulating localization as query-guided body-region selection. Benchmark results show that physical impact localization remains challenging for existing methods, motivating HAPACT as a dedicated benchmark to support physical impact reasoning in videos.
evidence_items.title: HAPACT: A Benchmark For Human-Centric Physical Impact Localization in Movies

evidence_items.summary: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.
evidence_items.title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing

evidence_items.summary: As assistants move from reactive answering toward proactive intervention, memory changes role: it no longer only supplies the answer to a query, it determines whether and when to speak at all. Prior work in this setting hands the system the relevant fact in context; we study the regime that makes the problem hard, where the evidence justifying an intervention must be mined from a long-horizon personal memory. We introduce ProPerMem, a benchmark for memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), pairing egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories (~618K tokens on average), human-verified trigger windows, and a protocol that scores content and timing jointly. Every baseline we evaluate performs poorly (at most 15%), including frontier models given summarized or retrieval-augmented memory. A controlled study explains why: with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window GPT-5.3-Chat reaches 96%; letting it choose the timing drops it to 38%, and replacing oracle evidence with retrieval drops it to 15%. Content and timing are separately necessary, and missing either is catastrophic. Guided by this, we build ProPerAgent (Proactive Personalized Agent) with a plug-and-play harness that surfaces memory from a graph-organized store and gates it down to what is worth interrupting for, plus a lightweight RL stage that curbs early and repeated firing. Without any training, ProPerAgent lifts strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5% on Qwen3.8-27B and 38% on GPT-5.3-Chat; RL post-training reaches 42.4%.
evidence_items.title: ProPerAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance

evidence_items.summary: Large language model based coding agents have made substantial progress on repository-level software engineering tasks. Existing repository benchmarks, however, usually start from a human-identified issue and evaluate whether a patch satisfies a functional signal. We present SWE-Prometheus, a benchmark for the broader task of improving repository engineering governance. Each task provides a fixed snapshot and an open-ended objective, requiring the agent to identify risks, prioritize interventions, and verify the resulting changes. SWE-Prometheus evaluates six governance dimensions through paired evidence, clean-environment probes, behavior gates, and two independent teacher ratings of the same evidence. The benchmark contains 60 repositories; ten models are evaluated on a shared 22-repository public subset, where mean Normalized Governance Improvement ranges from 0.0568 to 0.5760 and observed behavior-breakage rates range from 0% to 23%. On a frozen ten-repository batch, a repository-blind template obtains mean NGI 0.272, but its gains concentrate in Tests & CI, Quality Gates, and Documentation; it improves Reproducible Environment and Dependency & Security on none of the repositories. This baseline makes the distinction between adding governance artifacts and producing execution-backed improvements measurable. The no-op condition has median NGI zero and standard deviation 0.073; two teachers agree exactly on 57 of 60 dimension scores for the same no-op evidence. For the two highest conditional-mean systems, common-valid NGI is similar, while full-pool comparisons that include behavior failures favor Kimi-K3. These results show why repository-governance evaluation should report improvement, behavior preservation, evidence quality, and coverage together.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Prometheus: Measuring Engineering Governance Improvements in Real-World Repositories

evidence_items.summary: Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine deployment and Non-Engine Render in triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering. MeshSuite evaluates two deployment settings: Standard Deployment, using an opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; and Dedicated Deployment, using method-specific engine implementations to preserve appearance and compositing features. For mesh splatting, we also audit exported surfaces for topological and geometric integrity as downstream graphics assets. Our results show that engine deployment reduces image quality in both settings; among evaluated methods, MeshSplatting degrades least under Standard Deployment. Dedicated Deployment preserves most fidelity at roughly 5-33x the runtime of Standard Deployment across two deployment datasets. For mesh splatting, explicit connectivity and shared indexing remain limited: shared vertex indexing alone guarantees neither manifoldness nor global connectivity. These findings show that rasterizability is only part of graphics readiness and underscore the need to assess engine deployment. Project page: https://surrey-up-lab.github.io/MeshSuite.
evidence_items.title: MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering

evidence_items.summary: Log parsing turns free-text log lines into event templates and is the first step of most log-mining pipelines, yet parser behavior on mobile-platform logs remains poorly characterized. We present ABRLogParser, a multi-parser benchmark that expands the ABRLog Android bug-report dataset by applying thirteen classical parsers to its eight regular-expression block types: 342 files, 14 devices, 32.0 million log lines. Every (file, parser) pair yields a released structured output and template summary, and each parser is characterized by content (how aggressively it abstracts lines into templates) and by execution (coverage, failure modes, runtime). Abstraction spans a factor of 906 across parsers and throughput about fiftyfold; parsers carrying the LogPAI server-log defaults degenerate into near-identity transforms on Android; and we map where each one breaks down on large inputs. The corpus has no ground-truth templates, so the artifact is a substrate for parser comparison, not an accuracy benchmark.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Parser Benchmark over Android Bug-Report Logs

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.
evidence_items.title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth in reported software vulnerabilities, combined with substantial delays in manual Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) assessment, has created a critical need for automated and interpretable vulnerability scoring tools. When vulnerabilities remain unscored for long periods, organizations face greater difficulty in prioritizing patches and mitigation actions, which can leave exploitable weaknesses insufficiently addressed during a critical exposure window. This challenge is particularly important for the CVSS Base metrics, which form the foundation for severity assessment and are essential for timely risk evaluation. This paper presents WSymBERT, a neuro-symbolic approach for predicting CVSS v3.1 Base metrics by combining contextual language representations with expert-derived symbolic guidance through a symbolic-guided weighted pooling mechanism. We evaluate WSymBERT on two benchmark datasets, achieving mean accuracies of 96.2% on NVD and 94.7% on Combine across the eight CVSS Base metrics. Across the reported evaluations, WSymBERT achieved higher observed performance than the evaluated baselines, while attribution-based analyses indicated greater emphasis on security-relevant evidence under the specified evaluation protocol.
evidence_items.title: WSymBERT: a weighted neuro-symbolic model for interpretable CVSS prediction

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can render structured questionnaire variables as natural-language profiles, but their value in mental-health screening cannot be judged from a single fixed-threshold score. We evaluated LLM prompt conditions in a cross-questionnaire benchmark for predicting screen-positive status on the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) among undergraduates. The intended application was an offline methodological benchmark using previously collected questionnaire data, not a shorter alternative to direct SDS administration. Methods De-identified records were assigned to Development (n=1,951), Test (n=2,186), and Holdout (n=2,258) grade cohorts. We evaluated logistic regression, XGBoost, and 12 model-prompt conditions at the fixed 0.5 threshold and at thresholds selected only in Development-validation. We also examined paired bootstrap differences, ranking stability, scale correlations, grouped ablations, cohort shift, calibration intercepts and slopes, alternative expected calibration error specifications, representative repeated calls at temperatures 0 and 0.1, sex-stratified performance, and per-1,000 screening scenarios. Results At the fixed 0.5 threshold on Test, GPT E1, Gemini E2, and XGBoost achieved macro-F1 values of 0.732, 0.730, and 0.674. At Development-derived thresholds of 0.38, 0.50, and 0.174, the corresponding macro-F1 values were 0.702, 0.730, and 0.660. At the Development-selected specificity target, XGBoost achieved a Test macro-F1 of 0.738. Pairwise intervals showed no clear fixed-0.5 macro-F1 difference among the three highest-ranked LLM conditions. XGBoost yielded the lowest Brier scores. The combined-sample Spearman correlation between SDS and SAS was 0.60. Together with the ablation results, this correlation indicated predictive information distributed across overlapping questionnaire groups rather than dependence on a single measured group.
evidence_items.title: SDS screen-positive prediction from structured questionnaires in university students: a comparative evaluation of large language model prompting strategies

evidence_items.summary: Brazilian public-safety agencies release structured crime statistics but withhold the free-text narrative field of police reports, which is rich in modus operandi and contextual information, because it contains personal data protected by the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD). We address this deadlock for robbery reports with a fully local (on-premise) two-stage anonymization pipeline: a deterministic regular-expression stage for structured personally identifiable information (PII) and a pluggable semantic layer (dedicated NER, local LLMs served by Ollama, union and chained hybrids, and Microsoft Presidio as a system baseline). We contribute (i) an expert-annotated gold standard of 996 robbery narratives, released with the source code; (ii) an entity-level evaluation protocol whose headline metric is safety recall (how much PII actually did not leak), complemented by a re-identification-criticality analysis and bootstrap confidence intervals; and (iii) an empirical benchmark of nine engine configurations quantifying the safety–utility trade-off. The union of spaCy and qwen3:8b over the regex stage reaches the highest macro safety recall (0.986, 95% CI [0.972; 0.994]; micro 0.973) and is the most conservative (highest-recall) option, while qwen3:8b alone gives the best overall balance (safety recall 0.966, precision 0.80, micro-F1 0.826, text retention 96%) and is our recommendation for general use. In this configuration, direct identifiers (names, documents, phones, e-mails) are removed at 99–100%, with residual leakage concentrated in location quasi-identifiers. Safety recall measures PII removal, not residual reidentification risk: these figures bound leakage rather than certify anonymity. We recommend qwen3:8b for general supervised anonymization, and the union when leakage must be minimized, and discuss conditions for replication across Brazilian police forces.
evidence_items.title: Local Anonymization of Free-Text Robbery Police Reports in Brazilian Portuguese: a Safety-Recall-Oriented Multi-Model Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Cloud misconfiguration is a leading cause of data breaches in production cloud environments, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has amplified this risk by letting a single insecure configuration propagate across an entire cloud estate in one deployment. This paper presents an open-agent framework for intelligent compliance analysis of IaC configurations, integrating Open Policy Agent (OPA)-based Policy-as-Code enforcement with Large Language Model (LLM)-driven contextual reasoning in a single hybrid pipeline. Prior work has treated deterministic policy enforcement and LLM-based analysis independently; the proposed framework instead combines the precision of OPA-based Rego rule evaluation with the explanatory and remediation capabilities of an LLM to produce structured, audit-ready compliance evidence aligned to a formal control framework. The framework is instantiated with a custom 16-rule Rego policy library spanning three NIST SP~800-53 control families Access Control (AC), System and Communications Protection (SC), and Audit and Accountability (AU) across eight AWS resource types, and evaluated on 231 labeled Terraform configurations derived from the IaC-Eval benchmark. The OPA enforcement layer achieves 96.9\% precision, 90.5\% recall, and 93.6\% F1 score. The LLM enrichment layer, guided by a deterministic safeguard against LLM recall errors and explicit prompt-level format constraints, produces reliable, audit-ready control mappings and remediation guidance across 16 violation types. The performance advantage over an industrial static-analysis baseline (Checkov) is confirmed statistically significant via McNemar's exact test ($\chi^2=13.0$, $p<0.001$), demonstrating that the hybrid approach delivers compliance analysis outcomes that neither paradigm achieves alone.
evidence_items.title: An Open-Agent Framework for Intelligent Compliance Analysis in Infrastructure as Code Using Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This study evaluates how LLMs interpret Words of Estimative Probability (WEPs) in Brazilian Portuguese compared to English. We translated an English benchmark and compared multilingual models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Flash) against a region-specific model (Sabiá 4). Our findings reveal a “tail smoothing” phenomenon, where models systematically compress extreme probabilities. Notably, while Gemini 3 Flash demonstrated remarkable cross-lingual stability, GPT-5.1 exhibited significant calibration degradation. Counterintuitively, when measured against the English human baseline, Sabiá 4 displayed the most aggressive distribution compression. These results suggest a complex dynamic: either linguistic fine-tuning does not ensure alignment, or it actively captures a culturally specific pragmatic ambiguity in Brazilian Portuguese. This exposes the vulnerabilities and nuances of deploying deploying LLMs in nuanced semantic tasks in Brazilian Portuguese.
evidence_items.title: Tail Smoothing and Cross-Lingual Volatility: Evaluating Estimative Uncertainty in Large Language Models for Brazilian Portuguese

evidence_items.summary: Automatic auscultation is usually evaluated on the ICBHI 2017 database, where published scores depend on the split and the metric adopted. This work measures what a deployable model reaches under a fixed protocol: the official split, five seeds, patient-level bootstrap intervals, and an equivalence margin fixed in advance. Six configurations are compared, a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) trained from scratch, a closed-form continuous-time (CfC) recurrent network, and two pretrained models, MobileNetV3 on ImageNet and PANNs CNN6 on AudioSet. The compact CNN (556 500 parameters) obtains an ICBHI score of 0.460±0.017 and a binary area under the curve (AUC) of 0.572, with a patient-level interval of [0.515,0.630]. No pretrained configuration discriminates detectably better, and equivalence within the margin holds only between the CNN and its 8-bit integer (INT8) version. That level needs its baselines: a classifier that always predicts Normal scores 0.500, above every trained configuration, and an audio-free indicator of the recording device reaches an AUC of 0.582. The discrimination of the CNN ranges from 0.627 on the most represented device to 0.468 on the least, and the CfC stays at chance, which irregular event timing does not change. Quantized to INT8 with the classifier in floating point, the CNN occupies 0.58 MB and runs in 30.4 ms per cycle on a Raspberry Pi 5 without thermal throttling. Replacing the official score by a per-class macro average raises the figure by 0.121 to 0.183 on the same predictions.
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Benchmark of Compact, Pretrained, and Continuous-Time Models for Respiratory Sound Classification at the Edge

evidence_items.summary: Gold Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) provide investors with exposure to gold prices without requiring direct ownership of physical gold. Differences in fund expenses, benchmark replication and other operational factors may cause individual ETFs to perform differently. This study evaluates five selected Gold ETFs in India—Kotak, SBI, Nippon India, HDFC and Axis—over the period from 1 April 2021 to 30 March 2026. The analysis uses daily net asset values (NAVs), a domestic Indian gold-price series denominated in Indian rupees, and Nifty 50 index values. The analytical framework includes cumulative returns, compound annual growth rate (CAGR), annualised volatility, the Sharpe ratio, correlation, regression and tracking-error analysis. Three hypotheses are tested using the Friedman test, Newey–West heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) tests of mean active returns, and HAC-robust regression analysis. The domestic gold-price series generated a cumulative return of 232.19%, compared with 208.10%–216.46% for the five ETFs and 52.01% for the Nifty 50 price index. Kotak recorded the highest cumulative return among the five ETFs, the highest Sharpe ratio and the lowest tracking error. The Friedman test identified statistically significant differences in daily-return rankings among the ETFs. After Holm adjustment, Kotak exhibited statistically significant negative mean daily active returns relative to gold, whereas the corresponding results for the other four ETFs were not statistically significant. HAC-robust regressions also indicated significant positive relationships between each ETF's returns and gold-price returns. The findings demonstrate that absolute returns, risk-adjusted performance and tracking efficiency represent distinct dimensions of Gold ETF performance. Keywords: Gold ETFs, NAV, risk–return analysis, Sharpe ratio, tracking error, domestic gold prices, Nifty 50, hypothesis testing.
evidence_items.title: Performance, Risk and Benchmark Tracking of Selected Gold ETFs in India: A Comparative Study with Domestic Gold Prices and the Nifty 50 (2021–2026)

evidence_items.summary: General-purpose LLMs asked to output a structured AI-ness verdict can serve as text detectors at near-zero cost, and their availability is governed less by model quality than by the free-tier policies of the gateways that serve them. This report benchmarks 20+ models across four gateways (OpenRouter free pool, NVIDIA NIM free tier, Google AI Studio free tier, and a local multi-account router) on a 48-text in-sample corpus and a 48-text disjoint holdout drawn from HC3, all scored through the same strict-JSON prompt, a fixed decision band (AI >= 0.69, HUMAN = 0.60). Three findings stand out. First, model choice dominates tuning: identical prompts and parsers span 0.31 to 1.00 corpus accuracy. Second, each gateway enforces a materially different regime -- OpenRouter has two 429 classes that require opposite remedies, Google's per-model daily quota (nominally 20) delivers a volume that is per model and per project (5-46 requests in one window observed) and stacks linearly with extra project keys, and NVIDIA free serving windows open and close within hours -- so a free model's measured accuracy and its usability as a live lane are separate, per-gateway questions. Third, in-sample perfection does not transfer: a lane that erred zero times on the corpus its band was fitted on produced a false negative out of sample. Part II (window 2026-10-13 to 2026-10-17) adds four findings and one retraction. (1) Accuracy does not survive listing: the lane Part I ranked first was delisted by its gateway four days after its window closed (HTTP 410, permanent), and another advertised model answers 404 on every real call while still appearing in GET /v1/models -- so availability must be probed per model, per gateway, on the day of use, and a catalogue listing is not a health check.
evidence_items.title: Free-Tier LLM Gateways as AI-Text Detectors: A Dated Benchmark of Model Accuracy, Quota Regimes, Availability Churn and Out-of-Sample Stability

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs), like human learners, are frequently exposed to new visual concepts, but how they map novel visual references to language after exposure remains largely underexplored, particularly when those references contradict prior knowledge from pre-training. To study this, we present the Novel Visual References Dataset (NVRD): 19,176 images spanning 90 visual concepts across different levels of visual novelty, each with up to 20 increasingly perturbed versions of the original object to probe generalization. Unlike prior work on visual augmentations of familiar concepts, NVRD comprises entirely novel, open-ended stimuli constructed from scratch, mirroring how humans encounter genuinely new concepts. We evaluate 3 open- and 2 closed-source models alongside 2,400 human judgments for direct human-model comparison, and find that (i) models struggle to acquire novel concepts in-context when they contradict prior knowledge, and (ii) while models and humans show correlated sensitivity to visual perturbations, models significantly overgeneralize, extending learned labels to stimuli that humans reject. We contribute NVRD as a corpus and benchmark for research on visual concept learning in both humans and machines.
evidence_items.title: Would you still call this Dax? Novel Visual References in VLMs and Humans

evidence_items.summary: Understanding people often requires inferring what they feel or want from how they behave rather than from what they state outright. We ask whether language models can make these inferences, and how they do so. We introduce Theory-of-Mind Stories (ToMStories), an evaluation dataset of ~6,000 short synthetically generated narrative vignettes, each paired with a multiple-choice or open-ended question about a character's emotion, fear, motivation, or emotional wound. These psychological states are conveyed implicitly (showing), explicitly (telling), or with conflict between dialogue and description. Evaluating thirteen open-weight models (1B-72B parameters), we find that the largest models match humans on multiple choice but not open-ended questions. Our analyses point to simplifications models make in both interpretation and generation of implicit psychological states, indicating that synthetic data can help us understand how models perform interpretation, but likely overestimates how well models interpret humans.
evidence_items.title: ToMStories: Interpreting Theory-of-Mind in Synthetic Narratives

evidence_items.summary: Dozens of deep architectures for time-series anomaly detection have been published since 2018, most of them reporting higher scores than their predecessors on the same handful of datasets. A series of critical studies now suggests that much of this progress is an artefact. The datasets have flaws that make them easy or mislabelled. The most common scoring protocol, point adjustment, inflates results so strongly that random scores can compete with trained models. And when classical or deliberately simple methods are run under the same conditions, they often match the deep ones. This review assembles that evidence. We describe the method families briefly, then examine the benchmark critiques, the evaluation metrics and their failure modes, and the large comparison studies. A small worked example, constructed by hand and labelled as such, shows the arithmetic of point adjustment. We end with a reporting checklist and with the open question of whether pretrained time-series models change the picture. Apart from that worked example, no new result is reported.
evidence_items.title: Time-Series Anomaly Detection: Benchmark Flaws, Evaluation Metrics and Strong Baselines

evidence_items.summary: Identifying Internet-facing industrial control system (ICS) devices is essential for asset inventory, vulnerability assessment, exposure measurement, and security monitoring. These tasks require information about the vendors, types, and models of exposed ICS devices beyond the presence of an industrial protocol. However, developing and evaluating device identification methods remains constrained by the scarcity of labeled traffic from Internet-facing ICS devices. Existing public ICS datasets are largely collected from testbeds or designed for intrusion detection, providing limited support for studying identification across diverse device instances and changing Internet measurement conditions. We present ICSLibrary, a dataset and benchmark covering 2,205 labeled endpoints and 165 models across three industrial protocols: Modbus/TCP, EtherNet/IP, and S7comm. We construct the dataset through Internet-facing ICS service discovery followed by repeated protocol-specific probing at different times and scanner locations, collecting network traffic and device information. These measurements capture response variability under Internet measurement conditions, and we derive paired traffic views to examine the contributions of instance information and explicit model identifiers. Experiments reveal that accurate recognition of previously observed endpoints does not consistently translate into effective identification of new endpoints of the same model. Performance varies across protocols and collection conditions, and explicit model identifiers can contribute to identification even through statistical traffic features. A complementary response-based case study finds that limited identity information mostly leads to abstention, but can also result in unsupported model confirmations. ICSLibrary provides a foundation for developing and evaluating ICS device identification methods for asset inventory and exposure monitoring.
evidence_items.title: ICSLibrary: A Dataset and Benchmark for Identifying Internet-Facing Industrial Control System Devices

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides 10,000 reproducible instances of the one-dimensional Bin Packing Problem, accompanied by solver-certified integer and linear programming optima, deterministic heuristic packings, optimality certificates, and associated metadata. In the Bin Packing Problem, items with positive integer weights must be assigned to identical bins of a fixed capacity. Every item must be packed exactly once, without exceeding any bin’s capacity. The objective is to minimise the number of bins used. The collection supports computational experiments in combinatorial optimisation, integer programming, linear programming relaxations, approximation algorithms, packing heuristics, and lower-bound techniques. It also provides a resource for algorithm benchmarking and teaching in operations research and computer science. The benchmark includes ten item counts: n = 12, 20, 28, 40, 60, 80, 120, 200, 400, and 800, with bin capacities of 100, 500, or 1,000. Ten instance families are represented: uniform, small-item dominated, large-item dominated, bimodal, clustered, near-half-capacity, near-capacity with fillers, complementary pairs, planted feasible packings, and search-selected quartets. Each family contains 1,000 instances, with 100 at each item count. The search-selected family deliberately targets the recorded heuristics and supports stress testing rather than unbiased estimates of their general performance. Each instance includes its exact ordered item weights and capacity, optimal IP and LP objective values, a verified optimal packing, integrality gaps, generation seed and parameters, structural statistics, solver settings, runtimes, and supporting bounds and certificates. Five deterministic heuristic solutions are supplied: Next Fit, First Fit, Best Fit, First Fit Decreasing, and Best Fit Decreasing. Every instance is feasible and has solver-certified IP and LP optima.
evidence_items.title: Bin Packing Benchmark Dataset
