evidence_items.summary: This dataset documents experimentally induced cracks in reinforced concrete test specimens produced under controlled laboratory conditions. It comprises five reinforced concrete specimens, each tested as one experimental series under stepwise three-point bending in a hydraulic loading frame, resulting in 37 load stages and 74 crack-segment observations. Crack widths were measured using Digital Image Correlation and a crack magnifier. The measurements are complemented by photographic images and laser scans. The dataset contains classified and colored point clouds. In addition, quantitative information on crack lengths, crack widths, and the coordinates of the crack centerlines is provided. The dataset also includes the captured images together with the corresponding intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters. By linking image data with registered 3D point clouds, the dataset supports metric analysis of crack geometry and the evaluation of methods for automated crack detection on concrete surfaces. Compared to existing datasets, it combines image-based and point-cloud-based data and enables metric quantification of cracks.
evidence_items.title: CrackQuant: Multimodal dataset for the detection and quantification of cracks in concrete using image and spatial data

evidence_items.summary: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.
evidence_items.title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents

evidence_items.summary: Due to rapid advances in Generative AI, commercial video generation tools can be used to produce fabricated surveillance footage that can fool both human viewers and automated synthetic video detectors. Since these tools are so widely accessible, a malicious user can create a harmful video clip at minimal cost. The production and dissemination of such videos in high-stakes settings, such as crime reporting and elections, can misdirect emergency response efforts or distort political discourse. Existing deepfake video datasets, used by the research community to develop deepfake detection algorithms, exhibit two limitations: (1) they emphasize benign web content rather than footage of possibly malicious activity, and (2) they rely on older or open-source generators that do not represent recent advances in generative systems. We assemble CCtv DeepFakes (CCDF), a video deepfake dataset, to address both gaps. CCDF contains 1840 videos (460 real and 1380 generated) spanning 16 crime and accident categories, with generated content produced using three leading commercial systems: Grok Imagine, Google VEO 3.1, and OpenAI Sora 2. CCDF is a highly realistic, small-scale, manually annotated dataset targeting evaluation of detection models. We release three versions of the dataset: the raw generated data, a cleaned version in which video metadata are standardized between real and synthetic samples to prevent detectors from exploiting trivial cues, and an altered version simulating low-effort post-processing attacks. We evaluate CCDF with ten recent state-of-the-art detectors covering different detection approaches. Our results suggest that these approaches do not reliably distinguish CCDF's generated videos from real ones, despite their strong reported performance on existing datasets. These results further confirm the benefits of the CCDF dataset for advancing research in DeepFake detection.
evidence_items.title: CCDF: A Benchmark Dataset for Deepfake Detection in Surveillance Footage

evidence_items.summary: Physical AI requires models to ground visual and linguistic understanding in real-world environments while accounting for environmental constraints and execution feedback. We introduce MachEmbodied-VLM (ME-VLM), a unified vision-language model with two variants, 4B and 35B-A3B, that brings together embodied cognition and multimodal agent capabilities. Our work emphasizes physical perception and spatiotemporal reasoning, together with planning, interaction, and outcome assessment in both digital and physical environments. We construct training data spanning embodied and multimodal agent tasks, including execution observations and feedback to support outcome assessment and decision refinement. The training pipeline comprises embodied capability injection, separate reinforcement learning of embodied and multimodal-agent experts, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation that consolidates their complementary capabilities into a single model. Experiments show competitive performance on both embodied and agent benchmarks, as well as on autonomous-driving and embodied-navigation tasks. For edge deployment, visual token compression, W4A8 quantization, and hardware-software co-optimization enable on-device inference of the 4B variant on the M100, reducing prefill latency from 400 ms to 188 ms. Project Page: https://machembodied.com/ME-Brain/ME-VLM.html Code Repository: https://github.com/MachEmbodied/ME-VLM
evidence_items.title: ME-VLM: A Unified VLM for Embodied Cognition and Agent Coordination

evidence_items.summary: Underwater images often suffer from severe color distortion, low contrast, and a hazy appearance due to wavelength-dependent light absorption and scattering. Simultaneously, existing deep learning models exhibit high computational complexity, which limits their practical deployment for real-time underwater applications. To address these challenges, this paper presents a novel underwater image enhancement model, called Adaptive Frequency Fusion and Illumination Aware Network (AQUA-Net). It integrates a residual encoder-decoder with dual auxiliary branches, which operate in the frequency and illumination domains. The frequency fusion encoder enriches spatial representations with frequency cues from the Fourier domain and preserves fine textures and structural details. Inspired by Retinex, the illumination-aware decoder performs adaptive exposure correction through a learned illumination map that separates reflectance from lighting effects. This joint spatial, frequency, and illumination design enables the model to restore color balance, visual contrast, and perceptual realism under diverse underwater conditions. Additionally, we present a high-resolution, real-world underwater video-derived dataset from the Mediterranean Sea, which captures challenging deep-sea conditions with realistic visual degradations to enable robust evaluation and development of deep learning models. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that AQUA-Net performs on par with SOTA in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations while using less number of parameters. Ablation studies further confirm that the frequency and illumination branches provide complementary contributions that improve visibility and color representation. Overall, the proposed model shows strong generalization capability and robustness, and it provides an effective solution for real-world underwater imaging applications.
evidence_items.title: AQUA-Net: Adaptive Frequency Fusion and Illumination Aware Network for Underwater Image Enhancement

evidence_items.summary: Federated prompt learning enables vision-language models like CLIP to collaboratively adapt lightweight soft prompts across distributed clients without sharing raw data. However, existing federated prompt learning methods are designed primarily for supervised settings with labeled client data and assumed relatively stable training distributions. At test time, source-free federated prompt tuning remains largely unexplored. Clients may receive unlabeled target samples with heterogeneous, often non-IID distributions that differ substantially across clients and from the source training distribution, causing locally adapted prompts to drift in different directions and reducing the effectiveness of federated aggregation. In this work, we explore Source-Free Federated Test-Time Prompt Tuning (SF-FTTPT), where distributed clients collaboratively adapt soft prompts on unlabeled test streams without access to source data. Our study reveals that conventional federated aggregation methods struggle under heterogeneous client distributions, as locally adapted prompts become increasingly specialized and difficult to combine effectively. To address this challenge, we propose FedRAPP, a personalized aggregation framework that combines reliability-aware client assessment, server-side exponential moving-average prompt memory, and similarity-guided peer aggregation. FedRAPP selectively incorporates information from reliable and compatible clients while preserving local specialization, enabling more robust adaptation under distribution shift. Extensive experiments across nine CLIP benchmark datasets and ImageNet variants demonstrate that FedRAPP consistently outperforms standard federated aggregation baselines under heterogeneous client distributions while maintaining the efficiency advantages of prompt-only adaptation.
evidence_items.title: FedRAPP: Federated Test-Time Prompt Tuning for Vision-Language Models with Reliability-Aware Prompt Personalization

evidence_items.summary: Object hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs) is usually measured by checking each object a caption names against the image. Most benchmarks and detectors alike treat every object mention as a claim that the object is present. This assumption fails when a caption names an object without asserting it, as in "a bench for people to sit on", which mentions people without claiming that any are in the image. We call such mentions non-assertive. Treating them as hallucinations inflates the error rates attributed to models that use such language. To separate them from real hallucinations, we introduce NAME-Bench (Non-Assertive Mention Evaluation Benchmark), 25,497 object mentions from captions that five VLMs generate for COCO images. Each mention is labelled concrete (asserted and present), hallucinated (asserted and absent), or non-assertive, and non-assertive mentions are further divided into four subtypes: depictive, purpose, negation and hedged. All the hallucination detectors that we evaluate flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations, at rates between 14% and 80%. Adding non-assertive mentions to detector training as negatives largely corrects this on LLaVA-1.5. On the four newer VLMs, a comparable correction takes five to ten times more data, and the detectors then catch fewer real hallucinations. These findings show that current detectors conflate mentioning an object with asserting it, and that this conflation is harder to undo on the four newer VLMs than on LLaVA-1.5. Hallucination evaluation should therefore separate what a caption asserts from what it merely mentions.
evidence_items.title: Not Every Mention Is a Claim: Rethinking Object Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal-conditioned guidance for blind and low-vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users. VISTA contains $\sim$1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision-language models zero-shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal-directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.
evidence_items.title: VISTA: A Multimodal Egocentric Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Perception and Assistance to Blind and Low-Vision Users

evidence_items.summary: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.

evidence_items.summary: Cost Per Correct is a small benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on cost-effectiveness rather than accuracy alone. Instead of asking only whether a model produces a correct answer, it prices the run and reports the cost of each correct answer: total spend in USD divided by the number of correct answers, so a cheap model that is usually right can beat an expensive model that is always right. Version 1.0.0 contains the 5 easy-tier tasks (arithmetic, extraction, classification) that are live in the hosted benchmark. Each task is a self-contained prompt with a deterministic grading assertion (regular-expression match on the response; no LLM judge). The benchmark was created by Karmendra Pandey and first published as a public benchmark on Kaggle Benchmarks on 11 October 2026 (Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge entry), where the live leaderboard remains: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/karmendra8386/cost-per-correct In the first hosted run (11 October 2026), Gemini 2.5 Flash passed all 5 tasks (leaderboard score 100.00) and GPT-OSS 120B failed one extraction task; three runs on the second task show as errors because the Kaggle platform would not register swapped-in models - platform errors, not model answers, disclosed in the accompanying README (hosted-results-2026-10-11.csv) and in the entry write-up at the time. Costs are accounted with tokenecon (software DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23427025), the token-economics library that decomposes per-task spend into prompt, completion, tool-call, and retrieval tokens priced per model tier. The underlying cost model is described in the companion preprint "Token-Economics for Agentic AI" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23195511). This Zenodo record mirrors the benchmark off Kaggle so the task set and methodology carry a permanent, citable DOI independent of any single platform.
evidence_items.title: Cost Per Correct: benchmark tasks for cost-per-correct-answer evaluation of LLM agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains supplementary data supporting the study “In vitro evaluation of Chios mastic gum cytotoxicity in canine cancer cell lines.” The Excel workbook contains six supplementary tables reporting the effects of three Chios mastic gum preparations—terpenoid-rich preparation, mastic oil, and powdered mastic gum—on canine cancer cell viability assessed using the MTT assay. The worksheets correspond to the following cell lines:• Table S1: AXA, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S2: AXC, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S3: ORI, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S4: NK, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S5: DENNY, canine hemangiosarcoma.• Table S6: 17CM98, canine malignant melanoma. The workbook includes individual cell viability measurements for untreated controls, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) vehicle controls, and treatment groups, together with absorbance measurements used for concentration–response analyses and estimation of half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀). Treatment groups include concentrations of 5, 25, 50, 100, and 200 µg/mL. Concentrations are expressed in µg/mL, and normalized cell viability is expressed as a percentage. “Abs570” denotes absorbance at 570 nm. Abbreviations used in the workbook include T (terpenoid preparation), Ol (oil preparation), Pw (powder preparation), DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide), and IC₅₀ (half-maximal inhibitory concentration). The dataset is provided as an Excel workbook (.xlsx) within a ZIP archive. Experimental methods and statistical procedures are described in the accompanying manuscript.

evidence_items.summary: Overview This record provides the reproducibility materials accompanying the manuscript A Cross-Dataset Robustness Benchmark for Plant Disease Recognition under Controlled-to-Field Domain Shift. Benchmark and Reproducibility Materials The benchmark harmonizes PlantVillage, PlantWild v2, and PlantDoc into a shared 16-class disease taxonomy. It evaluates controlled-to-field domain shift under fixed model configurations, source-domain checkpoint-selection rules, and documented evaluation procedures. The package includes the frozen dataset split manifest, exact-content duplicate-audit records, experiment configurations, software environment information, seed-level results, class-wise performance summaries, and completion records for 126 original benchmark runs. Version 1.1.0: Validation and Reproducibility Evidence This version preserves the original benchmark records and adds supplementary validation and reproducibility evidence developed during the manuscript's second revision. Visual integrity audit: Complementary pHash/dHash and ResNet-50 feature-based near-duplicate retrieval, ORB-assisted geometric evidence, and documented manual decisions for 581 prioritized image pairs. Performance sensitivity: Fixed-checkpoint, test-subset sensitivity results for all 126 original runs based on confirmed cross-role image overlaps. Field-to-field evaluation: PlantWild v2-to-PlantDoc and PlantDoc-to-PlantWild v2 tests using six existing source-validation-selected checkpoints. Training-budget analysis: Optimizer-update counts, selected-checkpoint information, source-validation histories, and balanced-to-in-domain comparisons. Auxiliary experiment provenance: Reconciliation of the 16 representative A1-A4 SAM/Performer records with their original data partitions and checkpoint-selection procedures. Evaluation scope: Documentation of shot-dependent class eligibility and the distinction between unseen target domains and held-out target test partitions.

evidence_items.summary: The discovery rate p ₐ governs diversification in Cuckoo Search (CS) and is conventionally set to 0.25. Its optimal value depends on the landscape; its schedule shape does not. Holding shape constant and sweeping p ₐ over 51 replications, median error rises monotonically with p ₐ on smooth unimodal functions. Still, it falls monotonically on the rugged multimodal Michalewicz function, improving sixteen-fold across the range tested. Conversely, fixing the arithmetic run-average and varying only shape across six schedules separates them over twenty benchmark functions — but not because shape matters: rank tracks the geometric mean of the realised rate ( r = 0.891) and time spent below 0.10 ( r = −0.869), not direction of change. Renormalising on the geometric mean reverses the ordering, moving the cubic schedule from first of six to last with its shape unchanged. The discovery rate acts through where the search operates, not the trajectory taken, and no single-moment normalisation separates shape from level. These results reinterpret Mareli and Twala (2018), which concluded that an exponentially increasing schedule improves CS. We identify two defects: a criterion that ranks by dispersion rather than quality, and a specification that lets the exponential arm run at a mean p ₐ of 0.430 against a nominal cap of 0.25. Under a corrected criterion, that arm ranks last, and a constant schedule at matched level exceeds it. We propose CSAD, a stagnation-adaptive scheme that raises pₐ when the incumbent stalls and decays it when refinement pays; it is competitive at d = 10 but the worst arm at higher dimensions, a failure we diagnose rather than omit. Instrumentation shows the natural explanation—that higher pₐ buys escapes from local optima—is only half correct: it accounts for precision lost on smooth landscapes but not the gain on rugged ones, where diversity and relocations both fall as p ₐ rises.
evidence_items.title: Level, Before Shape: Landscape-Dependent Control of the Discovery Rate in Cuckoo Search

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the experimental, reconstructed, reference, and derived validation data associated with the manuscript: “Experimental validation of quantitative soft X-ray ptychography at the carbon K-edge.” The dataset provides the data used to evaluate the quantitative agreement between experimentally reconstructed soft X-ray ptychography (SXP) images and independently constructed reference maps for nominally 300 nm polystyrene nanoparticles. The archive includes: Raw and processed STXM data acquired across the Carbon K-edge. Experimental Carbon K-edge NEXAFS spectra of polystyrene reference material and nanoparticles. Energy-dependent optical constants (β and δ) derived from the experimental absorption data and Kramers–Kronig analysis. Reconstructed SXP amplitude and phase data at five selected Carbon K-edge energies. The final multimode ptychographic reconstruction used for reconstruction-validation analyses. Calculated optical-density (OD) and phase reference maps based on an idealized spherical-particle thickness model and independently determined optical constants. I0 data used for the STXM radiation-dose calculation. CSV datasets supporting probe-mode analysis, reconstruction reproducibility, synthetic-data reconstruction validation, particle-geometry sensitivity analysis, and radiation-dose calculations. The archive contains both original experimental/reconstruction data and derived machine-readable datasets supporting the quantitative analyses reported in the manuscript. The spherical nanoparticle model provides an idealized physical reference and is not intended to represent an independent measurement of the exact three-dimensional geometry of individual particles. This version expands the original dataset by adding raw STXM data and additional quantitative validation datasets supporting the revised analysis.
evidence_items.title: Data for "Experimental validation of quantitative soft X-ray ptychography at the carbon K-edge"

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a critical indicator of patient safety but are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. The potential of recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly generative large language models (LLMs), to identify ADEs remains understudied. This study aimed to compare the performance of multiple LLMs in identifying ADE-Drug relationships in inpatient and ambulatory clinical notes.


METHODS
We used clinical notes from the 2018 National NLP Clinical Challenge (n2c2) ADE dataset (inpatient; n = 505) and from outpatient encounters (n = 2555) between October 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, at a large academic medical center based in New England. Notes were pre-processed into snippets for model input. Evaluated Models included: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2-3B and their instruction fine-tuned variants (including low-rank adapters for Llama). Performance was assessed using both strict and relaxed evaluations (precision, recall, and F1) for all models, followed by manual evaluation (exact semantic match, partial match, missing ADE, drug mention only, not a drug, or wrong) of the two best-performing models.


FINDINGS
Of the 1048 notes in the local test split, 450 (42.9%) contained at least one ADE. The n2c2 test set included 202 notes, of which 155 (76.7%) contained at least one ADE. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were the top-performing models among those evaluated. GPT-4o consistently outperformed GPT-4o-mini in ADE extraction across both datasets, with higher F1-scores (0.524 vs. 0.381) and a more balanced precision-recall profile. Both models captured ADEs effectively in explicit and complex clinical contexts, although limitations included misclassification of pre-existing allergies and occasional conflation of therapeutic indications with adverse effects. GPT-4o achieved higher exact match coverage and fewer errors across clinical notes, indicating more reliable performance in both inpatient and ambulatory settings.


INTERPRETATION
This work establishes a foundation for integrating LLM methods into real-world drug safety surveillance, with direct implications for improving patient safety.


FUNDING
None.
evidence_items.title: Relationship extraction for adverse drug events in clinical notes using large language models: a retrospective cross-sectional study.

evidence_items.summary: Traditional AI models and large AI models, such as large language models, represent fundamentally distinct paradigms. Large AI models have demonstrated expert-level performance in specific medical domains. However, concerns about medical bias have attracted growing attention from the medicine, sociology, and AI communities. Although related research is expanding rapidly, existing efforts remain fragmented and are often shaped by discipline-specific assumptions, terminology, and evaluation criteria. A general understanding of medical bias in large AI models is still lacking. We searched databases of peer-reviewed publications and preprint archives and screened records against predefined eligibility criteria. In total, we included 92 studies and organized the findings into three core themes: the taxonomy of medical bias, methods for bias detection, and strategies for bias mitigation. We show that medical bias in large AI models spans a wide range of medical scenarios and clinical specialties. Persistent challenges include the absence of unified fairness definitions, insufficient evaluation benchmarks and representative datasets, limited automated bias detection methods, and inadequate real-world validation. Medical bias is not an isolated failure mode but an intersectional challenge shaped by model design, clinical context, patient diversity, and healthcare inequities. Addressing this challenge requires moving beyond fragmented evaluations toward clinically grounded, reproducible, and deployment-aware approaches that align technical fairness research with real-world healthcare needs.
evidence_items.title: A scoping review of bias in large AI models for medicine and healthcare

evidence_items.summary: This study empirically validates a theoretically grounded framework linking Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) infrastructure components to adaptive digital assessment outcomes. Drawing on Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles and learning analytics theory, we developed and tested a structural model examining how MMLA infrastructure is associated with educational practice. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 476 educators and instructional designers across diverse educational contexts in India. The initially proposed 11-construct framework integrating UDL principles with MMLA infrastructure underwent systematic empirical validation using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). A rigorous three-iteration refinement process reduced the initial 44-item instrument to a validated 24-item scale measuring seven constructs. The final validated model comprised MMLA infrastructure components (data quality, technology platforms, real-time analytics) and educational outcomes (adaptive intervention, formative feedback, inclusive assessment, SRL support). Real-time analytics emerged as the dominant predictor across all outcomes (β = 0.546, f2 = 0.421, large effect on adaptive intervention), while MMLA technology demonstrated consistent moderate effects, and MMLA data showed limited direct association. Together, MMLA infrastructure explained 19–46% of the variance in adaptive assessment practices. Notably, UDL constructs failed to achieve acceptable psychometric properties despite theoretical grounding, revealing important insights about measurement challenges in practitioner self-reports. Findings suggest institutions should prioritise real-time analytics capabilities over raw data collection or basic technology infrastructure. The validated 24-item instrument enables practitioners to benchmark MMLA implementation and identify infrastructure gaps. This study provides the first empirically validated framework linking MMLA infrastructure with adaptive assessment outcomes, distinguishing data quality, technology platforms, and real-time analytics as separate constructs with differential effects. The UDL measurement challenges contribute to implementation science by revealing gaps between theoretical articulation and practical measurement.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal learning analytics infrastructure and adaptive digital assessment

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
Artificial intelligence (AI) classifies routine electroencephalograms (EEGs) with expert-level accuracy, but interpretation of long-term EEG monitoring (LTM) remains reliant on time-intensive visual review. We evaluated whether autoSCORE, a clinically approved implementation of SCORE-AI integrated into an EEG reader, achieves expert-level diagnostic accuracy for LTM interpretation and whether expert-supervised use reduces review time versus conventional analysis.


METHODS
A fixed-and-frozen AI model was tested on an independent single-center dataset of 78 adult patient LTM recordings (52 normal, 26 abnormal), with epilepsy monitoring unit discharge diagnosis as the external reference standard. The AI model was benchmarked against two expert panels (three readers each); Panel 1 reviewed autoSCORE EEG detections (hybrid approach), and Panel 2 interpreted full recordings (conventional approach). Diagnostic accuracy and time to diagnostic decision were assessed for fully automated, hybrid, and conventional approaches. Interrater reliability (Gwet's AC1) was evaluated for hybrid and conventional interpretation.


RESULTS
Interrater reliability was significantly higher for hybrid than conventional approach (AC1 = .81, 95% confidence interval [CI] = .73-.89 vs. AC1 = .43, 95% CI = .32-.53; p < .001). Review time was markedly reduced (median [interquartile range (IQR)] = 2.2 [.5-4.3] vs. 52.4 [33.2-62.9] min, mean [95% CI] = 2.9 [2.5-3.2] vs. 50.8 [46.5-55.2] min, p < .001), a 95.8% median reduction (IQR = 95.6-96.3). Diagnostic performance comparisons were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni procedure across all 63 tests. The hybrid approach showed significantly higher sensitivity than conventional interpretation (.88, 95% CI = .77-.97 vs. .69, 95% CI = .57-.81; adjusted p = .006). Its numerically higher diagnostic accuracy versus conventional interpretation (.75, 95% CI = .66-.83 vs. .68, 95% CI = .61-.74) was nonsignificant after correction (adjusted p > .99). Hybrid approach diagnostic accuracy was significantly greater than fully automated analysis (.75, 95% CI = .66-.83 vs. .55, 95% CI = .44-.65; adjusted p < .001).


SIGNIFICANCE
Expert oversight of AI-assisted categorization of interictal epileptiform and nonepileptiform EEG abnormalities improves interrater reliability and efficiency, increases diagnostic sensitivity versus conventional interpretation, and increases diagnostic accuracy versus fully automated analysis in adult LTM.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted categorization of interictal abnormalities in adult long-term electroencephalographic monitoring: Comparable diagnostic accuracy with marked efficiency gain.

evidence_items.summary: This study presents a novel automated framework for the calibration and validation of rain-on-grid (RoG) hydrodynamic models at the catchment scale, with specific application to the TUFLOW HPC platform. The proposed approach establishes an integrated and automated workflow that links rainfall input directly to flood response, enabling efficient calibration of key hydraulic parameters, including Manning’s roughness, initial loss, and continuous loss. The framework combines ensemble-based parameter sampling, automated model execution, data-driven surrogate modelling, and evolutionary optimization algorithms (EAs) to systematically explore parameter combinations within the defined calibration ranges. Three modelling techniques—Random Forest (RF), Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and Gradient Boosting (GB)—are employed to approximate model responses from an ensemble of hydrodynamic model simulations, thereby accelerating the calibration process and reducing computational costs. Furthermore, three EAs, consisting of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Invasive Weed Optimization (IWO), and Differential Evolution (DE), are applied. The optimization objective is defined as minimizing the discrepancy between simulated and reference inundation extents, quantified through total inundated area derived from benchmark inundation datasets. The entire process is implemented in a MATLAB-based script that automatically controls TUFLOW simulations, iteratively adjusts parameters, and evaluates model performance without manual intervention. The framework is tested in a small catchment case study under multiple design rainfall events (50-, 100-, and 500-year return periods). Results demonstrate close agreement between the simulated and reference inundation areas, with differences of less than 1% across all scenarios. These findings indicate satisfactory predictive performance within the studied calibration range. The key novelty of this study lies in the integration of surrogate-assisted optimization within a fully automated calibration environment tailored for RoG models. Furthermore, the developed MATLAB code is made publicly available via GitHub, promoting transparency, reproducibility, and potential broader application in hydrodynamic flood modelling.
evidence_items.title: A Hybrid Computational Intelligence Framework for Automatic Calibration of Catchment Scale Hydrodynamic Flood Models

evidence_items.summary: Deep-learning models for dermoscopy are usually chosen on the basis of accuracy and discrimination, with limited attention to the energy and carbon costs that accompany model development, retraining, and clinical use. If clinical AI is to be governed responsibly, these operational dimensions need to enter the discussion alongside conventional diagnostic metrics. We compared three widely used dermoscopic classification architectures on both clinical performance and environmental cost, and asked how energy-aware reporting might fit into the broader practice of clinical AI governance and algorithmovigilance. The HAM10000 dataset (10,015 dermatologist-labelled dermoscopic images from 7470 unique lesions, seven diagnostic classes) was split at the lesion level into training, validation, and test sets, so that every image of a given lesion was assigned to a single partition. ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B3, and Vision Transformer B/16 were fine-tuned in TensorFlow/Keras on a single NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU. Each architecture was trained three times; metrics were computed separately per run and are reported as mean ± standard deviation. We measured accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), macro- and micro-averaged sensitivity and specificity, per-class sensitivity, and calibration (expected calibration error, Brier score), with lesion-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals and Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests. Training and inference energy were measured directly by sampling board-level GPU power through the NVIDIA management interface; carbon emissions were re-computed under four electricity-grid scenarios. No statistically significant difference in accuracy was detected between any pair of architectures (ResNet-50 0.807 ± 0.002, EfficientNet-B3 0.817 ± 0.002, Vision Transformer B/16 0.808 ± 0.006). Vision Transformer B/16 required 3.07 times the training energy of EfficientNet-B3 (0.0630 ± 0.0038 vs 0.0205 ± 0.0010 kWh per run) and 4.32 times the inference energy (0.307 vs 0.071 Wh per 1,000 images), without a detectable advantage on accuracy (− 0.89 percentage points, 95% CI − 2.47 to + 0.64), AUROC (+ 0.0026, 95% CI − 0.0034 to + 0.0090) or melanoma sensitivity (+ 0.044, 95% CI − 0.026 to + 0.109). The comparison between the two convolutional networks was different in kind: EfficientNet-B3 consumed 43% more training energy than ResNet-50 and returned a significantly higher melanoma sensitivity (+ 0.102, 95% CI + 0.038 to +0.167). Parameter count did not predict energy use—the 10.8-million-parameter EfficientNet-B3 consumed more training energy than the 23.6-million-parameter ResNet-50. Thermal-design-power estimates of inference energy were 2.7–13.8 times the measured values. Changing the electricity grid changed absolute emissions but left the ranking of the three architectures unchanged. Energy is not a decision rule on its own, but it cannot enter a decision at all unless it is measured. Measuring it here produced two different answers rather than one: additional energy corresponded to a statistically significant and potentially clinically important absolute gain in melanoma sensitivity in one comparison, and to no detectable gain in the other. We do not claim that Vision Transformer B/16 and EfficientNet-B3 are equivalent—the study was not designed as a non-inferiority comparison and no clinical margin was pre-specified—but an advantage that cannot be demonstrated does not discharge the burden of justifying a threefold difference in energy use. We argue that energy use, carbon emissions, hardware configuration, calibration, and inference cost should be reported in clinical AI studies as a matter of course, and integrated into pre-deployment evaluation and post-market monitoring of medical imaging models.
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic performance and energy consumption of deep learning models for dermoscopic image classification

evidence_items.summary: Wireless IoT deployments spend most of their energy keeping every node awake even when their measurements are statistically redundant. This paper presents the Adaptive Sensor Sleep Management (ASSM) framework, which analyses temperature and humidity streams online to decide how many nodes need to stay awake. ASSM combines a sliding-window statistical engine, a K-means stage that selects spatially representative nodes, and a phase detector that separates stable from transitional periods using the derivative of the smoothed signal, with all thresholds estimated online from past samples only. During stable phases a small subset of nodes remains active; during transitions every node is woken. We evaluate ASSM on a realistic 100-node model built from an 86,401-record Solapur-mimicking dataset by adding per-node calibration offset, measurement noise and drift, and we benchmark it against random, round-robin, fixed-duty, variance-adaptive and prediction-based baselines with an ablation and a multi-metric fidelity analysis. Across eight random seeds ASSM keeps the network mean to about 0.19% and significantly outperforms random selection (p = 0.008), although stronger baselines—fixed-duty, variance-adaptive and dual-prediction—achieve lower mean error; ASSM’s value is that it is training-free, interpretable and keeps no per-node model. A full-link energy model including switching and gateway-compute overhead shows a net saving of about 55% at the operating point, remaining above ~ 46% under communication-overhead stress, and the controller scales near-linearly to 10,000 nodes. Rare local events depend on periodic-wake and threshold-override safeguards rather than the sleeping subset.
evidence_items.title: An adaptive statistical and clustering-based sensor sleep management framework for energy-efficient IoT networks

evidence_items.summary: Conventional validation schemes may overestimate model robustness in agricultural deep learning when spatial domain shifts are not explicitly considered. This study evaluated convolutional neural networks for pasture biomass estimation using the CSIRO Image2Biomass dataset within a multi-seed Leave-One-State-Out (LOSO) framework. A total of 24 experiments combined four Australian geographical domains, two architectures (ResNet50 and EfficientNet-B0), and three random seeds (42, 123, and 2025). Performance was assessed using WRMSLE, MAE, RMSE, and R2. Seed-to-seed training variability was summarized using standard deviations across three random seeds, while 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for test WRMSLE were estimated by resampling the held-out test samples within each seed-level LOSO run. A metadata-based Random Forest was included as a non-image baseline. ResNet50 achieved mean test WRMSLE values ranging from 0.869 to 1.460 across held-out domains, whereas EfficientNet-B0 ranged from 0.911 to 1.519. The Random Forest baseline outperformed both CNN architectures in New South Wales and Western Australia, suggesting that structured ecological metadata can remain highly competitive when image-based models are transferred to unseen regions. To examine the visual basis of prediction errors, a systematic Grad-CAM audit was conducted using 40 activation maps derived from the five lowest- and five highest-error samples in each domain. The resulting attention patterns suggested domain-dependent model behavior and provided qualitative evidence consistent with reliance on contextual visual cues; however, the quantitative vegetation-attention measure should be interpreted as a coarse diagnostic proxy rather than a ground-truth segmentation metric. Overall, the combination of multi-seed LOSO validation, seed-level variability analysis, baseline benchmarking, and systematic XAI auditing constitutes a pre-deployment diagnostic framework for identifying generalization risks in agricultural computer-vision systems operating under spatial uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating domain generalization in agricultural deep learning through multi-seed LOSO validation and explainable AI

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the pilot evaluation of the DIINA (Diagnostic, Interactive, and Instructional Needs Assessment) framework for assessing instructional content generated by large language models (LLMs). The deposit contains a blinded evaluation matrix covering 20 instructional items across four thematic clusters: Basic Machine Learning, Advanced Neural Architectures, Applied Modeling, and Socio-Technical Implications. Each item was evaluated under two experimental conditions: (A) DIINA-refined outputs and (B) baseline outputs. These comparisons yielded 40 blinded case–condition units. Two raters evaluated each unit using a five-point Likert scale across four dimensions: Technical Accuracy, Pedagogical Quality, Linguistic Accessibility, and Fairness/Accountability. The resulting dataset contains 80 rating records with no missing values. The deposit includes: (1) the evaluation matrix in Excel format, including the blinded evaluation sheet; (2) the rating protocol and rubric definitions; (3) an inter-rater agreement audit and descriptive agreement summary; and (4) documentation of the item-generation and refinement workflow. Methodological note: The two raters assigned identical scores across all 40 case–condition units in each of the four rated dimensions. The resulting ICC point estimates were 1.000, with an estimated residual mean square of zero. Because this pattern creates limitations for conventional F-based inference and confidence-interval estimation, confidence intervals and F-based significance tests are not reported as inferential results. The perfect observed agreement is reported descriptively and should be interpreted cautiously. It may reflect protocol-driven calibration, shared rating anchors, or pilot-level data-generation procedures rather than independent, naturalistic rating variation. This dataset is released to support methodological transparency and reproducibility of the pilot workflow.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Firms increasingly track how often large language models (LLMs) and AI answer engines mention, rank and recommend their brands, yet the audits behind these “AI visibility” metrics reach conflicting conclusions. This scoping review, reported under PRISMA-ScR, maps 38 empirical studies (2024–2026) that query LLMs and measure outcomes at the brand or business level, and appraises them against nine measurement-validity criteria drawn from marketing measurement theory. The evidence base is young and fragile: 35 studies are not peer reviewed, half come from authors with commercial stakes in visibility services, and two vendor groups account for 12 papers. Few studies validate scores against external brand or market benchmarks (2) or repeat measurement over time (7), and results are sensitive to paraphrasing, query language and the number of draws. Drawing on consideration-set theory, I propose a two-stage account that can reconcile many apparent contradictions: inclusion in an answer (membership) appears to track how extensively a brand is documented online, while selection among included brands may be more responsive to attribute evidence, a conjecture the evidence supports only partly. Designs that supply a candidate list observe only selection. Six propositions and a minimum design and reporting standard for brand-visibility audits follow.
evidence_items.title: Measuring brands in machine answers: A scoping review and validity framework for large language model brand-visibility audits

evidence_items.summary: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) requires sustained patient education, self-management, medication use, pulmonary rehabilitation, symptom monitoring, and guideline-concordant clinical management. Large language models (LLMs) may expand access to conversational health information, but their value depends on more than factual accuracy. Objective: To map empirical evidence on LLMs and LLM-based generative artificial intelligence systems in COPD-related care and health management, summarize application domains and evaluation outcomes, and identify priorities for future research. Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported using PRISMA-ScR. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched from inception through September 10, 2026. Empirical studies evaluating an LLM or LLM-based generative AI system in COPD-related patient education, health information, pulmonary rehabilitation, medication management, or guideline-based clinical management were eligible. Data were charted and synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results: The search identified 327 records; 34 duplicates were removed, and 293 records underwent title/abstract screening. Of these, 281 were excluded, and 12 full-text reports were assessed. Four full-text reports were excluded, leaving eight studies. Five studies focused primarily on patient education or health information, one on pulmonary rehabilitation, one on COPD medication management, and one on guideline-based clinical management. Accuracy and information quality were the most common outcomes. LLMs often produced clinically acceptable responses, but limitations included incomplete information, high reading grade levels, outdated guideline references, response variability, and differences across models and task formats.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Care and Health Management: A Scoping Review

evidence_items.summary: Predicting ship turnaround time at ports is an operationally valuable regression problem on heterogeneous, text-rich tabular data. We ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can match purpose-built Machine Learning (ML) on this task, using a leakage-controlled pipeline over seven years of Brazilian (ANTAQ) data. On a fixed 200-berthing test set, with 20 seeds and seed-paired statistics (Wilcoxon, Cohen’s d), we compare five families that read the same cases: classical ML on engineered tabular features plus multilingual sentence embeddings; frontier LLMs (Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-V3) prompted zero-, 5and 20-shot; a small generative LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B) fine-tuned on 100–6000 serialized records; an encoder with a regression head fine-tuned on 100–12000 records; and a tabular foundation model (TabFM) reading the raw table in-context. Tuned XGBoost attains R2 ≈ 0.73. Every prompted configuration stays at R2 ≤ 0 and in-context examples do not help; generative fine-tuning barely clears zero, reaching only R2 ≈ 0.10 at 6000 examples. The encoder is the only text regime to rise substantially above R2 = 0, reaching ≈ 0.43 at 12000 examples yet still trailing all ML. In contrast, TabFM, with no task training, matches or beats a data-matched XGBoost at every budget (100–6000; R2 up to ≈ 0.60), leading the low-data regime, though full-data XGBoost still wins and TabFM is far costlier at inference. The predictive signal is tabular, not textual: text-only LLMs miss it, whereas a tabular foundation model recovers it in-context and engineered boosting wins at scale.
evidence_items.title: Traditional Machine Learning versus Large Language Models for Predicting Ship Turnaround Times at Brazilian Ports

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can translate ambiguous requirements into executable tests whose assertions conflict with the accepted behavior. Evaluating such tests requires distinguishing behavioral compatibility from fault-detection strength. Methods We present ReqTestAgent, an execution-grounded workflow that connects requirement interpretation, testing-knowledge retrieval, test generation, and feedback from canonical execution and mutation testing. We evaluate 100 requirement instances formed from 25 Orchid/BigCodeBench tasks, each with lexical, semantic, syntactic, and vagueness variants, using a reference implementation available to the evaluator. Comparisons include three generation baselines, their verifier-enhanced counterparts, and component ablations. Results The generation baselines fail the canonical implementation on 51%–68% of instances, whereas all verifier-enhanced methods achieve 100% canonical pass. ReqTestAgent achieves 92% qualified suites and a macro-averaged effective mutation score of 0.678, compared with 0.655–0.670 for the verifier-enhanced baselines. Removing verification reduces its effective score to 0.216. Across instance–mutant evaluations, ReqTestAgent kills 492 of 756 mutants, a pooled rate of 0.651; this rate weights instances by their mutant counts. A comparative execution trace shows how explicit domain assertions detect faults missed by the verifier-enhanced baselines. Discussion Execution feedback provides the principal validity improvement in this controlled setting. The workflow links interpretation records to executable checks, while the evaluation establishes canonical compatibility as a prerequisite for interpreting mutation-based test strength.
evidence_items.title: ReqTestAgent: execution-grounded language-model agents for acceptance testing under requirement ambiguity

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic in the United States has been a major public health crisis. We developed OUD-REY ( OUD R isk E valuator at 1 Y ear) - a deep learning model that uses longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data from the All of Us research program to predict risk of OUD at one year for patients with an opioid prescription. On internal validation, OUD-REY achieved an AUROC of 91.2% and AUPRC of 77.0%. We leveraged a pretrained language model to accommodate thousands of unseen, out-of-vocabulary clinical features in a patient’s longitudinal EHR history. We externally validated our model on a new dataset released by All of Us that was temporally separated from our development set and on a dataset containing ~6 million patients from medical centers of the Veterans Affairs (VA) nationwide over a span of 20 years. On external validation, our model had an AUROC and AUPRC of 86.4% and 23.1% (OUD prevalence of 2.9%), respectively, on our temporally separated All of Us validation set. It had an AUROC and AUPRC of 85.5% and 19.5% (OUD prevalence of 3.5%), respectively, on the VA dataset. Our fairness auditing showed that the model was generally fair for patients with different genders, race, and ethnic backgrounds. This model may potentially improve prevention and care of OUD.
evidence_items.title: A generalizable deep learning model for predicting opioid use disorder using language modeling for cross-EHR data harmonization

evidence_items.summary: Assessment is most powerful when understood as a leadership-driven process of continuous improvement—iterative, evidence-informed, and oriented toward genuine learning rather than compliance. However, the coordination costs of meaningful assessment have historically exceeded most programs’ capacity to sustain it. This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, and in particular retrieval-augmented reasoning environments, can function as leadership-support tools that change the conditions under which assessment becomes practically feasible without displacing the human judgment it requires. Drawing on leadership education and assessment scholarship, we develop a three-level framework—individual and course, program, and institutional—and present six practice-based use cases illustrating AI-supported assessment at each level, including an AI-populated curriculum alignment matrix and an AI-assisted synthesis of external program reviews. We also directly address the tensions practitioners must navigate: data contamination from AI-generated student work, reliability-validity trade-offs, the limitations of AI detection tools, and the faculty professional development gap. Implications for assessment leaders are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Leading Continuous Improvement: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Assessment in Higher Education

evidence_items.summary: Avaliar modelos de linguagem em domínios específicos, como o Direito do Consumidor, é um desafio devido à escassez de recursos padronizados em português brasileiro. Para resolver esse problema, introduzimos o OABench-Consumidor, um benchmark composto exclusivamente por questões de Direito do Consumidor da primeira fase do Exame de Ordem Unificado (OAB), cobrindo as edições de 2010.1 a 2025.2. Este artigo descreve a coleta e a estruturação dos dados. Além disso, a utilidade do benchmark é demonstrada através da avaliação do modelo fundacional Qwen3-8B e de uma versão ajustada. O modelo especializado obteve 64,84% de acurácia (59/91), superando os 51,65% (47/91) do modelo base. O benchmark oferece um recurso direto para avaliar sistemas de Inteligência Artificial nessa subárea do Direito.
evidence_items.title: OABench-Consumidor: Um benchmark para avaliação de modelos de linguagem em Direito do Consumidor

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Contamination by microplastics is an emerging environmental problem that is widely distributed across continental aquatic environments and may cause ecological impacts. This study evaluated the occurrence, concentration, and chemical and morphological characteristics of microplastics in surface waters and sediments from Lake Canaçari, comparing two areas with different land-use patterns within a floodplain system in the Central Amazon. Microplastics were detected in all sampled areas. In surface water, concentrations ranged from 0 (no microplastic particles detected in one sample) to 1,000 microplastics·m⁻ 3 (405 ± 298 microplastics·m⁻ 3 ), while in sediments, they ranged from 7 to 307 microplastics·kg⁻ 1 (77 ± 104 microplastics·kg⁻ 1 ). No significant differences in microplastic concentrations were observed between fishing and human-settlement areas. The particles were predominantly blue fibers (< 1,000 μm). Among the spectroscopically analyzed particles, polyethylene was the most frequently identified polymer, while copper phthalocyanine pigments, including Pigment Blue 15 and Pigment Green 7, were also detected by FTIR and/or Raman spectroscopy. Overall, the results suggest that Lake Canaçari may act as a transport pathway, redistribution zone, and retention compartment for microplastics; however, seasonal sampling is needed to confirm how these processes vary throughout the hydrological cycle. These results reinforce the role of Amazonian floodplain systems in the regional dynamics of microplastics and highlight the need for monitoring and management strategies that incorporate seasonal hydrological connectivity at the basin scale.
evidence_items.title: Microplastic contamination in surface water and sediments of Lake Canaçari, Central Amazon, during the dry season

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Preserving historical analogue seismograms and observational documents is vital for maintaining an accurate, long-term record of regional seismic activity and safeguarding irreplaceable information on seismic past events. Historically shaped by shifting political eras, resource constraints, and changing technological paradigms, Romanian seismology relies heavily on systematic conservation to bridge early observations with modern digital monitoring systems. This study presents the ongoing efforts to inventory and preserve the legacy seismological records stored at the Timisoara Seismological Observatory, covering six key historical stations in southwestern Romania: Timisoara (TIM), Susara (SSR), Gura Zlata (GZR), Buzias (BZS), Banloc (BANR), and Siria (SIRR). Out of an estimated 150,000 analogue records (smoked paper, photographic paper, and ink on paper), over 58,000 ink-on-paper seismograms spanning 1977–2017 have been chronologically sorted and catalogued into the Heritage Legacy Inventory of Seismograms in Romania (HELIOS-R). Furthermore, high-resolution scans (1200 dpi) and standardized metadata were generated for 45 seismograms corresponding to 17 nuclear explosion tests (1979–1992) to contribute missing southwestern Romanian data to the Nuclear Explosion Legacy Data (NELD) repository. These systematic preservation initiatives ensure uninterrupted data continuity, enrich national and international databases, and provide crucial data for re-evaluating historical events, refining seismic hazard assessments, and conducting global nuclear monitoring research.
evidence_items.title: Saving Legacy Seismological Data for South-Western Romania

evidence_items.summary: This study presents an integrated pipeline that transforms anomaly-detection outputs from global fitness-market data into data-faithful narratives. Using a 132-country panel and a 2019 baseline, we analyze observed post-COVID-19 recovery through 2025, while treating 2026 only as a modelled extension. Four complementary detectors—regional-median deviations, linear-regression residuals, Random Forest residuals, and Isolation Forest—are combined through method agreement and mapped to a rule-based typology. A deterministic, template-based Natural Language Generation (NLG) component then produces short, medium, and complete explanations from tabular evidence. In 2025, 14 countries were consensus anomalies; Guyana exemplified market growth without participatory expansion, with revenue recovery of +401.43%, participation recovery of -2.06%, and a 403.50-point gap. All 132 narratives passed automatic factual-consistency checks. These checks validate field preservation rather than fluency, usefulness, or explanatory quality; human evaluation remains future work.
evidence_items.title: Data-Faithful Natural Language Generation for Explaining Fitness-Market Anomalies

evidence_items.summary: Diagnosing production incidents is still largely manual: on-call engineers gather logs, errors and deployment history from separate tools before they can reason about a cause. Large language models (LLMs) can suggest root causes, but a model that sees only an incident summary lacks evidence, and an unchecked suggestion can mislead. This paper aims to give an LLM agent the evidence it needs while keeping a human in control. We present Phase 1 of an open, four-module platform: a non-blocking Java SDK that captures exceptions, latency and deployments; a multi-tenant Spring Boot backend that groups repeated errors into incidents by stack hash; a FastAPI service in which a tool-calling LLM investigates each incident only through audited APIs; and a dashboard where an operator approves or rejects every suggestion. We evaluate it by injecting seven kinds of real faults into an instrumented service. All 21 trials were detected, with mean detection times of 8–12 s for exception faults and 25–45 s for resource faults, and no incident was raised in 8 min of fault-free operation. The SDK added a median of 14 µs per captured error and stayed non-blocking when the backend was down. A successful investigation used about 11k–24k tokens and two to three minutes; of five graded suggestions, two were correct, two partly correct and one wrong despite a confidence of 0.78. The results show that telemetry-grounded investigation is practical for small teams, and that self-reported confidence must not replace human review.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Incident Response Platform for Cloud Applications: Telemetry-Grounded Root-Cause Investigation with Human Approval
Evaluation of Natural Lightscape Perception in Suzhou Garden Architecture

evidence_items.summary: Alopecia areata (AA) is an autoimmune condition that results in hair loss, significantly impacting quality of life. As TikTok emerges as a major platform for health-related information, concerns about the spread of misinformation have arisen. This cross-sectional study aims to evaluate the quality, reliability, and understandability of “most liked” AA-related TikTok videos. Videos were categorized as healthcare providers (HP) or non-healthcare providers (NHP). Two reviewers independently assessed the videos, using validated tools – Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for audiovisual content (PEMAT A/V), modified DISCERN (mDISCERN), Video Information and Quality Index (VIQI), Global Quality Scale (GQS), and AloCheck, a study-specific content-coverage tool. Among 93 included videos, only 26% were created by HPs, who scored significantly higher across all quality metrics: mDISCERN (3.0 vs. 1.5, p<0.01), GQS (3.5 vs. 1.5, p<0.01), VIQI (13.75 vs. 11.0, p<0.01), and PEMAT A/V (≥10: 66.7% vs. 26.1%, p<0.01). HPs focused on clinical aspects (87.5% vs. 40.6%, p<0.01), whereas NHPs emphasized psychological aspects, such as body image (37.5% vs. 63.8%, p=0.02). Findings reveal a gap between quality and user engagement, highlighting the risk that lower-quality information reaches a wide audience. Bridging this gap is essential to support the delivery of high-quality, reliable, and engaging health information to the public.
evidence_items.title: Cross-sectional evaluation of TikTok video quality on alopecia areata
Reliability Evaluation under Delta Shock Model for Dependent Intershock Times

evidence_items.summary: Visual grounding aims to localize the image regions based on a textual query. Given the difficulty of large-scale data curation, we investigate how to effectively learn visual grounding under data-scarce settings in this paper. To address the data scarcity, we propose a novel framework, POBF (Paint Outside the Box and Filter). POBF synthesizes images by inpainting outside the box, tackling a label misalignment issue encountered in previous works. Furthermore, POBF leverages an innovative filtering scheme to select the most effective training data. This scheme combines a hardness score and an overfitting score, balanced by a penalty term. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets demonstrate that POBF consistently improves performance, achieving an average gain of 5.83\% over the real-data-only method and outperforming leading baselines by 2.29\%-3.85\% in accuracy. Additionally, we validate the robustness and generalizability of POBF across various generative models, training data sizes, and model architectures.
evidence_items.title: Paint Outside the Box: Synthesizing and Selecting Training Data for Visual Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Due to privacy restrictions, there's a shortage of publicly available speech recognition datasets in the medical domain. In this work, we present VietMed - a Vietnamese speech recognition dataset in the medical domain comprising 16h of labeled medical speech, 1000h of unlabeled medical speech and 1200h of unlabeled general-domain speech. To our best knowledge, VietMed is by far the world's largest public medical speech recognition dataset in 7 aspects: total duration, number of speakers, diseases, recording conditions, speaker roles, unique medical terms and accents. VietMed is also by far the largest public Vietnamese speech dataset in terms of total duration. Additionally, we are the first to present a medical ASR dataset covering all ICD-10 disease groups and all accents within a country. Moreover, we release the first public large-scale pre-trained models for Vietnamese ASR, w2v2-Viet and XLSR-53-Viet, along with the first public large-scale fine-tuned models for medical ASR. Even without any medical data in unsupervised pre-training, our best pre-trained model XLSR-53-Viet generalizes very well to the medical domain by outperforming state-of-the-art XLSR-53, from 51.8% to 29.6% WER on test set (a relative reduction of more than 40%). All code, data and models are made publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/MultiMed/tree/master/VietMed.
evidence_items.title: VietMed: A Dataset and Benchmark for Automatic Speech Recognition of Vietnamese in the Medical Domain

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are usually chosen from leaderboards, which give one ranking for every application. On questions about objects that a scene suggests but does not contain, however, the model with the lowest error on the POPE hallucination benchmark is not the one with the lowest error on such questions. For yes/no questions about object presence, we show that the best model for a target domain can be predicted without running any candidate on that domain, given 650 to 1,200 labeled target items that calibrate a detector. We measure each model's reliance on a cue, a feature such as scene context or text in the image, by editing 100 labeled source images so that the cue suggests the wrong answer, and comparing with a matched control edit. Reliance predicts which VLMs are misled by physical sticker attacks (Spearman .93 on nine models not used to design the score) and which hallucinate on unedited COCO photographs, beyond what their tendency to answer yes explains. Shift-Reliance Alignment (SRA) scores a model by its source error on the labeled source questions plus its reliance multiplied by the shift. The shift is the proportion of target questions on which the cue misleads, and a detector estimates it on the unlabeled target images. SRA selects the model with the lowest score. In pre-registered tests on new images where most questions mislead, it lowered the error of the selected model from 30.4% under selection by source error to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages but, against its prediction, not on COCO. On CueDial, a benchmark we release that varies how often a cue misleads, selection by model confidence falls more than 40 percentage points behind the best model when overlaid text denies a visible object, and SRA stays within 3 points.
evidence_items.title: Shift-Reliance Alignment: Ranking Vision-Language Models by the Cues They Trust

evidence_items.summary: Description This dataset provides an evaluation set for single-image Centre-of-Figure (CoF) estimation of small and large Solar System bodies. It contains 5,000 synthetic grayscale images at a resolution of 2048 × 1536 pixels, with 1,000 images each of Itokawa, Bennu, Apophis, the Moon, and Mars. The dataset accompanies the paper "Prior Knowledge-Informed Centroiding CNN for Planetary and Small Bodies Navigation" (SPAICE 2026) and is released to support reproducible evaluation and comparison of centroiding methods on a common set of images. Dataset structure and usage The dataset is distributed as one ZIP archive per target body. Each archive contains: camera.yml: Camera parameters images/: Synthetic grayscale images labels/: Per-image annotations and scene metadata The release also includes: README.md: Dataset documentation, conventions, and usage instructions dataset manifest.yml: Dataset manifest (for versioning and source tracking) checksums sha256.txt: SHA-256 checksums for integrity verification LICENSE: Licensing information CITATION.cff: Citation metadata film centroiding model.onnx: The FiLM model evaluated in the associated paper, exported to ONNX A standalone Python loader based on NumPy, with an optional PyTorch Dataset interface and support for constructing the conditioning inputs used by the FiLM-based model described in the associated paper. The requirements.txt lists the python packages required to work with it. The README, loader, the onnx model and the additional metadata files are provided separately from the ZIP archives for direct access.
evidence_items.title: Prior Knowledge-Informed Centroiding CNN for Planetary and Small Bodies Navigation: Evaluation Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Existing evaluation benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) do not adequately capture the professional knowledge, normative constraints, and engineering calculations that characterize the electric power sector. Here we introduce PowerGLUE, a domain-specific benchmark for evaluating LLMs in this sector. PowerGLUE covers the six core business sectors of power systems, namely generation, transmission, transformation, distribution, dispatching, and electricity consumption, and consists of two complementary task categories, knowledge question answering and reasoning calculation, organized into seven subtasks. It is constructed from authoritative sources, including technical standards, registered electrical engineer examination questions, textbooks, and engineering cases, followed by a multi-stage quality-control process that combines automated verification and expert review; the current version contains 3,603 items. We evaluate seven representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across models, task types, and business sectors. Under the current item composition and scoring protocol, exact-match accuracy is generally higher on the reasoning-calculation track than on the knowledge-question-answering track, a pattern that suggests measurable differences between the two tracks, although differences in item difficulty and composition preclude direct causal attribution to knowledge or reasoning ability. PowerGLUE provides a systematic framework for examining the capabilities and boundaries of LLMs in safety-critical power applications.
evidence_items.title: PowerGLUE: A comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models in the electric power domain

organizations: Chinese University of Hong Kong Shenzhen
University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) may support hearing care, but evidence of clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a scoping review across eight databases, with searches updated in September 2026. Among 110 included reports, 95 empirical analysis units comprised 62 model-centered benchmarks, 31 application-oriented investigations, and two adoption surveys. Applications addressed assessment scoring, clinical documentation, rehabilitation content, biomedical evidence processing, psychosocial support, and research. Fourteen empirical units evaluated prototypes or target users; none tested prospective service deployment or comparative clinical impact. Privacy evaluation concerned attitudes or perceived confidentiality; no included study tested technical privacy safeguards. Current evidence supports selected task-specific capabilities, not established improvements in care. Future research should prioritize applications addressing defined hearing-care needs and compare them with usual care or simpler alternatives. Evaluation should measure patient and professional benefit, safety, privacy, accessibility, and workload rather than response accuracy alone.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models in Hearing Care

organizations: The Third People's Hospital of Yongzhou
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Pregnancy-related cardiometabolic complications remain important contributors to adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. However, risk-prediction models developed from a single dataset often have limited transportability, and the role of large language models in maternal risk stratification remains unclear. Methods We used two publicly available datasets: the Maternal Health Risk dataset and the Preeclampsia in Pregnant Women dataset. Low-risk, mid-risk, and high-risk labels were harmonised, and a binary high-risk versus non-high-risk endpoint was constructed. We compared several machine-learning models and undertook internal cross-validation, external validation, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and sensitivity analyses. Structured records were subsequently converted into label-free case narratives; DeepSeek and Qwen were evaluated under different prompting strategies, and the concordance between keywords in large language model explanations and machine-learning feature importance was examined. Results In internal validation, HistGradientBoosting showed the strongest overall performance, with a macro-averaged F1 score of approximately 0.876. Performance declined in external validation, in which multiclass accuracy was approximately 0.389. Across sensitivity analyses, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.437 to 0.528. Among the large language model configurations, Qwen with few-shot chain-of-thought prompting performed best, with an accuracy of approximately 0.583 and a macro-averaged F1 score of approximately 0.467. Explanatory keywords generated by the large language models most often concerned blood glucose or diabetes, blood pressure or hypertension, haemoglobin or anaemia, previous complications or medical history, and proteinuria.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning and Large Language Models for Maternal Cardiometabolic Risk Prediction Across Harmonised Public Pregnancy Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate health education materials, but their suitability for patient‐facing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) education remains insufficiently evaluated. We assessed the information quality, understandability, actionability, readability, text structure and source transparency of HIV patient education materials generated by six LLMs or artificial intelligence platforms. Methods In this cross‐sectional study, 100 common HIV patient education questions across 10 domains were submitted once in English to ChatGPT 5.4‐Thinking, DeepSeek‐V3.2, Doubao, ERNIE Bot 5.0 Preview, Ant Afu and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding 600 responses. Responses were evaluated using Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT‐P), EQ IP‐36, DISCERN, Global Quality Score (GQS), artificial intelligence response quality metric (AIRM), Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmarks and seven readability indices. Platform comparisons used paired Friedman tests with Wilcoxon–Holm post hoc analyses; topic analyses used question‐level aggregation followed by Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn–Holm comparisons. Results Significant family‐adjusted differences were observed across platforms for all prespecified text‐structure, quality/understandability/actionability and readability outcomes. At the topic level, five of six text‐structure outcomes, PEMAT‐P Understandability, PEMAT‐P Actionability, the exploratory PEMAT‐P composite score and all seven readability indices differed significantly after family adjustment, whereas EQ IP‐36, DISCERN, GQS, AIRM and JAMA did not. Overall actionability was limited and readability demands were high. Conclusions LLM‐generated HIV patient education materials showed substantial cross‐platform and topic‐level heterogeneity. These findings support the use of LLMs as expert‐reviewed drafting tools rather than independent patient education sources.
evidence_items.title:
Information quality, understandability, actionability and readability of large language models for
                    <scp>HIV</scp>
                    health education: A cross‐platform evaluation
