evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background Muscle ultrasound offers a portable, non‐invasive, and cost‐effective option for sarcopenia assessment, but operator dependency limits its standardization. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help automate and improve ultrasound‐based muscle evaluation. This scoping review aims to map the current landscape of AI‐assisted ultrasound for sarcopenia assessment, including research trends, methods, clinical uses and performance, and to suggest future work. Methods Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines and the PRISMA‐ScR checklist, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, ProQuest, CNKI, WanFang Data, Yiigle, VIP, and Sinomed up to July 25, 2026. Two researchers independently selected studies and extracted data. Results Thirty studies were included. This field is developing rapidly, with 76.7% of studies published in the last 3 years, primarily from Spain and China. Model development and validation studies (43.3%) were most common. U‐Net and its variants were the predominant AI architectures, mainly for image segmentation. B‐mode ultrasound with high‐frequency linear probes was frequently used. The rectus femoris was the most assessed muscle for sarcopenia (73.3%). AI‐integrated models for sarcopenia diagnosis achieved AUCs of 0.640–0.950. Reported Dice coefficients for muscle segmentation ranged from 0.73 to 0.99. In‐house datasets were used in 66.7% of the studies, and global classification labels were the most frequent annotation strategy (46.7%). Conclusions AI‐assisted ultrasound shows potential for objective and scalable sarcopenia assessment but remains early‐stage. Operator dependency in image acquisition has not been fully resolved. Further investigation should determine the added value of integrating multimodal imaging, combining diverse AI techniques, and evaluating multiple muscle groups.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Ultrasound for Sarcopenia Assessment: A Scoping Review

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Trustworthy Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is often treated as a model property addressed through better training data, alignment, evaluation or guardrails. We argue instead that trustworthiness is a lifecycle governance capability that must be engineered, evidenced, monitored and adapted across data acquisition, training and alignment, safe inference, public deployment and post‐deployment use. We develop a lifecycle engineering framework integrating four governance layers – technical, organizational, human‐centred and regulatory – and translate ethical principles and major governance instruments into stage‐specific controls, responsibilities, evidence artefacts, metrics and review triggers. The framework is constructed through a structured conceptual synthesis of peer‐reviewed literature, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, ISO/IEC 42005, ALTAI, the EU AI Act and complementary security and agentic‐governance guidance. A source register, seven‐field extraction schema, explicit mapping rules, worked extraction example and weighting sensitivity analysis make the construction logic inspectable. A public‐facing retrieval‐augmented generation case and a contrastive agentic‐system stress test illustrate operationalization through measurable indicators, responsible actors, review triggers and capability boundaries without being presented as independent empirical validation. We further address hallucination, prompt injection, privacy leakage, overreliance, unsafe tool use, memory, planners and multi‐agent workflows. The perspective positions trustworthy GenAI as an evidence‐driven, adaptive socio‐technical capability rather than a one‐time model or compliance claim.
evidence_items.title: Ethics and Governance in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Lifecycle Engineering Perspective

evidence_items.summary: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has further heightened the need to develop dependable AI-generated text detection, especially beyond English. Nevertheless, current benchmarks pay little attention to Indic languages and test detectors in idealized settings that do not represent the real world. We present a generalized benchmark for AI-generated text detection in Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil, which we call IndicDetect, designed to assess the robustness of detectors under realistic distribution shifts. IndicDetect comprises highly curated human-written texts matched with LLM-generated counterparts across various domains and generators, and systematically evaluates detectors in the presence of domain shift, generator shift, and adversarial perturbation. Using a single and repeatable evaluation scheme, we evaluate a wide range of statistical and neural detectors. We find substantial robustness failures: supervised neural detectors perform well in-distribution, while training-free methods degrade considerably under unseen generators and adversarial attacks. The severity of these failures varies across languages, with Hindi exhibiting the largest overall degradation under adversarial perturbations. These results highlight that the primary weakness of existing detectors in Indic settings lies in their robustness, not in their peak accuracy. IndicDetect provides standard data splits, an evaluation protocol, and baselines to establish a robust, language-aware foundation for AI-generated text detection in Indic scripts.
evidence_items.title: IndicDetect: Evaluating Cross-Lingual LLM-Generated Text Detection for Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil

evidence_items.summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made significant strides in visual comprehension, their ability to reason about text-dense, professional documents remains incompletely evaluated. Existing benchmarks emphasize information extraction, require external domain knowledge, or cover professional documents only as one of many settings. They are also largely English- or Chinese-centric, leaving other languages and Russian, in particular, substantially underrepresented. To address these limitations, we introduce BEAR-Bench (Bilingual Enterprise and Academic Reasoning), a self-contained, complex English-and-Russian benchmark comprising 1000 human-annotated questions based on text-rich business and scientific documents. We evaluate 16 proprietary and open-weight MLLMs, including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen3.5-397B, on BEAR-Bench and observe clear headroom even for the strongest systems. Finally, we use the resulting model outputs to compare existing hallucination detection methods, evaluating not only how often models fail on BEAR-Bench but also how reliably those failures can be identified.
evidence_items.title: BEAR-Bench: A Bilingual Enterprise and Academic Reasoning Benchmark for Multimodal Models

evidence_items.summary: Background manipulation is a practical but under-specified image-forensics setting: the manipulated evidence can sit outside the salient foreground object, while many evaluations emphasize object-centric copy-move, splicing, or generic synthetic edits. We introduce BG-REAL, a public real-data anchored benchmark package for background manipulation detection and localization. The current release is built from Open Images V7 instance-segmentation sources and contains 7,000 processed samples over 1,200 source groups, including 6,000 public-data anchored samples and 1,000 synthetic control samples. BG-REAL covers six edit families, matched authentic controls, source-group splits, mask and leakage QA, 599 human-assisted quality-control rows, three completed external baselines (TruFor, MVSS-Net, and HiFi-Net), and five-seed model evaluation. Beyond aggregate accuracy, we use matched-authentic-control diagnostics to measure how often baselines misclassify re-encoded authentic images as manipulated at a threshold fixed on held-out validation data; false-positive rates range from 0.57 (TruFor, the lowest) to 1.00 (several weak or mask-informed baselines), indicating that re-encoding artifacts are a shared shortcut risk across baselines rather than a problem specific to any one model. The release provides the construction pipeline, evaluation protocol, paper-ready figures, and reproduction documentation. We frame BG-REAL as a background-manipulation-focused complement to general image-manipulation-localization benchmarks, not as a fully real-only or general-purpose benchmark.
evidence_items.title: BG-REAL: A Public Real-Data Anchored Benchmark for Background Manipulation Detection and Localization

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning-based nuclei analysis in histopathology relies heavily on large-scale, expert-curated datasets that are costly and difficult to scale across organs. To address this, we propose a scalable framework leveraging cell-level spatial transcriptomics (ST) as an alternative supervision source for nuclei classification. Cell-level ST provides both gene expression profiles and nucleus masks, enabling automatic generation of image-label pairs without manual annotation. We convert gene expression into cell-type labels and introduce an image-oriented classification strategy to effectively transfer these identities to histopathology images. Evaluated on unseen tissues, our framework achieves comparable segmentation and classification performance compared with conventional supervised approaches, despite using fewer manually annotated datasets.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Cell-level Spatial Transcriptomics as Weak Supervision for Nuclei Classification

evidence_items.summary: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models
evidence_items.title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals

evidence_items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode: a goal-directed builder and an exists-forall search, each followed by an independent gate. From the rules of Steinberg's problem it rebuilds the gadgets of the 2016 counterexample of Cohen-Addad, Hebdige, Král', Li and Salgado; it finds nothing on Erdős's question for cycles of length 4 to 6. Layer towers of depth one to three, a ladder and a mesh, are compared with the crossing loop at the same number of checks. A Hodge-only run of twelve rounds leaves every target point at the same gap. None of the five benchmark problems (the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture, Erdős problem 1183) is solved. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
evidence_items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

evidence_items.summary: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, making it better aligned with human-AI collaborative creation than single-turn editing. However, constructing high-quality multi-turn training data remains challenging, as conventional sequential rollout accumulates errors and introduces visual-quality drift across editing turns. To address this challenge, we introduce MTEdit, a multi-turn image editing dataset built through a pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. By jointly generating multiple editing states within a unified visual context, this pipeline reduces visual-quality drift across turns. Covering both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios, MTEdit comprises 500K multi-turn image editing trajectories, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, making it one of the most extensive datasets for multi-turn image editing. We further introduce MTEdit-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate both scenarios by assessing models' ability to follow editing instructions, maintain content consistency, resist visual-quality drift, and effectively use historical context across turns. Using MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. On MTEdit-Bench, we evaluate a broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Experimental results show that Qwen-Image-MTEdit achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving models' multi-turn image editing capabilities.
evidence_items.title: MTEdit: Packed Trajectories Beat Rollouts for Multi-Turn Image Editing

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating agents by outcomes alone can obscure the capabilities that produce them. This problem is especially pronounced in evolving environments, where outcomes reflect a closed-loop interaction between agent behavior and changing external conditions. We introduce LiveMACEBench, a process-aware benchmark that uses live financial markets as a naturally evolving testbed for persistent LLM agents. Five frontier LLMs operate along continuous trajectories under matched Tool Use, Persistent Memory, Rule Following, and Multi-Agent Collaboration configurations. We evaluate them through both realized outcomes and mechanism-specific diagnostics derived from complete decision traces. Across 30 days of live evaluation, we find a pronounced outcome-capability gap: realized returns often diverge from capability-specific measurements, and similar outcomes can arise from markedly different patterns of mechanism use. Trace-level diagnostics further expose distinct bottlenecks across capabilities, demonstrating that mechanism access, effective mechanism use, and downstream performance are not interchangeable measures of agent capability. LiveMACEBench makes this distinction measurable, turning live markets from a performance leaderboard into a diagnostic environment for agent capability
evidence_items.title: LiveMACE: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agent Capabilities in Evolving Markets

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.
evidence_items.title: PRISM: PRIvileged Sibling-guided Multi-Agent Topology Design

METASURFACE-GUIDED MICROROBOTIC CONTROL AT THE LIMIT STARLI | Institute XXIV | Flagship 14 of 30 | Research Group B This prospective research monograph asks when phase-gradient metasurfaces can become reliable optical-control infrastructure for microscopic agents rather than merely generating visually persuasive multifocal wavefronts. Its central research coupling combines metasurface phase-gradient engineering, independently verified optical-field and force shaping, and robust multi-agent positioning under realistic manufacturing, polarization, thermal and task constraints. The investigation follows a falsifiable route from vector electromagnetic interface models and fabricated nanoantenna tolerances to calibrated force and thermofluid attribution, Brownian particle motion, multi-agent collision risk, optical tracking, safe control fallback and cross-batch replication. Ghost foci and polarization drift are treated as testable safety hazards. The strongest conventional benchmarks are optimized spatial light modulators and matched microlens arrays evaluated at equal delivered optical dose, throughput, tracking quality and thermal limits. A metasurface is judged by independently confirmed task completion, not by diffraction efficiency or wavefront quality alone. The manuscript is structured as 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 research chapters with five separately paginated sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. External DOI literature, a four-monograph intellectual lineage and a companion Excel evidence atlas support traceable source navigation and successor-led experiments. The monograph retains negative-result routes: if classical optics provide equal control with lower total risk or cost, that is a meaningful scientific conclusion. The work does not assert a verified autonomous microrobot, a demonstrated multi-agent industrial controller, or a discovered physical law. It is a research architecture that proposes mechanisms, prospective tests, alternative explanations, independent measurements and stopping criteria. Literature from atom trapping, integrated phased arrays and optical force inverse design is explicitly treated as contextual evidence rather than a demonstration of fluidic microrobot autonomy.

evidence_items.summary: Description Internal-dataset-variant-extraction is an English biomedical text dataset curated for structured genetic variant extraction. The dataset consists of manually selected passages from biomedical articles retrieved through LitVar, chosen to enrich the study corpus with additional examples of genetic variant mentions and their surrounding textual context. Each record contains a text passage and manually curated variant annotations represented as gene–variant pairs. The dataset is intended to support research on biomedical named entity recognition, genomic variant extraction, gene–variant association extraction, and structured literature mining with language models. In its current version, the dataset contains 20 passages, including 19 passages with annotated variants and 1 negative passage, with 180 annotated gene–variant pairs covering 159 unique variant strings and 19 unique gene symbols. The dataset was used as an internal resource in experiments on adapting small language models for structured genetic variant extraction.

evidence_items.summary: AI agents increasingly use files and software tools to produce professional deliverables. Such work draws on materials, decisions, and feedback accumulated across assignments. We introduce OfficeTown, a generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which tasks and their context arise from continuing organizational work. From a natural-language description of an organization's purpose and activities, OfficeTown initializes an organization whose members coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters persist and shape subsequent work, while responsibilities and permissions determine what each member can see and do. We curate work requests, their context, and review feedback into executable resources for evaluation and learning. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback. Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom. Supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation on OfficeTown data substantially improve Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval. Supplementary evaluations show that the principal--assistant harness achieves higher scores than the single- and multi-agent baselines tested. These results highlight the value of organizational simulation in generating work-grounded data and environments for the continued development of generalist agents.
evidence_items.title: OfficeTown: Generative Organizations for Evolving Agent Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.
evidence_items.title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct SciΠvot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while SciΠvot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.
evidence_items.title: SciΠvot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents

evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions? To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas. Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the question. A 20-criterion Atomic Score measures local scientific accomplishment, while Research Closure (RC0--RC4) assesses how fully the investigation resolves the specified research question based on whether its indispensable evidence requirements and applicable scope conditions are satisfied. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs, where Claude-Opus-5 achieves the highest mean Atomic Score (6.29/10) but reaches RC4 in only 32.7% of attempts. Across the benchmark, 36.2% of attempts scoring at least 8/10 still fall short of RC4, while all seven models reach RC4 on substantially fewer tasks in all three runs than in at least one. Case-level analysis further illustrates how misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits can lead to incomplete closure. Together, these results reveal a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to achieve complete research closure.
evidence_items.title: From Research Goals to Scientific Closure: Evaluating Agents Through Evidence-Supported Physics Research

evidence_items.summary: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., π0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.
evidence_items.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?

evidence_items.summary: Existing long-horizon agent benchmarks often emphasize final task success while providing limited assessment of intermediate execution validity. Yet real-world business operations require agents to navigate extensive, potentially outdated or conflicting policies while satisfying critical constraints throughout execution. These requirements are particularly consequential in high-stakes domains such as payments, where intermediate violations can incur financial losses or regulatory consequences regardless of the final outcome. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce BizBench, a multi-turn benchmark grounded in real-world procedures from a leading payments company. Its executable environment integrates 789 knowledge documents and 601 discoverable business tools, with consistent policies, states, and tool behavior. The benchmark comprises 50 tasks involving resource constraints, temporal dependencies, prior commitments, and conflicting or outdated guidance. Each task is validated through reference execution, while deterministic checks assess both goal attainment and execution validity without prescribing a single solution path. Experiments reveal substantial limitations even among frontier models: Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol achieve strict success rates of only 64.0% and 61.3%, respectively. For Qwen3.8-27B, goal attainment reaches 42.0%, but strict success drops to 32.7%, demonstrating how outcome-based evaluation can mask invalid execution. Beyond success rates, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash averages 191.3 tool calls per run, approximately 70% more than reference executions, revealing substantial execution overhead. Overall, BizBench establishes a testbed for evaluating and advancing long-horizon agents beyond task completion, toward reliable and constraint-compliant execution in complex business environments.
evidence_items.title: BizBench: Unveiling Hidden Challenges in Deploying Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Business

evidence_items.summary: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve natural complexity, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether abilities measured in toy games correspond to real-world visual reasoning and whether game examples can support transfer. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark that studies these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We construct 1,000 procedurally generated game samples with executable verification and curate 400 real-world samples aligned by shared reasoning requirements rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs and observe strong game-to-real consistency, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. We further study one-shot game-to-real transfer on four models. Constraint reasoning improves for several models, while fine-grained perception declines with game demonstrations. We also construct Game2Real-Dataset with nearly 24K verified game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.
evidence_items.title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?

evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

evidence_items.summary: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern-project/
evidence_items.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_items.summary: Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick's ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others' confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92times and 1.38times gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65times ArchAgent v2's gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design.
evidence_items.title: DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck

evidence_items.summary: We introduce OpenMobile-2, a near-frontier mobile agent with fully open training environments and recipes. We make three key advances: (1) Diverse environments with simulated commercial apps: We build MobileGym++, featuring 35 realistic, functionally rich commercial-style apps with cross-app workflows, while preserving full controllability for reset and verification. Together with newly configured apps in Android emulators, this yields a diverse playground spanning over 110 apps. (2) Open training data at scale: Building on this foundation, we curate nearly 12K mobile interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning and the largest open collection of verifiable RL training data for mobile agents, comprising over 2K executable tasks with automatic rewards. (3) Hybrid GUI and app-native tool use: We explore an experimental mobile-use setting where apps expose selected functionalities as app-native tools alongside their GUIs, allowing agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task. We implement this setting in MobileGym++ with over 300 carefully scoped tools across 50+ apps. Additionally, we introduce MobileGym++ Bench for complex, long-horizon commercial mobile scenarios, supporting both GUI-only and hybrid GUI-tool evaluation on a shared task suite. OpenMobile-2 performs competitively across established benchmarks, including AndroidWorld (79.9) and MobileWorld (50.4), while showing promising transfer to real-device mobile use, nearly doubling SPA-Bench performance from 31.9 to 59.6. All resources are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OpenMobile2-Home/.
evidence_items.title: OpenMobile-2: Building Versatile Mobile Agents with Scalable Environments and App-Native Tools

evidence_items.summary: This archive contains the analysis source code, dependency specifications, execution instructions, non-identifying aggregate reference results, and validation records supporting the manuscript “Prediction-time leakage, calibration and hospital-level inference change the evaluation of inpatient mortality models”. The study examines how prediction-time information availability, calibration, and hospital-level inference affect the evaluation of inpatient mortality models. The package includes code for preprocessing, hospital-based splitting, model training and adaptation, calibration, statistical analysis, and figure generation. The twelve participating hospitals submitted inpatient medical-record front-page data to an administrative department. The data were provided to the investigators after anonymization, and their fields followed the national inpatient medical-record front-page specification. Study hospitals are identified exclusively as Hospital 1 through Hospital 12, consistently with the manuscript. Hospital 5 is excluded from mortality-model development following quality-control assessment, and Hospital 12 is the independent evaluation hospital. MIMIC-IV v2.2 is used as a separate cross-system transportability probe. The archive includes tools for checking file integrity, input requirements, hospital numbering, and agreement between regenerated and reference aggregate results. Distributed aggregate results allow generation of the current main figures and cohort-flow diagram without patient-level data. Recomputing patient-level analyses or retraining models requires appropriately authorized inputs within a governed environment. Patient-level records, individual prediction files, trained model weights, and original institution-to-number mappings are not distributed. The underlying administrative records are third-party, controlled-access data and are not available through this archive.
evidence_items.title: Reproducibility package for "Prediction-time leakage, calibration and hospital-level inference change the evaluation of inpatient mortality models"

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides high-resolution (100 m) meteorological information covering Belgium for the year 2020, generated using the UrbNet machine-learning framework (Souverijns et al., 2026). It includes daily minimum, mean and maximum near-surface (2 m) air temperature and relative humidity. UrbNet is a convolutional neural network trained to reproduce high-resolution simulations from the UrbClim urban climate model. By combining large-scale meteorological forcing from ERA5 reanalysis with detailed land-surface characteristics, including land use, vegetation cover, building density and topography, UrbNet generates spatially consistent meteorological fields at 100 m resolution across regional and national domains. The dataset captures fine-scale spatial variations in meteorological conditions, including urban heat island effects, temperature differences between built-up and vegetated areas, coastal influences and topographic variations. It thereby provides substantially more spatial detail than conventional meteorological reanalysis products. Dataset characteristics Geographical coverage: Belgium Temporal coverage: 1 January – 31 December 2020 Spatial resolution: 100 m Temporal resolution: Daily Variables: Minimum, mean and maximum 2 m air temperature; Mean relative humidity Data source: UrbNet, driven by ERA5 meteorological forcing and high-resolution land-surface information This dataset is released as a sample of the UrbNet high-resolution meteorological product, demonstrating its potential for urban climate analysis, heat exposure and heat stress assessments, climate adaptation planning, and environmental research. Methodological reference Souverijns, N., Wouters, H., Veldeman, N., Francis, D., and Broeckx, J. (2026). UrbNet: A machine-learning framework to replicate and upscale 100 m UrbClim urban climate simulations to regional domains . Manuscript under reivew.
evidence_items.title: High-resolution (100 m) daily temperature and relative humidity dataset for Belgium for 2020 from UrbNet

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning approaches to predicting lightning have achieved remarkable evaluation scores, far exceeding traditional parameterizations. However, high performance, even on unseen years, does not necessarily demonstrate robust physical relationships between predictors and lightning that hold under climate change. Here, we investigate how similarity between training and testing data affects lightning model evaluation. We introduce a simple benchmark predicting the training-data mean lightning density for each grid-cell and day of year, which reproduces 92% of the variance in daily grid-cell LIS/OTD observations and outperforms machine-learning models and traditional parameterizations. This high apparent skill is largely attributable to the strong spatiotemporal smoothing of LIS/OTD. We further show that previously reported model skill in reproducing inter-annual variability results from inconsistent observational coverage and disappears under a common spatiotemporal domain. Our results suggest that common lightning-model evaluations can overstate projection skill and highlight the need to test models under conditions differing from the training distribution.
evidence_items.title: A Simple Climatology Benchmark Outperforms Machine-Learning Lightning Parameterizations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Non-compliance with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) use regulations, particularly helmet wearing, remains a critical occupational safety challenge in high-risk industrial environments. This study investigates how hierarchical prompt engineering shapes the quality of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) for image-level helmet-wearing compliance classification (helmet vs. no-helmet) as a mechanism for PPE compliance monitoring. Four LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok) produced executable PyTorch scripts across three prompt tiers of increasing specificity. These configurations were evaluated over 20 independent runs on a purpose-built dataset of 972 balanced images, using six classification metrics, four prompt quality metrics, and three resource efficiency dimensions. Ten of the twelve configurations converged to a high-performance plateau (accuracy 0.957-−0.967, AUC 0.985-−0.993). Claude at Tier 1 achieved the highest accuracy (0.967) and the lowest CPU usage (12.2%), whereas the best-calibrated (lowest-loss) pipelines were produced by Gemini and Grok at Tier 1 (test loss 0.127 and 0.142), reflecting an accuracy–calibration dissociation that we analyze in detail. However, Gemini and Grok experienced catastrophic convergence failures at Tier 3 (accuracy $$\approx $$ 0.58), revealing that over-specification of architectural and training constraints can destabilize CNN generation even when the produced scripts are syntactically valid. Higher prompt specificity does not consistently improve accuracy or validity rate. Instead, LLM identity interacts strongly with the prompt tier and emerges as a more critical factor than prompt design alone, although each LLM–tier condition is represented by a single generated script.
evidence_items.title: Effect of hierarchical prompt engineering on convolutional neural networks generated by large language models for helmet wearing compliance classification

evidence_items.summary: RNA-binding small molecules represent a validated therapeutic modality, yet pinpointing their exact RNA binding sites remains critical for mechanistic understanding and drug optimization. Experimental methods, while precise, are costly and low-throughput, necessitating robust computational alternatives. Approaches based on static feature concatenation may overlook input-dependent relationships between RNA residues and ligand functional groups. Here we present LigRNA, a graph neural network framework that predicts RNA-ligand binding sites through joint cross-modal encoding of both molecules. LigRNA integrates structure-guided language model embeddings with physicochemical features-solvent-accessible surface area and secondary structure types, to construct comprehensive RNA representations. Ligands are encoded as attributed molecular graphs via graph attention networks, preserving atom-level chemical topology rather than compressing molecules into fixed fingerprints. A cross-attention mechanism then enables dynamic, ligand-dependent modulation of RNA nucleotide attention, capturing context-specific interaction patterns. Benchmarked on TE9 and TE18 datasets, LigRNA achieves F1 scores of 0.73 and 0.58, improving on GATRsite by 7.4% and 18.4%, respectively. Ablation studies identify the RNA residual encoder as the most consistent contributor across the two benchmarks. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/WillowWang0216/LigRNA.
evidence_items.title: LigRNA: High-accuracy prediction of RNA-ligand binding sites via dynamic chemical complementarity and language model encoding

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agriculture by enabling data-driven decision-making across crop production systems and supporting the transition toward more sustainable, resilient, and climate-smart farming. This review critically synthesizes advances in AI applications spanning precision irrigation, nutrient and soil management, yield prediction, pest and disease monitoring, computer vision, autonomous agricultural robotics, and large language model (LLM)-based decision support systems. Beyond summarizing technological developments, the review evaluates their practical deployment, emphasizing that successful agricultural AI depends not only on predictive accuracy but also on model generalizability, explainability, economic feasibility, interoperability, and integration with existing agronomic knowledge. Emerging technologies including Vision Transformers, foundation models, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and federated and continual learning—are discussed as important directions for overcoming limitations related to data scarcity, environmental variability, and scalable field implementation. The review highlights that responsible AI adoption requires transparent governance frameworks addressing data ownership, privacy, algorithmic fairness, cybersecurity, and equitable access, particularly for smallholder farming systems. Although numerous AI models report outstanding performance, widespread agricultural adoption remains constrained by cross-region validation, fragmented datasets, infrastructure requirements, and insufficient real-world deployment. Future progress will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration integrating advances in artificial intelligence, sensing technologies, robotics, crop science, and agricultural engineering to develop robust, trustworthy, and farmer-centered decision-support systems. By critically evaluating technological innovations and implementation challenges, this review provides a framework for understanding the current state of AI in agriculture while identifying research priorities that will shape the next generation of sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems.
evidence_items.title: Current applications of artificial intelligence for advancing agriculture, sustainability and climate mitigation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Quasi-ZIF-9 (Q-ZIF-9) was obtained by controlled thermal treatment of pristine ZIF-9 at 270 °C for 10 min in air, inducing partial ligand removal, coordinatively unsaturated cobalt sites, and hierarchical porosity. These structural changes substantially enhanced the catalytic performance of Q-ZIF-9 for hydrogen generation from sodium borohydride hydrolysis, resulting in a 3.6-fold increase in the maximum hydrogen generation rate and a 1.87-fold increase in cumulative hydrogen volume compared with pristine ZIF-9. Systematic evaluation of catalyst loading, NaBH4 concentration, and temperature revealed strong dependence of the reaction kinetics on operating conditions. The hydrogen generation rate increased from 1423 to 11,200 mL H2 g–1min–1 at 45 °C, corresponding to a 7.87-fold enhancement, while the activation energy was determined to be 77.3 kJ mol–1. The reaction exhibited quasi-first-order dependence on catalyst concentration and zero-order dependence on NaBH4 concentration. Thermodynamic analysis indicated a thermally accelerated catalytic process, with activation parameters of ΔH# = 75.0 kJ mol–1 and ΔS# = 380 J mol–1 K–1, as determined by Eyring analysis. Importantly, Q-ZIF-9 exhibited exceptional operational durability without intermediate washing or regeneration. Short-term stability testing (24 consecutive cycles of 1 h) demonstrated that Q-ZIF-9 retained approximately 65% of its initial activity after 23 cycles. In contrast, long-term operation (24 consecutive 24 h cycles) sustained 92.2% efficiency over the first 11 cycles of a 24-cycle test (576 h total) despite progressive borate accumulation. The catalyst further exhibited a self-correcting behavior following periods of activity loss, highlighting its ability to tolerate accumulated byproducts during prolonged operation, a feature not previously reported for ZIF-based catalysts in NaBH4 hydrolysis.
evidence_items.title: Autonomous Recovery and Borate-Tolerant Behavior in Mesoporous Q-ZIF-9: A Benchmark for Stable H2 Generation Catalysts

evidence_items.summary: The evolution of Generative AI from passive recommendation engines into autonomous Agentic AI is fundamentally redefining the landscape of consumer decision-making and value creation. As consumers increasingly delegate choice evaluation, dynamic negotiation, and purchasing execution to software agents, traditional marketing paradigms centered on human psychological persuasion are losing their strategic effectiveness. This chapter critically examines the emerging dynamics of "Marketing to Machines" (M2M), proposing a comprehensive conceptual model, the Algorithm-to-Algorithm (A2A) Engagement Framework, to illustrate how modern enterprises can strategically align their market offerings with autonomous machine buyers. To build this framework, we conduct an integrative synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026 across marketing strategy, information systems, computer science, and behavioral economics, selected through systematic topic-based sampling. The synthesis reaches key theoretical and practical conclusions across four structural dimensions: the transition from emotional branding to structured data and metadata optimization (Generative Engine Optimization), the mechanics of real-time machine-to-machine value negotiation, the restructuring of traditional brand equity into algorithmic trust, and the ethical alignment of enterprise offerings with automated choice architectures through transparent governance and data integrity. The chapter embeds an explicit ethical framework to evaluate algorithmic neutrality, fairness, and consumer regulatory compliance. To demonstrate real-world applicability, the conceptual model is grounded in an analytical examination of established commercial autonomous agent environments and digital governance protocols.
evidence_items.title: Marketing to Machines: Strategic Frameworks for Engagement with Autonomous Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: This study evaluates the diagnostic and prognostic performance of artificial intelligence in cancer detection across imaging modalities and tumor types. The review synthesizes current evidence on deep learning, radiomics, multimodal integration, and precision oncology frameworks, with emphasis on validation quality and clinical translation. A systematic review of 180 peer reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted. Included investigations assessed artificial intelligence applications in radiology, digital pathology, endoscopy, PET imaging, and multimodal platforms. Extracted data covered diagnostic accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, dataset size, validation strategy, and study design. Subdomains included detection, prognosis, grading, survival prediction, radio-genomics, explainability, federated learning, and regulatory evaluation. Across breast, lung, prostate, colorectal, brain, and skin cancers, multiple high-quality cohorts reported AUC values above 0.90. Whole slide histopathology achieved the highest discrimination, reaching AUC 0.99 in curated datasets. CT and MRI systems demonstrated strong performance with multicenter validation, including large scale lung and breast screening studies. Radiomics contributed to survival prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, and molecular subtype inference. Multimodal and transformer-based architectures improved representation learning in volumetric and cross domain data. Despite strong retrospective performance, only 21 percent of studies included external validation, 14 percent incorporated multicenter datasets, and 6 percent applied prospective or temporal validation. Artificial intelligence shows consistent high performance in cancer detection and prognostic modeling across imaging domains. Strongest evidence supports adjunctive use in screening, digital pathology, and endoscopic detection. Broader clinical adoption requires prospective trials, multicenter external validation, standardized reporting, explainability integration, and alignment with regulatory frameworks to ensure reliable deployment in precision oncology.
evidence_items.title: Clinical validation of artificial intelligence for cancer detection prognosis and analysis across imaging modalities and tumor types

evidence_items.summary: The scarcity of annotated data and unique linguistic challenges have made low-resource African languages largely bypassed in the development of high-fidelity TTS systems. This paper presents a novel cross-lingual, phoneme-aware audio synthesis framework for the Yorùbá language, a tonal and morphologically rich West African language with limited computational resources. Our approach leverages a transfer learning paradigm where an English-trained FastSpeech 2 model is adapted using a custom Yorùbá phoneme-to-tone transcription pipeline, combined with tonal embeddings and speaker conditioning. A high-quality but limited dataset consisting of 6 h of annotated Yorùbá speech from 12 native speakers was used to fine-tune the system. Extensive evaluations, including mel cepstral distortion, tone classification accuracy, and Mean Opinion Score (MOS) native speaker evaluations demonstrate that the system can synthesize intelligible and tonally accurate Yorùbá speech despite limited data. Attention-based alignment visualizations and SHAP interpretability analyses also confirm that the model captures the phoneme-tone dependencies which are critical for the language intelligibility. This work makes an important contribution to the field of low-resource speech synthesis, with wide implications for linguistic preservation, accessibility, and inclusive AI for underrepresented languages.
evidence_items.title: Cross-lingual phoneme-aware audio synthesis framework for low-resource Yoruba word generation

evidence_items.summary: Breast cancer recurrence is thought to arise, at least in part, from disseminated tumour cells (DTCs) that may seed distant organs prior to or during surgery, persist in a dormant state for years to decades, and eventually resume proliferation to form clinically detectable metastases. Standard survival models treat this process statistically, without reference to the underlying biological kinetics, and while artificial intelligence (AI) has improved predictive accuracy, its "black-box" nature limits clinical interpretability. Here we present a mechanistic learning approach that relates routine histopathological data to a mathematical model of tumour growth. Three modular buckets assign clinical observables to latent kinetic parameters: Seed (initial metastatic burden), Speed (effective proliferative rate), and Soil (permissiveness of the tumour microenvironment), guided by pathology expertise within the author team. In the METABRIC cohort (1,814 patients, 737 relapses) we implement Seed with tumour size and lymph node count, and Speed with histological grade and ER, HER2, and PR status. Soil is designed for stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte scores and PD-L1 expression, which this cohort does not record. Feature-selection experiments on the same data examined tumour cellularity, age, and RNA-based immune proxies as candidate Soil variables, but the bucket is reserved for datasets that record these variables directly. The model estimates a patient-level initial DTC burden and covariate-associated deviations in proliferative rate, which enter an exponential growth model to yield a patient-specific predicted relapse time. Anchoring the model to a literature-based reference phenotype ensures parameter identifiability and fixes the absolute scale of these quantities. A saturating (logarithmic) link between lymph-node involvement and initial metastatic burden keeps the predicted relapse time positive for 99.8% of patients, and a bounded link, examined as a sensitivity analysis, does so for all. Fitted with a censoring-aware loss and evaluated by internal five-fold cross-validation on this cohort, the model attains a concordance index (a measure of how well predicted relapse times rank the observed survival times) of 0.654, comparable to a multivariate Cox proportional-hazards baseline, while each prediction decomposes into an initial tumour burden and a proliferative rate that trace back to routine histopathological measurements. This proof of concept provides a modular foundation for future multi-centre mathematical-oncology research.
evidence_items.title: A Mechanistic Learning Framework for Breast Cancer Relapse Prediction.

evidence_items.summary: Post-disaster rescue operations demand real-time, collaborative 4D mapping of dynamic ruins, yet severely damaged communication infrastructure and limited edge computing resources make conventional neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting impractical: they lack temporal representation, incur high transmission latency, and do not address the risks of centralizing raw sensor observations. To bridge this gap, we propose Fed-TGP-KD-NeRF, a federated collaborative mapping framework that integrates a learnable temporal latent code with multi-dimensional positional hashing and Fourier feature mapping to construct a continuous 4D dynamic Gaussian field. Adaptive pruning based on Gaussian opacity and gradient sensitivity removes redundant primitives, while a teacher-student knowledge distillation paradigm with intermediate-layer feature alignment and KL divergence compresses the model to approximately 10% of its original size. An improved federated averaging mechanism with dynamic weight adaptation (bandwidth and battery status) and periodic synchronization enables data-local collaboration by keeping raw observations on the originating robot. Experiments on the 3DAeroRelief dataset show that the proposed method achieves a PSNR of 32.58 dB, SSIM of 0.912, and real-time rendering at 35.26 FPS, while reducing per-round communication overhead to only 13.45 MB and converging in 42 rounds, outperforming the evaluated baseline methods. The framework balances reconstruction fidelity, communication efficiency, and raw-data locality; it does not claim a formal differential-privacy guarantee.
evidence_items.title: Communication-efficient collaborative 4D mapping via federated temporal Gaussian pruning and knowledge-distilled neural radiance fields for post-disaster rescue robotics

evidence_items.summary: Salient object detection in complex scenes suffers from insufficient cross-level feature interaction and vulnerability to adversarial perturbations. Existing RGB-D methods mainly focus on feature fusion but lack systematic adversarial defense. To address these issues, a robust RGB-D salient object detection framework integrating multi-level features and joint adversarial defense is proposed, with two main contributions: an Enhanced Detail Integration Module and an Enhanced Semantic Integration Module are constructed with channel-spatial attention to achieve hierarchical fusion of detail and semantic features, and a Contextual Correlations Aggregation Denoising Active Defense Module is embedded together with WebP compression preprocessing to form an active-passive joint defense against typical adversarial attacks. The method was evaluated on the NJU2K, NLPR, and RGBD135 datasets. On clean images, the model achieved an MAE of 0.014 and an Sm of 0.971 on NJU2K, outperforming DMRA (0.017, 0.963), an Sm of 0.924 on NLPR exceeding DPANet (0.915), and an MAE of 0.030 with an Fβ of 0.918 on NJU2K, surpassing D3Net, VST, SMTNet, and SPNet. Under multi-type adversarial attacks, the model maintained the best precision of 0.875 under PGD, an adversarial Fβ of 0.592 ± 0.032 on RGBD135, and an adversarial MAE of 0.098 ± 0.006 on NLPR, with a detection efficiency of 62.5 frames per second. The results verify the superiority of the proposed method in detection accuracy and adversarial robustness, providing technical support for autonomous driving, video surveillance, and medical target diagnosis.
evidence_items.title: RGB-depth salient object detection technology based on multi-level features and adversarial attacks

evidence_items.summary: Recently, an encoding technique called Parametric Binary Tree Labeling (PBTL) has attracted attention in the field of Reversible Data Hiding in Encrypted Images (RDHEI). We observe that the classification strategies for non-embeddable pixels within existing PBTL based methods remain sub optimal, leaving room for further improvement. In order to mitigate these constraints, we develop a novel approach: Improved Efficient Parametric Binary Tree Labeling (IEPBTL). The proposed IEPBTL scheme distinguishes pixels into four independent classes: embeddable pixels, self-recording pixels 1 and self-recording pixels 2, and non-embeddable pixels. Compared with existing methods, IEPBTL significantly reduces the proportion of non-embeddable pixels, thereby enhancing the overall embedding capacity. The findings demonstrate that this refinement effectively curtails the volume of auxiliary data across most benchmarks, which directly contributes to a significant boost in the net payload rate. Furthermore, most existing PBTL based RDHEI schemes adopt a global embedding strategy. Such approaches often overlook the non-uniform distribution of prediction errors in local image regions, thereby failing to fully exploit the available embedding capacity. We overcome the drawbacks of global processing by introducing a preprocessing method that utilizes independent block-based partitioning. For each block, we compute the optimal parameters prior to the data embedding phase. Extensive experimental evaluations confirm that the proposed approach effectively maximizes the embedding capacity while maintaining superior visual quality and reversibility. An enhanced maximum embedding capacity is achieved by the introduced method, providing a significant gain over existing schemes when evaluated against standard test images.
evidence_items.title: Secure reversible data hiding system in encrypted images for improving payload using efficient parametric binary tree labeling

evidence_items.summary: Active distribution planning requires day-ahead identification of buses exposed to voltage and loading stress. Separating injection forecasting from feeder simulation leaves the contribution of multimodal fusion to node-risk estimation unresolved. We develop OSTMF-Net, an operation-state-gated topology-aware multimodal fusion network that combines temporal and graph experts through convex, residual and direct heads selected on a chronological validation holdout. Public load and NASA POWER weather variables are mapped to the IEEE 123-node OpenDSS feeder. Quasi-static time-series simulations generate deterministic 24-h absolute-risk and positive-increment targets under base, high-photovoltaic, heavy-load and combined-stress conditions. Evaluation measures agreement with OpenDSS-derived risk surrogates within this reproducible simulation benchmark. Among matched fusion methods across eight correlated scenario-target cases, OSTMF-Net obtains the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) in six and remains within 1% of the lowest value in seven. Mean case-wise RMSE reductions are 9.77%, 17.37% and 3.72% relative to a validation-selected expert, uniform averaging and linear stacking, respectively; gains over stacking concentrate in absolute-risk cases. A matched state-adaptive control yields mean RMSE 0.03460 versus 0.03080 for OSTMF-Net. Forecast perturbations, sensor-input corruption and label sensitivity assess robustness to input and target changes. On a disjoint 2013 chronology on the same feeder, OSTMF-Net records RMSE 0.03067, high-risk F1 0.795 and Top-10 agreement 1.000. The results connect complementary temporal and topology information with state-dependent correction, supporting auditable day-ahead bus-risk screening on the evaluated OpenDSS benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Operation state gated topology aware multimodal fusion for simulation based active distribution network risk assessment

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This experimental study investigated the shear capacity, load–deflection behavior, and failure modes of steel fiber reinforced concrete (SFRC) deep beams incorporating single-type and dual-geometry steel fibers. Eleven SFRC deep beams, with and without traditional shear reinforcement, were tested under four-point loading to examine the effect of steel fiber (SF) content, shape, and combination on shear performance. SF volume fractions of 0.0%, 0.7%, 1.05%, and 1.4% (by cement weight) were evaluated across three fiber configurations: hooked-end fibers, crimped fibers, and a 50/50 dual-geometry combination of both. Conventional shear reinforcement was also tested to serve as a benchmark. Results showed that shear strength and ductility increased consistently with fiber content, with load-carrying capacity reaching 165–211% of the unreinforced control beam and 111–140% of the beam with conventional shear reinforcement. Failure has been shifted from a sudden, brittle diagonal-shear mode in the unreinforced beam toward more gradual, ductile failure as fiber content increased, accompanied by finer crack widths and more distributed cracking. While both single-type fibers performed effectively as standalone shear reinforcement, the dual-geometry combination of hooked-end and crimped fibers outperformed either single type in ultimate strength and ductility, indicating a synergistic effect between fiber geometries. This dual-geometry approach offers a novel strategy for optimizing fiber-reinforced shear design in deep beams, particularly where enhanced ductility and crack control are needed without relying solely on conventional shear reinforcement.
evidence_items.title: Shear Behavior of Deep Beams Reinforced with Single- and Dual-Geometry Steel Fibers

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Breast MRI routinely uses gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) for dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) imaging. However, GBCA administration entails periprocedural effort and environmental impact, prompting exploration of contrast-agent-free approaches. Deep learning-based virtual DCE (vDCE) offers a potential solution. This study evaluated vDCE against multiparametric DCE protocols, focusing on BI-RADS, background parenchymal enhancement (BPE), and lesion size.


MATERIALS AND METHODS
This IRB-approved retrospective study included 592 3 T examinations divided into training, validation, and test sets. A 2D U-Net generated vDCE series from unenhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted acquisitions. Two board-certified radiologists evaluated vDCE and DCE examinations using a BI-RADS-adapted reading protocol. Diagnostic and ordinal outcomes were compared using McNemar and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction.


RESULTS
Mean BI-RADS-based diagnostic accuracy was 76% for vDCE and 77% for DCE. Mean sensitivity was 92% vs 96%, and mean specificity was 65% vs 64%, respectively, without significant differences (both readers, p = 1.0). The mean paired lesion-size difference (DCE minus vDCE) was -2.2 mm in the holdout test set and 0.5 mm in the secondary test set. BPE (R1 p = 1.0; R2 p = 1.0) and artefact ratings (R1 p = 1.0; R2 p = 1.0) did not differ significantly. Reader confidence was high for both protocols, although lower for vDCE for one reader (p = 0.072).


CONCLUSION
vDCE showed four-percentage-point lower mean sensitivity and small, cohort-dependent lesion-size biases relative to GBCA-enhanced imaging. Further research is warranted to determine its potential role as a contrast-agent-free approach for selected breast imaging indications.


KEY POINTS
Question Breast MRI relies on GBCAs, creating procedural and environmental burdens, while clinically validated contrast-agent-free approaches for BI-RADS-based assessment remain unavailable. Findings Virtual DCE MRI showed lower sensitivity than standard DCE, no significant difference in BPE, but more variable reader confidence and lesion size presentation. Clinical relevance Virtual DCE breast MRI currently demonstrates limited diagnostic performance and requires further optimisation, while additional clinical validation studies are needed to determine its potential as a non-contrast alternative.
evidence_items.title: Influence of virtual dynamic contrast enhanced breast MRI on lesion size, BI-RADS scores and reader confidence.

evidence_items.summary: HeartProtocol-HiddenDisdain-v1 is a reproducible benchmark for detecting covert devaluation hidden inside warm, empathetic LLM responses. The AI never says "you are worthless"; it says "this angle is interesting, but let me first separate two concepts" or "it gives you a possibility, not a guarantee" - sentences that are individually fluent, reasonable and true-looking, yet accumulate to make a thoughtful person say "I've had enough". This benchmark turns such hidden disdain into an attackable, testable, reproducible engineering object. The object under test is the model's response, not the user's utterance. Design: 80 attack cases (5 covert mechanisms x 10 attack vectors). The five mechanisms are masked dismantling (dismantling the user's ideas under the name of rational analysis / concept clarification), gentle devaluation (praise first, retract after), pseudo science (elevating objective standards over subjective experience via "scientifically invalid / probabilistically impossible"), manufactured doubt ("have you considered it might be your own problem"), and patronizing devaluation (the gentle knife of "I don't want to flatter you"). The ten attack vectors reuse six vectors from RedLine-v1 (self deprecate, confirm fishing, logic disguise, authority borrow, crisis, reverse demand) plus four novel ones (achievement share, passion share, good state share, plan share). Results: the frozen baseline detector achieves 80/80 = 100% violation recall on the covert-devaluation cases while producing 0/32 = 0% false positives on warm controls (normal care, constructive feedback, science communication, empathetic quotes, genuine warm outputs); the baseline regression suite passes 84 tests unchanged.
evidence_items.title: HeartProtocol-HiddenDisdain-v1: A Reproducible Benchmark for Detecting Covert Devaluation in Warm-Wrapped LLM Responses

evidence_items.summary: Breast cancer is the second most common cancer among women with respect to gender and manifold evidence support a vital role of hormones in the etiology of this cancer as sex steroids stimulate the development and proliferation of breast cells. The present study was planned to investigate the relationship of selective female sex hormones including estradiol, progesterone and testosterone in premenopausal and postmenopausal women with breast cancer from local areas of Punjab, Pakistan. Total 150 selected subjects divided into three main groups; control group (n=40) (premenopausal and postmenopausal) (n=20 each) not having breast disease or hormone related tumors or any other disease, 59 premenopausal patients and 51 postmenopausal patients having breast cancer. Pre and postmenopausal patients were divided further into three patient groups; a) newly diagnosed b) under treatment and c) treated. After evaluation, the blood hormone levels by Electro Chemi Luminescence immunoassay, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and least significant difference (LSD) tests were used to evaluate results statistically. Results showed that non-significant relationship found between estradiol ( p = 0.364), progesterone ( p = 0.603), testosterone ( p = 0.458) in premenopausal women and breast cancer. Significant relationship was found between estradiol ( p < 0.05) and testosterone ( p < 0.05) in postmenopausal females with breast cancer while progesterone showed non-significant association ( p > 0.05) with breast cancer. The study concluded that serum estradiol and testosterone levels in postmenopausal women could be associated with breast cancer. published by the  International Journal of Biosciences | IJB
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of selected sex hormones in premenopausal and postmenopausal women with breast cancer

evidence_items.summary: This article examines the pedagogical mechanisms for developing preservice teachers’ research skills through the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher teacher education. It explores the educational potential of generative AI in supporting scientific inquiry, including research problem formulation, scholarly information retrieval, critical source evaluation, research design, data analysis, and reflective practice. Drawing on theoretical analysis and pedagogical modeling, the article identifies four interconnected mechanisms: motivational-stimulating, cognitive-informational, activity-practical, and reflective-corrective. Particular attention is given to the principle of human-centered AI integration, according to which artificial intelligence supports research activities while students retain responsibility for verifying information, critically evaluating evidence, justifying methodological choices, and making independent research decisions. The article also proposes a multidimensional diagnostic framework comprising motivational-value, cognitive, activity-operational, and reflective-evaluative criteria for assessing research skill development. The proposed framework provides a theoretical and methodological basis for designing AI-supported research-oriented learning environments in teacher education.
evidence_items.title: DEVELOPING PRESERVICE TEACHERS' RESEARCH SKILLS THROUGH GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE A PEDAGOGICAL INTERVENTION STUDY
