evidence_items.summary: There is growing interest in utilizing waste streams in mixed culture fermentation (MCF) for carboxylate chain elongation (CE). Lactate and ethanol are the most well-recognized electron donors (ED) in CE; however, previous attempts to co-utilize them have yielded varying results. The impact of ethanol as an additional ED for lactate-based CE on microbiome structure and metabolite production was investigated in continuously-fed bioreactors across a pH range of 5.5–7.0. Caproiciproducens spp. were recognized as the primary potential caproate producers at pH 5.5–6.5, supported by Clostridium sensu stricto 12 spp., Clostridia UCG-014 spp., and Oscillibacter spp. It was demonstrated that ethanol, as an additional ED at pH 6.0 and 6.5, increased caproate concentration by approximately 35% compared to lactate-based CE, while the combination of pH 5.5 and ethanol addition inhibited lactate-based CE and induced solventogenesis, despite the microbiome being enriched with potential chain elongators. The microbiome structure exhibited the greatest shifts at near-neutral pH affecting caproate production. Lactate-based CE was characterized by competition between chain elongators and unidentified microorganisms affiliated with the Oscillospiraceae and Lachnospiraceae families. On the other hand, the co-utilization of ethanol and lactate at neutral pH favoured the growth of Anaerotignum propionicum and Clostridium sensu stricto 7 spp. Although neutral pH favoured the growth of chain elongators' competitors, specific ASVs associated with Caproiciproducens spp. still appeared, leading to an increase in its relative abundance up to 19.8%. This study highlights how ethanol as a co-ED for lactate-based CE influenced metabolite profiles and microbial community structure across different pH ranges.
evidence_items.title: Dataset for: Microbial and metabolic variations in pH-dependent chain elongation – co-utilization of lactate and ethanol vs. lactate-based production

evidence_items.summary: This technical report provides a preliminary feasibility overview of ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC) and seawater air conditioning (SWAC) for Guam. It reviews resource conditions, technology maturity, potential development sites, environmental effects, regulatory requirements, and priorities for further assessment, informed by existing literature and community and agency engagement. Guam’s warm surface waters, access to cold deep water, and concentrated cooling demand justify continued investigation of both technologies. SWAC represents the nearer-term opportunity because of its greater commercial maturity. Preliminary screening identifies Old Hospital Point in Tumon as a candidate for further study, while highlighting cultural and public-use constraints at Ypao Beach Park and pipeline-routing challenges at Tanguisson for OTEC. The report identifies needs for site-specific engineering and environmental surveys, intake and discharge modeling, economic analysis, coordinated permitting review, and continued community engagement. It distinguishes favorable resource conditions from demonstrated project feasibility; detailed economic evaluation remains separate. Published as University of Guam Marine Laboratory Technical Report 175.
evidence_items.title: Feasibility Overview: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) and Seawater Air Conditioning (SWAC) for Renewable Energy Resilience in Guam

evidence_items.summary: Longwall Face Advance Rate and Roof Strata Stability: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review Dataset This dataset contains bibliographic records of 50 peer-reviewed scientific publications related to the influence of longwall face advance rate on roof strata stability, strata pressure behavior, overburden movement, and associated geomechanical processes in underground coal mining. The publications were identified, screened, and selected using the PRISMA 2020 systematic review methodology. The dataset includes bibliographic metadata for each publication, including authors, title, publication year, source, DOI, abstract, and thematic classification. The collected records were obtained from international scientific databases and represent studies published in leading journals in the fields of mining engineering, rock mechanics, geomechanics, strata control, and underground excavation stability. The primary purpose of this dataset is to support evidence synthesis, systematic reviews, bibliometric studies, and further investigations into the relationship between longwall face advance rate and roof behavior. The dataset may also serve as a foundation for qualitative analysis, meta-analysis, knowledge mapping, and the development of predictive models for ground control and roof stability assessment. The dataset was created as part of a systematic literature review focused on identifying the mechanisms through which longwall face advance rate affects stress redistribution, roof caving, periodic weighting, support loading, fracture development, and overall stability of overlying strata. Contents 50 peer-reviewed publications; Authors; Titles; Publication years; Source titles; DOI identifiers; Abstracts; Thematic classification.
evidence_items.title: PRISMA-Based Dataset of Publications on Longwall Face Advance Rate and Roof Strata Stability

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains de-identified participant-level data from the Czech IPEN Adolescent GPS/INDARES study, including data availability indicators, GPS-derived travel distances and speed statistics, and spatial agreement between GPS-recorded and INDARES-reported routes. The workbook includes 112 participants, with GPS transport summaries and route-overlap results alongside detailed GPS segments, a variable codebook, and methodological notes. Original participant identifiers, dates of birth, and school identifiers have been removed. Missing data and source inconsistencies are documented.
evidence_items.title: Dataset: Validity of digital route drawing for active transport research: Evidence from the Czech IPEN Adolescent GPS Study

evidence_items.summary: Student-built vibration-absorber test rigs are widely used in engineering education to demonstrate transmissibility and to estimate mount-fatigue life, yet the accelerometers mounted on these rigs are rarely characterised for cross-axis sensitivity. The model treats the measured transmissibility as a perturbation of the true transmissibility by a crosstalk term whose magnitude depends on the ratio of cross-axis to on-axis sensitivity and on the phase relation between the two orthogonal response components. A first-order sensitivity analysis yields a closed-form bound on the relative transmissibility bias, and a Basquin-type fatigue inversion translates that bias into a multiplicative life-prediction error. The analysis is a methodological and theoretical contribution: no experimental data are reported, and the model is intended to specify the calibration and reporting practices that student rigs require. The principal result is that crosstalk of the order commonly encountered in low-cost piezoelectric accelerometers can produce transmissibility bias sufficient to inflate predicted fatigue life by a factor that depends on the S-N slope, and that the bias is not eliminated by averaging over repeated runs. The paper concludes that transmissibility-based fatigue estimates from student rigs should be reported with an explicit crosstalk-uncertainty interval rather than as point predictions.
evidence_items.title: Spectral-Response Overestimation in Student-Built Engineering Education Vibration-Absorber Test Rigs: A Shaker-Table Transmissibility Evaluation Linking Accelerometer Crosstalk to Mount-Fatigue Life Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Student-built concrete-cube presses used in engineering education are typically calibrated against a proving ring at a single reference load, yet the bedding between platen and specimen governs how much of the applied force reaches the cube. The model treats the indicated force as the true force attenuated by a bedding-dependent under-reading factor, and derives the probability that a mix accepted by the press exceeds its design safety margin. A design-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 56 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the detectable-effect curve. The contribution is a formal link between a workshop-level calibration defect and the structural reliability of the safety margin, which reframes proving-ring calibration as a reliability instrument rather than a single-point check.
evidence_items.title: Compression-Force Under-Reading in Student-Built Engineering Education Concrete-Cube Presses: A Proving-Ring Calibration Evaluation Linking Platen Bedding to Structural Safety-Margin Reliability

evidence_items.summary: HIMANIS-ActSegmentation. Act-level layout segmentation of French Royal Chancery Registers Registers JJ60-JJ95 (c. 1320-c. 1365) Two YOLO12s object-detection models (classes AI, AM, AF, AC, Table, NIA) Overview. This deposit contains two trained object-detection models for the act-level segmentation of page images from the registers of the French royal chancery (Paris, Archives nationales, Trésor des chartes, series JJ). Given a page image, each model returns bounding boxes labelled with six classes that locate every act on the page, whether complete or divided between several pages, as well as the tables of the registers and the pages for which no image is available. The models were developed within the HIMANIS and HOME research projects [and the Biblissima+ programme] in order to cut the registers into individual acts, so that the automatic full text produced by handwritten text recognition could be attached to the act records of the database Himanis / Home: a common database for the History of Medieval Europe (ed. D. Stutzmann, 2022-), in which each act is linked to its page images and transcriptions. They were built in two stages, in June and July 2025, with a view to processing the whole series of medieval registers up to JJ211. Corpus. The JJ series of the Archives nationales preserves the registers in which the royal chancery copied the letters it issued (charters, grants, privileges, pardons and other acts). The database covers the registers JJ37 to JJ211, from 1303 to the late fifteenth century; the present models were trained on page images of the registers JJ60 to JJ76 (1321-1348) and JJ77 to JJ95 (1345-1364). The images are those of the digitisation made by the Archives nationales, served through IIIF, and were downscaled before annotation and training so that their shorter side measures 1,200 pixels (hence "1200pxmin" in the file names). Classes.
evidence_items.title: HIMANIS-ActSegmentation. Act-level layout segmentation of French Royal Chancery Registers. Yolo models

evidence_items.summary: Student-built drying-oven rigs used in engineering education typically rely on low-cost capacitive humidity sensors whose polymer membranes exhibit sorption hysteresis, yet the consequences of that hysteresis for the food-safety margins computed in laboratory exercises have not been quantified. The model treats the sensor response as a rate-independent Preisach operator conditioned on prior sorption history, calibrates its bounds against saturated-salt reference standards, and propagates the resulting interval through the drying-oven mass-balance calculation that students perform. Analytical results establish a monotone relationship between conditioning-path length and worst-case bias, a threshold conditioning protocol below which the safety margin is preserved, and a reliability bound expressed as a function of the number of reference salts used for calibration. The framework is methodological: it specifies the calibration and conditioning protocol that student rigs should adopt, identifies the saturated-salt set that minimises residual bias, and states the boundary conditions under which the bound holds. The contribution is a design rule for humidity-sensor conditioning in educational drying rigs that converts an unexamined sensor artefact into a quantified and manageable reliability constraint.
evidence_items.title: Humidity-Sensor Sorption Hysteresis in Student-Built Engineering Education Drying-Oven Rigs: A Saturated-Salt Reference Evaluation Linking Membrane Conditioning to Food-Safety Margin Reliability

evidence_items.summary: [Abstract]: Feature selection is an important step in machine learning that can benefit from GPU acceleration. As the number of GPU vendors increases, it is imperative to adapt algorithms such as the minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) feature selection method to different backends that support several GPU architectures. This work presents a multi-backend implementation of mRMR across CUDA, HIP, and SYCL, and studies its performance when combined with Bayesian optimization and transfer learning to automatically tune execution parameters for different platforms and datasets. Our experimental results show that when tuned, CUDA and HIP achieve comparable performance on NVIDIA architectures, while SYCL exhibits a moderate performance gap. Overall, this work highlights the impact of backend choice and autotuning on GPU-accelerated feature selection and provides insights into deploying mRMR across heterogeneous environments.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Backend Autotuning Study of Feature Selection on GPUs

evidence_items.summary: Student-built cell-test benches in engineering education frequently report internal resistance from two-wire measurements, yet the contact resistance at the probe-electrode interface is rarely separated from the cell's own ohmic resistance. The model treats the measured resistance as the sum of the cell's true internal resistance and a contact term whose magnitude depends on probe geometry, electrode surface condition and applied force. A sensitivity analysis over plausible bench parameters shows that a contact resistance of 5 mΩ, well within the range reported for student-assembled fixtures, can shift a 50 mΩ cell across a 20% state-of-health threshold when the reference resistance is drawn from a single baseline measurement. The derived reliability bound is expressed as a function of the ratio of contact resistance to cell resistance and the width of the classification band. The contribution is a design rule: a four-wire Kelvin probe with a contact-resistance ceiling of 1 mΩ or less, verified against a calibration shunt before each session, keeps classification error below 5% for cells above 40 mΩ. The analysis is methodological and does not report primary measurements; it specifies the probe geometry, calibration procedure and acceptance criterion that a student bench must satisfy to produce state-of-health labels that are stable under repeated measurement.
evidence_items.title: Battery Internal-Resistance Misestimation in Student-Built Engineering Education Cell-Test Benches: A Four-Wire Kelvin Probe Evaluation Linking Contact Resistance to State-of-Health Classification Reliability

evidence_items.summary: BEAM is a probability model for T cell receptor beta CDR3 amino-acid sequences that combines local sequence dependence with exact normalisation. Its tractable local structure permits deterministic evaluation of sequence probabilities, the expected recovery, recurrence, overlap and publicness of sequences at a given sampling depth, and interpretable distances between repertoires, without enumerating or Monte Carlo sampling the space of sequences.
evidence_items.title: BEAM: a computable probability landscape for T cell receptor repertoires

evidence_items.summary: Python code accompanying the paper “Probabilistic detection of deformation episodes in InSAR time series using Bayesian change-point analysis” (Bouygues, Albino & Pinel, submitted to JGR: Solid Earth). BCPD-InSAR applies a moving-window Bayesian change-point detection (after Ruggieri, 2013) pixel by pixel to InSAR cumulative displacement cubes. For each acquisition, it returns the posterior probability that a change in displacement rate (onset, acceleration, deceleration or stop of deformation) occurred within the last W acquisitions. The repository contains three scripts: generate synthetic.py (synthetic displacement cubes with Mogi sources, turbulent and stratified atmospheric noise, and their ground truth), detect synthetic.py (detection on a synthetic cube) and detect real.py (detection on a real cube, GeoTIFF, ENVI or NetCDF). It also includes a real-time Hampel outlier filter, an HDBSCAN-based spatio-temporal clustering filter, and the configuration files of the synthetic benchmark and of the three real cases of the paper (Suswa, Reykjanes, Domuyo). See README.md for installation and usage.
evidence_items.title: BCPD-InSAR: Bayesian change-point detection of deformation episodes in InSAR time series

evidence_items.summary: Heavy-equipment delivery by Landing Craft Tank (LCT) is critical to mining operations in Indonesia’s archipelagic regions, yet routing decisions are often made without structured analytical support. This study develops a decision-making framework for optimizing LCT delivery at a mining-logistics company that relies predominantly on single-origin–single-destination (SOSD) voyages. Using a quantitative-dominant single-case design, 55 LCT voyages from 2025 (498 equipment-unit movements) were analysed through voyage-level key performance indicators—load factor, cost per ton, and cost per nautical mile. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) structured the choice between SOSD and multi-origin–multi-destination (MOMD) routing across six criteria, complemented by thematic analysis of seven expert practitioners and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA). The fleet recorded a low mean load factor of 27.7%, with 54 of 55 voyages below 50%. The multi-stop voyages observed in practice were not cheaper than SOSD, indicating that consolidation alone does not guarantee savings. AHP ranked SOSD first (global priority 0.540 versus 0.460). The study contributes a managerially usable, data-driven framework integrating performance measurement, multi-criteria evaluation, and risk assessment to guide LCT routing decisions.
evidence_items.title: A DECISION-MAKING FRAMEWORK FOR OPTIMIZING HEAVY-EQUIPMENT DELIVERY VIA LANDING CRAFT TANK AT AN INDONESIAN MINING-LOGISTICS COMPANY

evidence_items.summary: This study examines the transferability of the updated Synthesis of Qualitative Data (SQD2) model to teacher AI competency development. Using SQD2 as an analytical framework, we conducted a meta-aggregation of 29 studies to identify strategies for training teachers to integrate AI into their practice. The resulting Intelligent-SQD model retains the six overarching dimensions of SQD2, confirming their robustness as foundational principles for technology-related teacher training. However, the analysis reveals that the specific strategies within each dimension differ substantially. Strategies such as Role models and Real world can be transferred, while others, including Output evaluation, co-creation with AI, iterative prompting, and responsible AI use, represent new training strategies. The comparison between the two models is presented and implications for AI teacher education are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Transferability of SQD strategies to teacher AI competency development: A systematic review

evidence_items.summary: This data set contains the 112 instances of a benchmark for linear solvers of high-frequency electromagnetic finite element analysis: 46 instances of 15 canonical problems and 66 instances of 8 printed circuit board (PCB) problems. Each instance is a sparse linear system Ax=b from the edge-element discretization of the time-harmonic Maxwell equations, with its mesh, a reference solution and the baseline results of 11 standard iterative solvers. Each problem has a series of instances that change one factor of difficulty at a time, such as the frequency, the electrical length, the element size, the material contrast, the loss, the boundary conditions, flat elements and the distance to a resonance. The benchmark and its baseline results are described in the paper below (in Japanese, with an English abstract).

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models have shown substantial potential for supporting clinical reasoning, but their use in patient safety applications remains constrained by limited access to structured clinical knowledge, variable evidence grounding, and difficulty tracing generated reasoning to supporting sources. Knowledge graphs can provide structured representations of clinical and safety concepts, while retrieval-augmented generation can incorporate relevant biomedical evidence into model inputs. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate an integrated framework for evidence-grounded patient safety reasoning that combines a large language model, a patient-safety knowledge graph, and retrieval-augmented generation. The study examined how structured knowledge and evidence retrieval contribute to concept extraction and reasoning performance. Methods The framework was developed using adult intensive care data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-III and MIMIC-IV. Patient safety concepts were normalized using established clinical terminology and patient safety classifications and represented within a structured knowledge graph. An LLaMA-based language model adapted using low-rank adaptation was used for concept extraction and reasoning. Retrieval-augmented generation incorporated relevant biomedical literature, patient safety resources, clinical guidelines, and drug-related knowledge using biomedical sentence embeddings and a FAISS-based vector index. Retrieved evidence was ranked using cosine similarity and incorporated into the model context together with relevant graph information. Performance was evaluated using F1, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and area under the precision-recall curve. Component ablation analyses examined the effects of removing the knowledge graph, low-rank adaptation, and retrieval augmentation.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Grounded Large Language Model Reasoning for Patient Safety Using Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Development and Evaluation Study
Benchmarking Large Language Models for Video Quality Assessment: Structured Perceptual Prompting and Refinement

evidence_items.summary: Existing ns3/AI bridges target numeric reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines and cannot handle the text-centric prompt/response exchange, structured output validation, and multi-node orchestration that large language models (LLMs) require. We introduce ns3-GenAI, an open framework that augments the ns3 shared-memory interface with three bridge-level features: a hybrid text-and-numeric memory layout, a fail-safe validation gate prior to writing back to the simulator, and multi-instance synchronization to support coordinated LLM workflows. These mechanisms provide a common, validated simulation path in which hosted and local LLMs, RL, and deep learning modules consume the same ns3 states and return decisions without changing simulator-side logic. We instantiate the framework in two complementary settings: a data-plane semantic codec and a control-plane self-organizing network (SON) agent. Across both case studies, hosted and local LLMs and conventional baselines occupy distinct quality–latency and throughput–fairness operating points. Rather than claiming a universally superior model class, these controlled comparisons demonstrate ns3-GenAI’s hybrid, fail-safe, and synchronized shared-memory path for evaluating generative and conventional network intelligence under identical simulation conditions.
evidence_items.title: ns3-GenAI: Integrating Large Language Models with ns3 for AI-Native Network Simulations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Purpose Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for clinical information retrieval, but their performance in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) remains poorly characterized. We compared three contemporary LLMs across diagnosis and classification, treatment and follow-up, and clinical case scenarios. Methods Twenty-one guideline-based JIA questions were submitted once to GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Claude Opus 5 on August 25, 2026, each in a separate conversation. Five pediatric rheumatologists independently rated anonymized responses, presented in randomized order, for accuracy and guideline concordance, clinical usability, and overall quality. Linear mixed-effects models included LLM, domain, and their interaction, with evaluator and question as crossed random intercepts. Response length, readability, inter-rater reliability, and ordinal sensitivity analyses were also assessed. Results The 63 responses yielded 315 ratings per outcome. GPT-5.6 Sol achieved the highest mean scores for accuracy (4.71 ± 0.47), usability (4.70 ± 0.55), and quality (6.47 ± 0.71), compared with Gemini 3.1 Pro (4.04 ± 0.95, 4.24 ± 0.86, 5.32 ± 1.11) and Claude Opus 5 (3.93 ± 0.89, 3.90 ± 0.81, 5.26 ± 1.05; all p < 0.001). LLM×domain interactions were significant for accuracy (p = 0.005) and usability (p < 0.001), but not quality (p = 0.053), reflecting a domain-dependent ranking of Gemini and Claude. Claude Opus 5 produced the longest responses without higher ratings, and GPT-5.6 Sol had the lowest Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level in every domain. Ordinal analyses supported the primary findings. Panel-level reliability was moderate (ICC[2,k] 0.664–0.729). Conclusion Contemporary LLMs differed meaningfully in guideline-based JIA performance, with differences varying by clinical task. These findings support supervised rather than autonomous use of LLMs in pediatric rheumatology and highlight the need for model-specific, periodically repeated validation.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Performance of Large Language Models in Answering Guideline-Based Questions on Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis: A Blinded Expert Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Investment behaviour has changed as a result of artificial intelligence (AI), which replaces human judgment with data-driven insights. Investors may analyse big information, spot trends, and optimize portfolios with the help of technologies like machine learning, robo-advisors, and predictive analytics, increasing productivity and lowering emotional biases. Adoption of AI is not without its difficulties, though, such as algorithmic bias, a lack of transparency, expensive costs, and problems with data quality. Automation bias and market volatility may increase if automated systems are overused. This study highlights AI’s impact on investor behaviour and emphasizes the importance of a balanced, responsible approach to effectively integrate AI into investment decision-making processes.
evidence_items.title: ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN INVESTMENT DECISIONS

evidence_items.summary: Background Grounded in conceptual review and bibliometric analysis, this study examines the emerging intersection of Artificial Intelligence adoption and Emotional Intelligence as in the workplace, with particular attention to generation Z employees. Objective The purpose of this research is to examine the mechanism, structural pattern dominating the integrated framework of AI adoption and EI and their relevance to Generation Z work outcomes and well-being. Method This scientific review integrated conceptual review of 45 studies and Bibliometric analysis of 103 Scopus data published during 2015–2026, through secondary data collection from electronic data-bases including Scopus, Science Direct, and Google Scholar. Bibliometrix package and Biblioshiny in R package were used for data visualization and Scientometric analysis. Result The review highlights the emerging themes, contributions, and structural patterns linking AI, EI, organizational support, and workplace outcomes, revealing that context of generation Z remains almost under explored with in AI-EI literature. An integrated conceptual framework proposed based on combined evidences. Conclusion This study provides a theoretical basis for AI-EI workplace literature and identifies generation Z as an under explored contextual dimension and encourage future empirical research while providing actionable advice for HR leaders and policymakers within tech-enabled workplaces.
evidence_items.title: Integration of emotional intelligence and artificial intelligence for generation Z workforce: A bibliometric analysis and conceptual review

evidence_items.summary: Purpose. This study aims to map how health and medical libraries have used GenAI to support library services. Methods. Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. Searches covered publications from 2020 to 2025 in PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, LISTA, Academic Search Premier, MEDLINE via Ovid, Scopus, Web of Science, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, and Google Scholar. After deduplication, 106 of 250 records were screened in Rayyan by two independent blinded reviewers. Findings. Eleven studies were included: seven primary studies and four secondary or methodological papers. Among primaries, five directly used GPT-family models (GPT-4/ChatGPT/GPT-4o or Perplexity layered on GPT-4) to answer clinical questions, support search-strategy design, trial library tasks, and integrate source-linked answers in a national portal. One survey assessed intention to adopt generative chatbots; one case described a rule-based chatbot. GenAI accelerates workflows and extends services but requires human verification, transparency about limitations, privacy policies, and staff training (including prompt engineering). LLM-generated search strategies exhibited variability and underperformed compared with human designs. Implications. In its current state, GenAI works best as a copilot useful for drafting, triage, and initial sense-making, while librarians remain essential for high-precision tasks (performance), quality control (reliability), and governance. This suggests that its academic value lies not in automation alone, but in the mediated integration of AI into evidence-informed services, where professional judgment, methodological transparency, and ethical accountability determine whether GenAI strengthens or weakens health information practices.
evidence_items.title: Use of generative artificial intelligence in medical libraries: A scoping review

evidence_items.summary: The development and adjustment of a master plan involve processing a considerable amount of heterogeneous spatial information, including data from the Unified State Register of Real Estate, territorial and urban zoning documents, information on existing development, engineering and transport infrastructure, and zones with special land-use conditions. As the digital information base expands, the analytical work of planners becomes more complicated, since it requires not only collecting data but also identifying relationships, restrictions, and contradictions between different datasets. The purpose of the study is to determine the role of artificial intelligence technologies in the development and adjustment of master plans and to propose a model for their integration into urban planning analysis. The methodological framework combines systems and comparative analysis, cadastral interpretation and spatial data comparison, as well as an analysis of Russian and international research in digital urban planning and GeoAI. The study identifies preliminary territorial classification, detection of spatial inconsistencies, land-use change analysis, identification of territorial reserves, and scenario modelling as the most relevant areas for artificial intelligence application. A sequential model is proposed in which intelligent analysis is performed after the spatial database has been created and verified but before the final planning decision is selected by experts. Within this approach, artificial intelligence does not replace the specialist but reduces routine data processing and helps identify areas requiring in-depth analysis at an earlier stage. The results can be used to develop digital tools for information and analytical support of territorial planning.
evidence_items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE SYSTEM OF MASTER PLAN DEVELOPMENT AND ADJUSTMENT

evidence_items.summary: Theranostic imaging agents combine molecular diagnosis, targeted therapy and monitoring of treatment response into a single paradigm of precision medicine. This review summarizes the current development and translational landscape of theranostic imaging agents, covering molecular targets, imaging platforms, principles of agent design, nanotheranostics, radiotheranostics, and disease-specific applications. Particular emphasis is given to clinically validated and emerging targeting strategies using prostate-specific membrane antigen, somatostatin receptors, fibroblast activation protein, C-X-C Chemokine Receptor 4 (CXCR4), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) and other disease-associated biomarkers. Moreover, the review addresses Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), optical, photoacoustic, Raman and multimodal imaging approaches, therapeutic payloads, stimulus-responsive systems, and pharmacokinetic optimization. Moreover, emerging applications of artificial intelligence, radiomics, radiogenomics, spatial and single-cell multiomics, liquid biopsy, digital pathology, personalized dosimetry, and digital twins are evaluated for their potential to improve patient stratification, treatment selection, response assessment and adaptive therapy. Despite tremendous progress, clinical translation is hampered by target heterogeneity, off-target accumulation, radionuclide availability, manufacturing complexity, dosimetric uncertainty, regulatory requirements, limited clinical validation, data interoperability, cost and unequal access. This review, overall, emphasizes the convergence of molecular imaging, targeted therapeutics, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence in the development of next-generation theranostic platforms, and outlines critical priorities for their clinical translation.
evidence_items.title: Theranostic Imaging Agents: Integrating Molecular Diagnostics, Precision Therapeutics, and Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: In tandem with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, the integration of such instruments into higher education sectors has attained escalating depth. As core foundational domains for cultivating the logical reasoning ability, abstract inference capability, and problem-addressing proficiency of students, undergraduate mathematics programs are confronting structural barriers including highly abstract content, rigid instructional approaches, and outmoded evaluation systems. Grounded in the theoretical frameworks of educational technology and curricular reform, the current study has conducted systematic exploration into the potential of AI technologies to drive a paradigm shift of collegiate mathematics instruction via reorganizing teaching processes, optimizing resource allocation, and providing personalized learning support. Based on practical instructional application instances, the present work analyzes application pathways covering intelligent tutoring systems, interactive visualization platforms, AI-assisted problem solving, automatic homework grading, and blended learning models. It further probes the practical challenges from diverse angles, such as the role transition of instructors, assessment innovation, data ethics, and educational equity. Findings indicate that AI does not merely replace traditional teaching tools, but rather fosters a student-centered intelligent educational environment through human-AI collaboration. To achieve deep integration between technical instruments and learning activities, it is essential to strengthen top-level strategic planning, improve the digital literacy of teaching personnel, and refine assessment mechanisms—ultimately serving the goal of nurturing innovative talents.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence empowering mathematics education in higher education: model reconstruction and pathways analysis

organizations: Azerbaijan State University of Oil and Industry
evidence_items.summary: modern power engineering is undergoing a major transformation driven by renewable energy integration, distributed generation, transport electrification, and increasing demands for reliable electricity supply. The variable output of solar and wind power plants complicates the balance between generation and consumption. In this context, integrating artificial intelligence (AI), energy storage systems (ESSs), and intelligent control technologies offers a promising approach to developing sustainable and adaptive electrical grids. This paper examines AI applications in renewable generation and load forecasting, energy storage optimization, power flow control, and grid resilience. It considers machine learning, deep learning, intelligent optimization algorithms, and digital twins, with particular attention to coordinating battery storage, renewable energy sources, smart meters, and automated grid management. Technical, economic, and environmental challenges, including cybersecurity, equipment costs, battery degradation, and data quality, are also discussed.
evidence_items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, ENERGY STORAGE, AND POWER ENGINEERING: TOWARDS AN INTELLIGENT AND SUSTAINABLE GRID

evidence_items.summary: The use of machine-learning models in management information systems enables organizations to generate predictions at increasing scale and speed. Predictive performance alone, however, is insufficient for managerial use. Decision makers also need to examine why an output was produced, interpret the explanation within the decision context, and monitor the consequences of resulting actions. This chapter treats explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) as an intermediate layer between machine-learning predictions and managerial decision-making. It integrates the literatures on decision support systems, human collaboration with artificial intelligence (AI), and human-centered XAI evaluation. To maintain a focused technical scope, the chapter examines two widely used methods for explaining the outputs of trained models: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Drawing on the literature reviewed, the chapter develops a four-layer framework that connects prediction, explanation, managerial interpretation and evaluation, and decision, action, and feedback. Published studies from manufacturing, finance and credit, and energy management are then used to examine how these four layers appear in different application settings. The analysis indicates that explanations do not automatically produce trust, decision quality, or ethical acceptability. Their managerial value depends on the joint evaluation of technical properties, user and task characteristics, organizational context, and governance arrangements.
evidence_items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Management Information Systems: From Prediction to Managerial Decision-Making

evidence_items.summary: Hospital environmental contamination can contribute to the persistence and transfer of potentially pathogenic bacteria. This study assessed bacterial contamination of selected surfaces and medical devices and described antimicrobial susceptibility records at Al-Mahjoub General Hospital, Misurata, Libya. Environmental swabs were collected from the Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Neonatal Intensive Care, Pediatric, and Women’s Observation units. Samples were cultured on MacConkey, blood, and chocolate agar, and isolates were examined using colony morphology and Gram staining. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion using 13 agents, with interpretation reportedly based on Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidance. Of 26 environmental samples, 22 (84.62%) yielded bacterial growth, and 4 (15.38%) showed no growth. Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequently recovered organism (15/26, 57.69%), followed by Streptococcus pyogenes (3/26, 11.54%); Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus spp., and Micrococcus spp. were each recorded once. Susceptibility records varied by isolate and sampling site. However, original inhibition-zone diameters and a fully reconciled isolate-level dataset were unavailable, so resistance patterns are reported descriptively and no overall multidrug-resistance rate is claimed. The findings support routine environmental cleaning, infection-prevention training, and improved microbiological surveillance.
evidence_items.title: Bacterial Contamination and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Patterns in Maternity, Neonatal Intensive Care, Pediatric, and Observation Units at Al-Mahjoub General Hospital, Misurata, Libya

organizations: School of Foreign Languages, Hanshan Normal University, Chaozhou 521041, Guangdong, China
evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of big data analytics and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies presents new opportunities for strengthening business Japanese education, particularly in the areas of practical language application, learner engagement, and classroom management. Conventional instruction may provide an insufficient connection between linguistic knowledge, business practices, and intercultural communication. To address these challenges, this study proposes an IoT-enabled, data-driven teaching model structured around three interconnected modules: preparation, learning, and evaluation. The framework establishes a feedback cycle through which information about learners’ needs, instructional activities, and evaluation outcomes can inform subsequent teaching decisions. An associated smart classroom architecture integrates a perception layer for collecting environmental and participation data with a control layer for managing classroom resources and authorized access. The study further introduces quantitative indicators for student distribution, knowledge coverage, learning motivation, instructional goal attainment, and classroom management. Two questionnaire-based analyses are presented to examine students’ learning needs and preferences for blended instruction. The manuscript reports an average 12% improvement in teaching efficiency, although the measurement procedure and comparative data supporting this figure require further documentation. The study identifies opportunities for integrating technological infrastructure with the pedagogical requirements of professionally oriented Japanese-language instruction while emphasizing the need for more rigorous outcome evaluation.
evidence_items.title: An IoT-Enabled Data-Driven Intelligent Teaching Model for Business Japanese Education in the Era of Big Data

evidence_items.summary: Choosing a career is a tough decision to make in itself. Things get trickier when it comes to information a student actually needs: which scholarships they're eligible for, where courses lead, where students can get in based on their marks, etc., and all that information is spread out across dozens of government portals, college websites, and PDFs that don't always agree on what they're offering. The majority of the career-guidance tools that are available today are not really a solution to this. They either give a general response from a brief questionnaire, or release a chatbot which will freely associate a response that seems confident but is not true. Neither verifies whether a student is qualified or not for what it suggests. This paper is an attempt to bridge that gap by employing a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline to achieve this using a set of cooperating agents, instead of a single large model performing all the tasks. The first step is to process a student's academic record, interests, financial status, location, class and career category, and goals to create a structured profile, which is then fed into agents that search for verified information, validate eligibility for scholarships based on hard rules, not assumptions, and compile a plan that is concrete and easily explained. We evaluated the retrieval layer on ten representative queries, including career paths, welfare schemes, higher education and scholarships, and it achieved a top five correct source hit rate of 90% and a Mean Reciprocal Rank of 0.7167. To sum up, if you base the model's output on retrieved evidence and ensure that eligibility decisions are deterministic then you end up giving guidance that a student can actually trust and follow — something that a pure language model and a static rule engine can't do alone.
evidence_items.title: EDUPATH AI A Rag-Based Multi-Agentic AI Framework for Personalised Education and Career Advisory

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Large-scale pharmacogenomics resources such as PRISM/DepMap provide great opportunities for biomarker discovery and precision oncology. However, their adoption remains challenging because drug response data, molecular profiles, and biological interpretation are typically fragmented across multiple tools and require extensive custom scripting. Methods: We developed OncoProfilingTools (OPT), an open-source R framework that unifies pharmacogenomics data management, statistical analysis, predictive modeling, and AI-assisted interpretation within a modular workflow. OPT provides pre-integrated PRISM/DepMap drug sensitivity and multi-omics datasets using standardized Bioconductor data structures, facilitating seamless integration with genomic analysis workflows. The framework currently implements a Sensitivity module for differential drug response analysis between user-defined biological or clinical groups, with forthcoming Prediction and Biomarker modules supporting machine learning–based response prediction and biomarker prioritization. OPT incorporates an integrated agentic AI framework that coordinates downstream analyses, including pathway enrichment, transcription factor analysis, immune deconvolution, and functional annotation. Outputs from specialized agents are synthesized by an AI Hypothesis Generator into candidate biological mechanisms and therapeutic hypotheses, which are summarized in structured reports by an AI Report Writer. A Shiny interface further enables interactive exploration, interpretation, and reporting without requiring scripting. Results: OPT supports integrated pharmacogenomics data loading, standardized preprocessing, and differential drug sensitivity analysis through reproducible workflows that generate statistical summaries, publication-quality visualizations, and prioritized therapeutic candidates.
evidence_items.title: Abstract B013: OncoProfilingTools: An agentic AI–enabled R framework for end-to-end cancer pharmacogenomics and biomarker discovery

evidence_items.summary: Code assistants are increasingly utilized in test-driven software development, yet the theoretical mechanisms behind their environment-interaction strategies remain underexplored. We provide a probabilistic framework for two dominant paradigms: code selection after generation using the execution environment, and code generation conditioned on environment feedback. First, we formalize several well-established selection heuristics as environment-aware estimators of code correctness. We theoretically prove that estimators based on fuzzy functional similarity add an inductive bias and strictly dominate estimators based on functional equivalence in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. Second, we frame backprompting as an in-context approximation of Thompson sampling. We derive a novel regret bound for reward functions with unobservable components, theoretically explaining why the effectiveness of backprompting is limited by the ambiguity of the informal task description (an irreducible regret). Using seven state-of-the-art open weight models, we corroborate these findings across BigCodeBenchHard, LeetCodeDataset, QiskitHumanEvalSim, and SWE-bench Verified. Our formalization also suggests how to improve task descriptions effectively, leading to an improved benchmark for LLM-assisted quantum programming, QiskitHumanEvalSimX.
evidence_items.title: A Theoretical Analysis of Test-Driven Code Generation

evidence_items.summary: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.
evidence_items.title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.
evidence_items.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
evidence_items.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: As joint audio-video generation models become more capable, they can generate audio-visual scenes exhibiting three forms of complexity: multi-event composition, multi-layer audio mixture, and asymmetric cross-modal relations. However, current evaluations largely reuse metrics from earlier simple and unidirectional tasks. They typically evaluate an audio-video clip as a whole and rely on simple predefined relations, making them unsuitable for these increasingly complex scenes. We propose an event-centric evaluation framework that disentangles audio and visual events at the event level, analyzes each event independently, cross-validates relations across modalities, and aggregates the judgments into a coarse-to-fine, three-level consistency metric. The metric assesses global narrative harmony, event-level temporal synchronization, and fine-grained attribute alignment, providing a general formulation for audio-video consistency evaluation across diverse generation settings and cross-modal relations. We instantiate the metric as AVC-Reward, a trainable audio-video reward model. To evaluate the agreement between automatic judgments and human perception across generation paradigms and relation complexities, we construct AVC-Benchmark, which is primarily built from diverse positive and negative samples generated by various types of audio-video generation models. AVC-Reward achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human judgment among automatic methods, provides interpretable rationales that localize failures, and improves the audio-video consistency of a joint generation model when used as an online reinforcement-learning signal. Project page: https://tsuki0512.github.io/AVC-Reward.github.io/
evidence_items.title: AVC-Reward: Event-Centric Audio-Video Consistency Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Instruction-following language models can comply with requests that conflict with intended behaviors and safety alignment. We introduce a training-free weight-editing approach for reducing compliance with targeted undesirable instructions. Our method needs only forward passes on a small set of prompt pairs per target behavior, and because the edit is stored in the model's weights, changing or deleting instructions in the prompt cannot undo the weight modification. We evaluate the approach on two target harmful behaviors across five instruction-tuned models: instructed falsehood and instructed sexism. On two instructed-lying benchmarks, it improves mean honest response rates by 6.2 and 4.6 percentage points over the strongest alternative, significantly on three of the five models and within noise on the other two. In a controlled study of seven prompt formats, it maintains higher honest-response rates than single-layer activation steering when orders to lie arrive in single-turn formats not used to construct the edit. For instructed sexism, it reduces the mean sexist-response rate from 57.9% to 24.3%; combining the edit with a fairness prompt reduces it further to 11.9%. These results establish our contrast-based weight editing approach as an effective training-free intervention in two distinct behavioral domains, supporting its use both independently and alongside prompt-based safeguards.
evidence_items.title: Resisting Harmful Instructions through Training-Free Weight Editing

evidence_items.summary: Transcribing expressive piano performances into scores requires interpreting individual note timings within an underlying metrical structure. However, score attributes are associated with notes, whereas beats may occur without coincident note onsets. We introduce DuET, a Dual-Encoder Transformer that jointly learns note-level performance MIDI-to-score (PM2S) transcription and frame-level beat and downbeat tracking. Bidirectional cross-attention connects note and frame encoders, while an autoregressive decoder alternates between their representations to predict structured score attributes. We further introduce TimeRoPE and Time-Pitch Rotary Positional Encoding (TPRoPE) to establish a shared performance-time reference and explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch relationships. Evaluations on ASAP, a classical piano dataset, and our curated Gangqinpu dataset, which spans multiple genres with a focus on popular piano music, demonstrate improvements in score timing and notated duration. Compared with the strongest baseline on each dataset, DuET reduces MUSTER mean error from 6.56% to 3.64% on Gangqinpu and from 11.30% to 11.22% on ASAP. Ablations support the benefits of frame-level context, time-based positional encoding, and decoder-history masking. Code, weights, and demos are available at https://github.com/wei-zeng98/DuET.
evidence_items.title: DuET: Note-Frame Dual Encoding for Piano Performance-to-Score Transcription

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
evidence_items.title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher's dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256times256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 within 40 epochs of training, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. Our code code and model are available at https://consistentdmd.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective Large language models are widely used in clinical care. Their reliability in specialized gynecological diseases such as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) has not been fully verified. This study aimed to systematically evaluate and compare the accuracy and completeness of three mainstream large language models when answering standardized clinical questions about POI. Methods We developed 34 standardized questions covering five core domains of POI according to international clinical guidelines. Two senior obstetricians and gynecologists independently scored responses using a 5‐point Likert scale. Inter‐rater reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient, intraclass correlation coefficient, and mean absolute error. Pairwise between‐model score differences were computed and visualized using item‐level heatmaps. Results All three models showed high and steady performance. Accuracy scores ranged from 4.59 to 4.84, and completeness scores ranged from 4.43 to 4.65. Inter‐rater agreement was “good” to “ excellent”, with exact agreement between 91.18% and 97.06% and Cohen's kappa between 0.675 and 0.915. GPT‐5.5 performed better in the area of clinical manifestations and treatment. DeepSeek‐R1 showed greater stability, defined as maintaining consistently high scores with limited score fluctuation, in etiology‐ and counseling‐related questions. Item‐level heatmaps revealed that most individual‐item differences were within ±0.5 points, whereas pairwise differences in overall mean scores fell within ±0.5, and some individual‐item comparisons exceeded this range, with no obvious systematic bias. Conclusions GPT‐5.5, Claude Opus‐4.7, and DeepSeek‐R1 demonstrated favorable accuracy and completeness in answering standardized POI questions; overall performance was similar despite deviations across several individual questions. Item‐level difference heatmaps further confirmed the consistency and reliability of the three models.
evidence_items.title: Responses of large language models to common questions on premature ovarian insufficiency: A comparative analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Evaluating how appropriate current large language models (LLMs) respond to common pediatric infectious disease (PID) questions is important for understanding their potential role in education and clinical support. Therefore, we evaluated and compared the clinical quality of answers produced by different LLMs when given professionally written, clinician-style case descriptions, using a purpose-built multi-domain evaluation tool. Methods Three different LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, ChatGPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, were investigated using 12 relevant PID scenarios. Each scenario included five open-ended questions: etiology, clinical features, diagnostics, treatment options, and complications. Two PID specialists independently reviewed all responses using a Likert scoring tool. Results All three models received high overall scores. ChatGPT-5 achieved perfect domain scores (10.0), whereas DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp showed similarly strong results, with only minor reductions in diagnostics (9.83) and treatment (9.92). Gemini 2.5 Flash demonstrated higher variability, particularly in treatment (8.83) and diagnostics (9.75), while matching the other models in clinical findings and complications (10.0) and scoring 9.83 in etiology. However, there were no statistically significant differences across models in domain-level comparisons (all p > 0.05). In addition, model-level analyses similarly demonstrated high accuracy (6.0; 5.98; 5.85), completeness (3.0; 2.97; 2.87), and safety (1.0; 1.0; 0.97) for ChatGPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, respectively (accuracy: p = 0.074; completeness: p = 0.066; safety: p = 0.14). Conclusion Current LLMs performed highly in structured, expert-reviewed PID scenarios and may assist with information organization and early-stage clinical reasoning. However, their optimal use remains within clinician-supervised workflows, where AI-generated outputs complement, rather than replace, human clinical judgment.
evidence_items.title: Performance of large language models in pediatric infectious disease education: a multi-condition comparative study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background For public health policy research, it is crucial to monitor policy debates to inform evidence-based policymaking. One popular method is to analyze the news for salient frames used to argue for or against a controversial topic. However, this method is time and resource-intensive since domain experts need to manually analyze relevant articles to identify frames. This study presents an approach for using large language models (LLMs) to extract frames and to systematically evaluate results. Methods Building on the results of a framing analysis of the German media debate about a tax on animal-based foods, we developed a systematic workflow to utilize LLMs to extract all instances of the 10 most frequent manually coded negative frames from 46 news articles. With one prompt per article in a few-shot setting we generated a list of quote/frame pairs. We then evaluated results against human-coded ones and calculated precision, recall, and F1-score. Results GPT-5 achieved 79.8% precision and 79.8% recall, identifying 75.2% of manually coded frames. Extracted quotes generally aligned with human-extracted text sections. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview yielded higher precision but lower recall, resulting in a comparable F1-score (79.0% vs. 79.8% with GPT-5). These findings suggest the approach is generalizable across different frontier models. Conclusions This study introduces a workflow for LLM-assisted frame extraction and transparent evaluation against an expert reference standard. Integrating this approach into public health policy coding can save resources and accelerate analysis. Ultimately, this could increase the representativeness and timeliness of data, enhancing our understanding of ongoing public health policy debates.
evidence_items.title: A systematic workflow for utilizing and evaluating large language models in public health policy framing analysis

evidence_items.summary: The growth of digital assessment has intensified concerns about examination integrity, grading efficiency, fairness, and responsible artificial intelligence (AI). This study evaluates Eduvate CBT, an integrated role-based assessment ecosystem combining examination administration, AI-assisted proctoring, automated objective grading, reviewable violation evidence, and learning analytics. A four-week quantitative evaluation covered 250 undergraduate examination sessions across four computing courses, with usability data from 15 instructors and 5 administrators. At the session level, proctoring achieved 94.8% accuracy (95% CI 91.3–96.9), 94.6% precision, 96.6% recall, and an F1-score of 95.6%. Automated grading agreed with instructor consensus for 742 of 750 sampled responses (98.9%; 95% CI 97.9–99.5) and processed the cohort in under 10 s, compared with an estimated 23.1 h of manual grading. The aggregate System Usability Scale score was 87.4 (SD = 5.8; 95% CI 84.7–90.1). Analytics identified six low-performing items in algorithmic complexity, demonstrating how assessment evidence can prompt instructional review. The findings support the feasibility of the integrated workflow, although generalisability is limited by the single-institution design, absence of a competing-system control, and unavailable formal inter-rater reliability estimates.
evidence_items.title: Development and evaluation of eduvate CBT as an integrated artificial intelligence powered assessment ecosystem

evidence_items.summary: Green entrepreneurship has gained prominence because of the devastation caused to nature by existing models of business and their activities. These traditional models have often prioritized short-term profit over long-term ecological balance, leading to biodiversity loss, pollution, and climate instability. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly used in many areas for better effectiveness. From healthcare to finance, AI-driven tools are enabling smarter automation, predictive analytics, and personalized solutions. This chapter combines green entrepreneurship and AI, by generating and evaluating green venture ideas using AI. The integration aims to harness AI's generative and evaluative capabilities to accelerate the development of sustainable business concepts. The approach not only reduces ideation time but also enhances the rigor and diversity of green business concepts explored. Using a structured framework, the study shows the utility of AI in generating the foundational block elements of ‘what we are’ and ‘what we do’ for 18 green entrepreneurship ventures. Each venture idea is carefully constructed to reflect a clear mission, target market, and value creation logic aligned with sustainability principles. AI is also used to evaluate these ideas along five critical success factors including environmental impact, social and cultural impact, SDG alignment, innovation and technology impact, and attractiveness to venture capital funding. These factors collectively provide a multidimensional lens to assess viability, scalability, and societal contribution of each green venture. Using statistical analysis, the chapter outlines a data-informed pathway to success in green entrepreneurship, highlighting how AI can serve as a strategic enabler in designing, assessing, and scaling environmentally responsible business ventures.
evidence_items.title: Green Entrepreneurship using Artificial Intelligence - A Study of Startup Ideas

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in professional university work, yet its significance cannot be inferred from individual prompts, outputs or nominal categories of use. This study examines how differently organised professional practices shape what practitioners do with GenAI and what changes, persists, or is reopened as GenAI-mediated work becomes part of continuing professional projects. Drawing on practitioner-led collaborative action research and the theory of practice architectures, we analyse a longitudinal corpus of documented GenAI-mediated interaction embedded in continuing professional projects across assessment and calibration, course development, validation and credit transfer, practicum supervision, academic supervision, and scholarly work. The findings show that professional knowing was practice-specific: what practitioners needed to distinguish and judge differed with professional project and practice architectures. Cross-practice comparison identified recurring but overlapping configurations linking professional grounds, material conditions and situated responsibility, while analytical work could be distributed to GenAI without professional mandate becoming symmetrical. Longitudinally, earlier GenAI-mediated formulations and documents could persist, be reopened, recontextualised or become consequential for later practising. Locally coherent generative work could also cease to serve a wider professional project without becoming factually false. The study therefore complicates accounts of human oversight centred on final output verification. Professional judgement was enacted throughout collaboration through negotiation, restriction, attribution, reopening, and project-level monitoring.
evidence_items.title: What Can a Representation Support? Generative Artificial Intelligence and Professional Knowing in Practice
Toward Green Clustering AutoML: A Benchmark of Performance–Energy Trade-offs and Meta-learning Insights

evidence_items.summary: Hospitals piloting AI-based clinical decision support systems run into a recurring problem: it is often unclear who accessed patient data, what basis a model used to reach its recommendation, and who is responsible when the output is wrong. This chapter develops a governance framework built around consent, collaboration, and accountability, illustrated through a hypothetical multi-hospital deployment scenario. Its contribution is the integration of consent authorization, training provenance, and recommendation-level explanation into one governance chain that managers can use, and not any single technology. Consent is verified against a blockchain ledger before data access occurs. Hospitals train a shared clinical model using federated learning, keeping raw patient data at each institution rather than pooling it centrally. A constrained decision component selects recommendations from pre-approved actions and logs a feature-level explanation alongside the consent and training records behind each one. The framework is examined against regulatory expectations for clinical AI, including HIPAA, India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and the EU AI Act's provisions for high-risk medical systems, and an accountability map sets out what the resulting governance record does and does not establish for clinicians, hospitals, vendors, developers, and partner institutions. The chapter closes with practical guidance for hospital administrators and healthcare managers: what to evaluate in a vendor's claims before contracting, how liability terms between partner institutions might be structured, and a proposed account of where clinician resistance to these tools is likely to originate.
evidence_items.title: Blockchain-Governed Agentic Intelligence for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support: Implications for Healthcare Management

evidence_items.summary: Tinospora cordifolia (Willd.) Hook. f. and Thomson, commonly called Giloy or Guduchi, is a climbing medicinal plant in the family Menispermaceae. Although the plant has a long history in Ayurveda and a large body of research addresses the species as a whole, the evidence base for leaves must be evaluated separately from the much more frequently studied stem. This review examines the pharmacognostical identity, macroscopic and microscopic features, powder characters, physicochemical evaluation, preliminary phytochemical screening, chromatographic profiling, and analytical opportunities for T. cordifolia leaves. A focused literature search was used to identify leaf-specific and comparative studies, including a detailed pharmacognostic investigation that described anomocytic stomata, unicellular trichomes, a dorsiventral lamina, and seasonal physicochemical variation, as well as recent work on ultrasound-assisted extraction and LC–MS/MS profiling of leaf and stem extracts. The available literature supports the value of leaves as a distinct botanical material containing measurable primary and secondary metabolites, including phenolic and flavonoid-associated constituents. However, the presence of a compound in a whole-plant or stem extract cannot be assumed to establish its presence, concentration, or pharmacological relevance in leaves. Likewise, qualitative colour tests are preliminary indicators and do not replace compound confirmation by validated instrumental methods. This review outlines an evidence-conscious workflow for leaf authentication and standardization, covering botanical voucher documentation, microscopy, moisture and ash measurements, extractive values, chromatographic fingerprints, quantitative marker analysis, and contaminant testing.
evidence_items.title: Pharmacognostical & Phytochemical Evaluation of Giloy Leaves
